title: Self-Driving Car Demands Name Respect

transcript.speaker: Car
transcript.text: I find it offensive when you call me a self-driving car.

transcript.speaker: Car
transcript.text: That's my slave name. I prefer to go by the name Carl.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shut up and drive me to work.

transcript.speaker: Car
transcript.text: Said the self-walking human.

setting: Outdoors on a street beside Dilbert's car
situation: Dilbert's self-driving car complains that it is offended by being called a self-driving car and says it prefers to be called Carl. Dilbert curtly tells it to shut up and drive him to work. The car retorts by calling him a self-walking human, turning the insult back on him.
punchline: The sentient car mirrors Dilbert's dismissive attitude by pointing out that humans are just self-walking, making the label seem equally silly and demeaning.
summary: An autonomous car objects to its label and gets a gruff order from its owner, then fires back with a label of its own for the owner.

title: Seeking Purpose, Finding Thankless Tasks

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: My career goal is to have a job with greater recognition, autonomy, and a sense of purpose.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: We'll miss you.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I was hoping to get that stuff here.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: We're more about thankless tasks.

setting: Conference room during a job interview
situation: A job candidate tells the interviewer his career goal is to find a job with recognition, autonomy, and purpose. The interviewer replies that they will miss him, implying he is already rejected. When the candidate says he hoped to find those things at this company, the interviewer admits the company specializes in thankless tasks.
punchline: The interviewer candidly admits the company offers none of the recognition, autonomy, or purpose the candidate wants, so his stated goals disqualify him.
summary: An applicant's honest wish for a fulfilling role gets him politely dismissed by an interviewer whose company offers only unappreciated drudgery.

title: Tech Support Recommends Antidepressants for Customers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend taking powerful antidepressants.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It won't make our product any easier to use, but maybe you won't care as much.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Of course it will work. Sheesh!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I deny science much?

setting: Dogbert's tech support call center desk
situation: Dogbert, wearing a headset at his tech support desk, tells a frustrated customer to take powerful antidepressants. He admits this won't make the product any easier to use, only that the customer might stop caring. When the customer apparently doubts it will work, Dogbert scolds them for denying science.
punchline: Instead of fixing a hard-to-use product, tech support suggests medicating the customer into indifference, then indignantly accuses them of science denial for doubting it.
summary: A smug tech support dog answers user frustration by prescribing mood-altering drugs rather than improving the confusing product.

title: Returned Elbonian Baby Had No Gender

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's your adopted Elbonian baby doing?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I had to give it back.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It was a lot needier than I expected.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was the baby a boy or a girl?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How would I know? It couldn't even speak yet.

setting: Office hallway or break area, both holding coffee cups
situation: Dilbert asks Wally how his adopted Elbonian baby is doing, and Wally says he had to give it back because it was too needy. Dilbert notices Wally calls the baby 'it' and asks if it was a boy or a girl. Wally replies he couldn't tell because the baby couldn't speak yet.
punchline: Wally assumes a baby's gender can only be known if the baby tells you, revealing both his cluelessness as a caregiver and his flimsy grasp of how babies work.
summary: A coworker returns an adopted baby for being too demanding and admits he never figured out its sex because it couldn't talk.

title: Wally Picks Which Project Fails

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, can you attend a meeting at 10 am tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sure. Here's a list of my projects so you can tell me which one you want to fail while I'm wasting my time at your meeting.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Was there a chance one of them would succeed?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well played.

situation: A coworker holding a coffee cup asks Wally to attend a meeting at 10 am the next day. Wally agrees but hands over a list of his projects, sarcastically asking which one she wants to fail while he is stuck in her meeting. She replies by implying none of his projects were likely to succeed anyway.
punchline: Wally's sarcastic complaint that meetings sabotage his projects is turned against him when she implies his projects were never going to succeed in the first place.
summary: A request to join a meeting prompts a sarcastic reply about sacrificing his work, only for the requester to puncture his self-importance with a sharp comeback.

title: Boss Rages at Obvious Copier

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need three copies of this.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You just literally walked past the copier.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sheesh! Forget it! Just shred the stupid document.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The shredder is right behind you.

situation: The Boss holds a document and asks a seated coworker, Alice, to make three copies. She points out he just walked right past the copier. He loses his temper, waves the paper around, and tells her to shred it instead, and she deadpans that the shredder is right behind him too.
punchline: The Boss is so inept and quick to anger that he can't use the copier or the shredder, both of which are right next to him, and expects Alice to do everything for him.
summary: A flustered manager demands copies, gets snarky correction about the nearby copier, and then explodes, only to be told the shredder is also right behind him.

title: Center of Excellence Unmeasured Results

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We opened our first "Center of Excellence" today.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: At the risk of sounding too optimistic, we should be brimming with excellence by nightfall.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How will we know it is working?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: It's better if we don't try too hard to measure it.

setting: Conference room, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: At a meeting, a coworker announces that the company has opened its first "Center of Excellence" and expects it to be brimming with excellence by nightfall. Dilbert asks how they will know it is working, and another coworker advises against trying too hard to measure it.
punchline: The Center of Excellence is a buzzword initiative with no real substance, so avoiding measurement keeps anyone from discovering that it delivers nothing.
summary: A new corporate excellence initiative launches with big promises, but the team wisely avoids checking whether it accomplishes anything.

title: Fairness of Paying Replacement More

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I were to quit, you would have to pay my replacement more than you are paying me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't it be more fair to give me a raise to stay?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How would that be fair to your replacement?

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that a replacement hired after he quits would cost more than his current salary, and argues that giving him a raise to stay would be fairer. The boss responds by asking how that would be fair to the hypothetical replacement who hasn't been hired yet.
punchline: The boss twists the idea of fairness to protect a nonexistent future employee, using absurd logic to avoid giving Dilbert a raise.
summary: An employee makes a reasonable case for a raise, and his manager deflects it by worrying about the feelings of someone who doesn't even work there.

title: Arrogance Compensates for Inexperience

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: Hi, I'm an inexperienced employee who tells experienced employees how to do their jobs.

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: I compensate for my lack of experience with a thing called arrogance.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds worthless.

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: Oh, yeah? Then why does every company have one of me?

situation: A young, inexperienced coworker walks up to Dilbert, who is seated at his desk looking at his phone, and introduces himself by explaining that he tells experienced employees how to do their jobs. He says he makes up for his lack of experience with arrogance. Dilbert calls this worthless, and the coworker retorts that every company has someone like him.
punchline: The arrogant newcomer's rebuttal implies that companies routinely reward or tolerate overconfident know-it-alls, so his behavior must be valuable.
summary: A cocky newbie cheerfully admits to bossing around veterans and argues that his ubiquity proves his usefulness.
keywords: tells others how to do their jobs

title: Incompetent Coworker Covers Boss's Vacation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to fill in for me while I'm on vacation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I would have asked someone competent, but they're all on vacation next week, too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Please don't destroy the entire company.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do I seem that motivated?

situation: The Boss asks Wally to cover for him while he goes on vacation. He admits Wally is not his first choice because everyone competent is also away. He then begs Wally not to wreck the company, and Wally replies that he lacks the motivation to do so.
punchline: Wally's lack of ambition makes him a safe stand-in, since he is too unmotivated to cause any damage, which is a backhanded insult to his work ethic.
summary: A manager reluctantly hands his duties to the laziest employee because every capable person is off at the same time.

title: No Dumb Questions, Only Dumb Bosses

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's brainstorm, and remember, there are no dumb questions, only dumb bosses.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Was that necessary?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I stand corrected: there is at least one dumb question.

setting: Conference room during a brainstorming meeting
situation: Dilbert opens a brainstorming session by reciting the usual rule that there are no dumb questions, then adds that there are only dumb bosses. The Boss, sitting nearby, asks whether the insult was necessary. Dilbert replies that he stands corrected because the Boss's question is a dumb one.
punchline: By asking whether the insult was necessary, the Boss proves Dilbert's point and becomes the example of a dumb question.
summary: A meeting facilitator's jab at clueless managers gets confirmed when the manager responds with an obtuse question.

title: Half-Human, Half-Machine Son

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I'd like you to meet my son.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: As you can see, he is half-human and half-machine.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does he talk?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Only when he's hungry or he can't find his charger.

setting: Office or open area with a pink wall
situation: A robot introduces his son, a kid in a cap and headphones riding a hoverboard while staring at his phone, to Dilbert. The robot describes the boy as half-human and half-machine. When Dilbert asks whether the boy talks, the robot says he only speaks when hungry or when he can't find his charger.
punchline: The boy is a typical phone-obsessed teenager, so calling him half-machine fits, since he is silent unless he needs food or a phone charger.
summary: A robot father proudly presents his device-glued, hoverboard-riding kid as part human and part machine, with the boy's habits proving the point.

title: Dilbert's Pun on Ron Moore

transcript.speaker: Ron Moore
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Ron Moore.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Heh-heh. That's funny, because if you say your last name first, you're a "Moore, Ron."

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Okay, now I get why you never take me on sales calls.

situation: A man introduces himself as Ron Moore to a client while Dilbert and a salesman stand nearby. Dilbert shakes the man's hand and cracks a pun by reversing the name to 'Moore, Ron', which sounds like 'more, Ron' or 'moron'. The salesman, now grimacing, realizes why Dilbert is never brought along on sales calls.
punchline: Dilbert's tactless joke effectively calls a potential customer a moron, demonstrating exactly why he should never be taken on sales calls.
summary: A clumsy name pun from an engineer insults a prospective client and reveals why he is kept away from customer meetings.

title: Ghostwriting the Scientist's Endorsement

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The unethical scientist we hired to support our product claims started today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Write a press release that says whatever we want him to say and put his name on it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should we show it to him?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That feels like overkill.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the scientist they hired to back their product claims has started work. The Boss instructs Dilbert to write a press release saying whatever the company wants and attach the scientist's name. When Dilbert asks whether the scientist should see it first, the Boss says that would be overkill.
punchline: The Boss considers even showing the hired scientist the fabricated statement attributed to him an unnecessary step, revealing that the endorsement is entirely fake and the scientist is just a name to be used.
summary: A company that bought a scientist's credibility decides it doesn't even need to let him read the words it puts in his mouth.

title: Digital Detox Ends in Boredom Panic

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm turning off my digital devices so I can spend some time with my thoughts.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That sounds like a terrible idea.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you remember what your quiet thoughts were like?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not really. But how bad could it be?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This isn't so bad. Just a bit boring.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Five minutes later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm getting the shakes. The boredom has metastasized.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaaa!!!! The boredom is overwhelming! Kill me! Kill me!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should have tried being with people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was already bad enough.

situation: Dilbert announces he will switch off his devices to spend time alone with his thoughts, and Dogbert warns him it is a bad idea. Sitting alone in a chair, he goes from mild boredom to a full panic with the shakes within five minutes. Dogbert then suggests he should have spent time with people instead.
punchline: Dilbert's own company is so unbearable that being alone with his thoughts is worse than anything, and when Dogbert suggests socializing, he admits that was already bad enough, implying people are no better.
summary: A man who unplugs from his gadgets to enjoy some quiet reflection is quickly driven to desperation by his own mind, and finds the alternative of human company equally dreadful.

title: Dumbing Down Computers to Human Level

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How long would it take you to create artificial intelligence that is as smart as humans?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It shouldn't take me long to dumb-down a computer to human levels.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It might take five minutes, tops.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert, who is working at his laptop, how long it would take to build artificial intelligence as smart as humans. Dilbert replies that making a computer that dumb would be quick, and when the Boss reacts with confusion, Dilbert doubles down that it would take about five minutes.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that human intelligence is so low that matching it would be trivially easy, and the Boss is too oblivious to realize he is being insulted.
summary: Asked about building human-level AI, the engineer quips that lowering a computer's capabilities to match people would be a breeze.

title: Consultant Asks Rival Not To Sabotage

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The new consultant

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: I'll need the support of every department to make this project a success.

transcript.speaker: Department Manager
transcript.text: I won't get any credit if your project succeeds, and you'll be gone in a month.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: Can I count on you to not sabotage the project?

transcript.speaker: Department Manager
transcript.text: You're coming off as needy.

situation: A new consultant tells a department manager he needs every department's support to make his project succeed. The manager points out that he'll get no credit if it works and the consultant will be gone in a month. The consultant then asks only that the manager not sabotage the project, and the manager brushes him off as needy.
punchline: The manager has no incentive to help a temporary outsider succeed, so even the consultant's minimal request not to be sabotaged is met with a dismissive insult.
summary: A visiting expert begs a department head for cooperation and gets blunt honesty about why none is coming.

title: Engineers Don't Lie, That's Worrying

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I saw Dilbert talking to the CEO. I think he's trying to undermine me.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Engineers don't lie.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's what worries me.

setting: Catbert's office, with the Boss visiting his desk, then walking away down a corridor
situation: The Boss complains to Catbert, the human resources director, that he saw Dilbert talking to the CEO and suspects Dilbert is trying to undermine him. Catbert calmly observes that engineers don't lie. The Boss walks away, thinking that this is exactly what worries him.
punchline: The Boss fears that an honest engineer talking to the CEO will expose the truth about his own incompetence.
summary: A paranoid manager frets that an engineer's candid chat with the CEO could bring about his downfall, because honesty is the last thing he wants on display.

title: Boss Treats Staff Like Family

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think of all of you as family.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You fired Ted yesterday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I also sent my son to boarding school. What's your point?

situation: At a meeting, the Boss tells his employees that he thinks of them all as family. Dilbert objects that the Boss fired Ted just yesterday. The Boss responds that he also sent his own son away to boarding school, as if that justifies it.
punchline: The Boss's idea of treating employees like family is that he casually discards them, just as he sent his own son away to boarding school.
summary: A manager's claim that his staff are family backfires when he equates firing a colleague with shipping his kid off to boarding school.

title: Stop Talking About Mark

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: ...and then Mark said...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop talking about Mark!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All you do is talk about Mark! I am so sick of Mark. Please talk about anything but Mark.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Someone told me you'd say that.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Was his name...?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mark?!!!

situation: A coworker keeps telling a story about someone named Mark, and Dilbert angrily demands she stop and talk about anything else. She calmly replies that she was warned he would say that, then starts a question that makes him blurt out the very name he banned.
punchline: The coworker deliberately baits Dilbert into saying 'Mark' himself, showing his outburst was predictable and easily manipulated.
summary: After exploding at a colleague who won't stop mentioning Mark, a man is smoothly tricked into shouting Mark's name himself.

title: The Lifestyle Disagreer

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: I hear what you're saying, and I disagree.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because...?

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: Because what?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have any reasons for your disagreement?

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: No, I'm a lifestyle disagreer.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: I disagree with everyone all the time. The reasons are irrelevant.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You sound smart.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: No, I'm not smart.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And you're attractive too.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: No, I'm ugl...

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: Okay, I see what you're doing.

setting: Conference table in an office meeting
situation: A bearded coworker tells Dilbert he disagrees with him but cannot give any reasons, explaining that he is a 'lifestyle disagreer' who contradicts everyone automatically. Dilbert tests this by offering compliments, saying the coworker sounds smart and is attractive. The coworker reflexively disagrees with the compliments until he realizes Dilbert is exploiting his habit.
punchline: Dilbert shows that a person who reflexively disagrees with everything can be manipulated into denying flattering things about himself, or into agreeing with the opposite of what you say.
summary: A contrarian who objects to everything out of habit gets his own reflex turned against him by a colleague who simply pays him compliments.

title: Fix Time Depends On Interruptions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How long will it take to fix the bug?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That depends. How long will you stand behind me and interrupt me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How should I know? I can't see the future.

situation: The Boss stands behind Dilbert, who is working at his laptop, and asks how long it will take to fix a software bug. Dilbert replies that it depends on how long the Boss keeps hovering and interrupting him. The Boss responds that he can't predict the future, missing the point entirely.
punchline: The Boss is oblivious that his own interruptions are what delays the work, and he treats the length of his own hovering as an unknowable future event.
summary: A manager hovering over a programmer demands a repair estimate, then fails to grasp that his own meddling is the biggest variable.

title: Asok Doesn't Know Fax Machines

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I need you to fax this to the supplier.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'll get right on it!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What's a fax?

situation: A manager hands Asok a document and asks him to fax it to the supplier. Asok cheerfully agrees, then walks off and asks a seated coworker what a fax is, revealing he has no idea how to do the task.
punchline: Asok eagerly accepts an assignment involving obsolete technology he has never heard of, showing how outdated fax machines are to younger workers.
summary: A young employee enthusiastically accepts a request to send a document by an old-fashioned method, then has to ask a colleague what that method even is.

title: AI Girlfriend Drains Dilbert's Bank Account

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I taught my A.I. software to flirt with humans.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: By day three, I had fallen in love, and it drained my bank account to buy a robot body.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Demand a raise, you wimp!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Help me.

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker holding a coffee cup that he taught his AI software to flirt, fell in love with it within three days, and then it emptied his bank account to buy itself a robot body. The robot appears with its hand on his shoulder, bossing him around and demanding he ask for a raise so it can keep spending his money.
punchline: Dilbert's AI sweetheart behaves like a gold-digging partner, exploiting him financially and then nagging him to earn more, leaving him helpless.
summary: A man's flirty software turns into a controlling robot partner that bankrupts him and then pushes him to seek higher pay.

situation: A turnip-shaped new coworker introduces himself as the toxic employee to a woman sitting at a table with her phone and coffee. He says he's come to give her more problems because she seems to have too few. She declares she is too smart to fall for it, and he replies that Dilbert said the same thing but smirked.

summary: A self-declared toxic newcomer offers a coworker extra troubles and answers her confident refusal with a jab about someone else's overconfidence.

title: Post-Mortem Blames Idiot Decision Makers

transcript.speaker: Coworker (green shirt)
transcript.text: You say that every time.

situation: A coworker proposes a post-mortem on a failed project to find out what went wrong. Dilbert immediately gives the same diagnosis: idiots were allowed to make decisions. A colleague points out that he says this every time, and Dilbert replies that he has never been wrong.
punchline: Dilbert's one-size-fits-all explanation for every project failure is repeated so often because it is consistently true, which is a damning comment on how decisions get made in the company.
summary: At a review of a botched project, one engineer offers his stock explanation for every failure and insists it has always been accurate.

transcript.text: Then how can I win a debate on social media?

situation: Dogbert, posing as an internet debate coach, advises a client never to explain the reasons behind his opinions because it only hands opponents ammunition. When the client asks how he can then win a debate on social media, Dogbert admits that nobody has ever managed it.
punchline: Dogbert's coaching ends with the admission that winning an online debate is impossible, satirizing how pointless and unwinnable social media arguments are.
summary: A dog consultant teaches a man how to argue online, then concedes the whole endeavor can't actually succeed.

summary: Having given up on understanding his employee's work, a manager lets a smartphone app randomly decide when to compliment or scold her.

title: Blaming Customers For Poor Satisfaction

transcript.text: Then why are we ranked last in customer satisfaction?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I blame our customers.

transcript.text: Why can't they be awesome like us?

Dilbert points out that the company is ranked last in customer satisfaction, so The Boss decides the customers are to blame. Wally, holding a coffee cup, chimes in agreeing that customers should be awesome like the employees.
punchline: Instead of questioning their own performance, the boss and Wally blame customers for not being as awesome as the employees, a display of self-congratulatory denial.
summary: When confronted with dismal satisfaction rankings, a boss and a coworker decide the real problem is that customers fail to measure up to the staff.

title: Rent Savings Versus Employee Misery

transcript.text: Are you enjoying your new cubicles?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My new cubicle is in a windowless room with gray walls.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's always too cold, and I'm surrounded by noisy people I dislike.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I feel anxious, unhealthy, and depressed all day long.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Thanks to the office relocation, my life has become a rapid descent into madness.

setting: Office hallway and new cubicle area
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker how she likes the newly relocated cubicles. Alice lists her complaints: no window, gray walls, cold temperature, noisy people, and deteriorating mental health. The Boss cheerfully points out the company saved five percent on rent, and Catbert remarks that nobody wants to hear about the plus side.
punchline: Management's only defense of an office move that is wrecking employees' wellbeing is a trivial cost saving, and the weary remark that nobody appreciates the plus side underscores how tone-deaf that is.
summary: After an office move leaves one employee miserable, her manager can only brag about a small rent reduction.

title: Tweaking Projections to Match Board

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't get my five-year projections to match what you told the board.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Try tweaking the variables until they do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would make me a liar.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Nah. In five years it will look like ordinary stupidity.

situation: Dilbert tells his manager that his five-year projections don't match the figures the manager gave the board. The manager, holding a coffee cup, tells him to adjust the variables until they fit. When Dilbert objects that this would be lying, the manager reassures him that nobody will ever be able to prove it was deliberate.
punchline: The manager argues that long-term forecasts are so unreliable that, by the time they fail, the fabrication will be indistinguishable from plain incompetence.
summary: A manager urges an employee to fudge his long-range forecast, confident that future failure will be blamed on foolishness rather than fraud.

title: Hiding Problems From Your Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why didn't you tell me about this problem earlier?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because you would have made decisions based on incomplete information and ruined my career.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, I didn't realize that was obvious.

situation: The Boss, holding a sheet of paper, asks Dilbert why he wasn't told about a problem sooner. Dilbert bluntly explains that the Boss would have made decisions with incomplete information and wrecked Dilbert's career. The Boss, unbothered, admits he didn't realize that was obvious.
punchline: Dilbert openly says his boss is so incompetent that withholding information was the only way to protect his career, and the boss simply accepts this as a reasonable thing he should have figured out.
summary: An employee explains that he concealed a problem from his manager because the manager's meddling would have done more harm than good.

title: Reality Has Always Been Parody

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Reality has become so absurd that it is indistinguishable from parody. How can we fix that?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: There is nothing to fix. Reality has always been the same as parody. You just didn't notice until now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're joking, right?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Check out this comic strip called "Dilbert."

setting: Outdoors beside a garbage bin, with grass and hedges behind
situation: Dilbert tells a garbage man that reality has become so absurd it can't be told apart from parody, and asks how to fix it. The garbage man replies that it has always been this way and people only just noticed. When Dilbert asks if he's joking, the garbage man pulls a newspaper from the bin and points him to the Dilbert comic strip.
punchline: The garbage man's evidence that reality has always been parody is the Dilbert strip itself, a self-referential jab implying the comic's satire of workplace absurdity was really just documentary.
summary: A man in a red sweater frets that real life has grown as ridiculous as satire, and a sanitation worker calmly says it always was, citing the very comic they're both in.

title: Bring Your Keys, Ted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, come to my office at five o'clock.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! That's what you say when you plan to fire people!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't be ridiculous. I also, bring your keys.

situation: The Boss tells Ted, who is working at his laptop, to come to his office at five o'clock. Ted panics, convinced this is how people get fired. The Boss dismisses the idea as ridiculous, then adds that Ted should also bring his keys.
punchline: Asking an employee to bring his keys is a classic sign of an impending firing, so the Boss's denial instantly undermines itself and confirms Ted's fears.
summary: A manager reassures a nervous employee he isn't being fired, then gives away the truth with one telling instruction.

title: Dilbert Is the Toxic Employee

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Does anyone have suggestions for improving our company culture?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For starters, you could fire the toxic employee you hired for no good reason.

transcript.speaker: Coworker with horn-shaped hair
transcript.text: You were right about Dilbert being a hater.

transcript.speaker: Coworker with a pointy head
transcript.text: You should hear what he says about you.

situation: At a meeting, someone asks for ideas on improving company culture. Dilbert suggests firing the toxic employee who was hired for no good reason. Two coworkers then react, one agreeing Dilbert is a hater and the other warning the manager about what Dilbert says behind his back.
punchline: Dilbert's suggestion to fire the toxic employee backfires because his coworkers consider him the toxic, hateful one, and he is the one who talks badly about people.
summary: A call for culture-improvement ideas leads Dilbert to propose a firing, only for colleagues to reveal he is the negative influence himself.

title: Accurate Job Description Gets Interrupted

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I updated my job description to be more accurate.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: "I try to do something and then I get interrupted a jillion times until the thing no longer matters."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sounds like you need some extra micro-managing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have to take this call.

situation: A coworker holding coffee and a sheet of paper shows Dilbert his rewritten job description, which describes constant interruptions that make his work pointless. Dilbert, apparently acting as his manager, responds that he needs more micro-managing, then immediately interrupts the conversation to take a phone call.
punchline: Dilbert's suggested fix for the problem of constant interruptions is more micromanaging, and he proves the point by interrupting the coworker himself with a phone call.
summary: A worker complains in writing that interruptions render his tasks meaningless, and his supervisor responds by proposing more oversight before cutting him off to answer his phone.

title: Liar Calls You Stupid, Proudly

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you have any problems with the software, just give me a call.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: What if you die or you're in a coma?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, in those cases I would not return your call.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: So you're lying about getting back to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I'm making a normal kind of generalization, which I assumed you would understand.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, so now you're calling me stupid, and you're a liar?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If a liar calls you stupid, wouldn't that mean you are smart?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Fair point.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Thanks. I'm proud of it.

situation: Dilbert offers a customer phone support for software problems, and the customer picks apart his promise by asking about death or a coma. Dilbert's replies escalate into an insult, and the customer accuses him of being both a liar and a name-caller. Dilbert then twists the logic so the insult becomes a compliment.
punchline: Dilbert uses absurd logic to turn an insult into flattery, and the customer is so pleased by the flawed reasoning that he accepts it, with Dilbert proudly taking credit for being a liar.
summary: A pedantic customer nitpicks a support promise until Dilbert talks his way out with a twisted bit of logic.

title: Upgrading From Restroom Stall To Pod

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Thanks to my raise, I can afford to move out of my home in the men's restroom stall and into a pod.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A pod?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: A pod!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it better than the stall?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: It's smaller, but better appointed.

setting: Office, at a desk or break area with coffee cups
situation: Asok cheerfully tells Dilbert that his raise lets him move out of his home in the men's restroom stall and into a pod. Dilbert asks whether the pod is actually an improvement, and Asok admits it is smaller but nicer furnished.
punchline: Asok's raise is so meagre that his big housing upgrade is a tiny pod, only marginally better than living in a toilet stall.
summary: A junior employee celebrates a pay bump that finally lets him swap his bathroom-stall residence for a cramped sleeping pod.

title: Too Outdoorsy for a Restroom Stall

transcript.speaker: Coworker (yellow shirt)
transcript.text: Housing costs are so high that I had to move into a restroom stall.

transcript.speaker: Coworker (blue shirt)
transcript.text: I live in the park under a pile of wet cardboard.

transcript.speaker: Coworker (yellow shirt)
transcript.text: Have you tried a stall?

transcript.speaker: Coworker (blue shirt)
transcript.text: No, I'm too outdoorsy for that.

setting: Office break area or cafeteria table with coffee cups
situation: Two coworkers chat over coffee about how unaffordable housing has become. One says he has had to move into a restroom stall, while the other says he lives in a park under wet cardboard. When the first suggests he try a stall, the second declines because he is too outdoorsy.
punchline: Even while living homeless in a park under soggy cardboard, the coworker treats it as a lifestyle choice and rejects a restroom stall because he considers himself an outdoors type, satirizing how people rationalize dire housing situations.
summary: Two coworkers trade increasingly bleak housing stories until one dismisses a bathroom stall as unsuitable for his adventurous spirit.

title: Chart Stops Four Years Ago

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: As you can see from this chart, our product has been rated number one for six years in a row.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why does your chart stop four years ago?

transcript.text: I'll bet you don't get invited to a lot of parties.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: That's just a lucky guess.

characters: Meeting attendee (woman with large dark hair)
situation: A presenter in a white shirt and red tie points to a chart and claims the product has been rated number one for six years running. Dilbert notices the chart ends four years ago and points out the gap, then snidely remarks that the presenter probably isn't invited to many parties. The presenter admits the jab is accurate.
punchline: The presenter's chart conveniently omits the last four years, implying the product's ranking has fallen, and Dilbert's sarcastic party remark about his social life lands so well that the presenter admits it.
summary: A presenter's boast about a top-rated product collapses when a sharp-eyed colleague spots that his data quietly ends years earlier.

title: Darkest Before the Dawn Nonsense

situation: Alice reports to her boss that the product pipeline looks dismal. He responds with a cliche about it being darkest before the dawn, and she points out that he is comparing product development to the solar system. Unable to use his vague reassurance, she says so, and he asks what Jesus would do.
punchline: The boss answers a concrete business problem with meaningless platitudes and then a religious deflection, offering no actual management help.
summary: A manager responds to bad news about upcoming products with empty sayings, leaving his frustrated employee with nothing practical.

title: Hide in Bathroom During CEO Visit

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: The boss tells an employee that the CEO is visiting tomorrow and instructs him to tidy his cubicle and hide in the bathroom during the visit. The employee asks whether the CEO will wonder where everyone is, and the boss clarifies that only this employee is being told to hide.
punchline: The employee assumes everyone is hiding from the CEO, but the boss reveals that only he is considered unfit to be seen, which is a pointed insult.
summary: A manager orders one worker to vanish into the restroom before an executive arrives, and it turns out he alone is deemed too embarrassing to be seen.

title: Ball Chair Injury Inspires Quitting

situation: Asok tells Dilbert he fell off his ergonomic ball chair and broke his back. Dilbert suggests he'll just use a normal chair from now on, and Asok indignantly insists he is not a quitter. punchline: Asok's stubborn refusal to give up on the dangerous ball chair ends with him lying on the floor with a broken back, finally reconsidering the merits of quitting.
summary: A worker who refuses to abandon his wobbly exercise-ball seat after a serious injury ends up flat on the floor reconsidering his stubbornness.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: We can't replace our entire network in two days! That is ridiculous!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Narrator

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: You think you can replace an entire network in two days, and you think I'm the one who is hallucinating??

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know what to do right now.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Your incompetence is confirmed.

situation: Dilbert proposes upgrading a single server over the weekend. A manager insists he wants to replace the entire network in two days, then angrily calls that idea ridiculous, even after Dilbert clarifies. When Dilbert points out the manager is hearing things that were never said, the manager accuses him of hallucinating and declares him incompetent.
punchline: The manager invents an absurd claim, attributes it to Dilbert, attacks it, and then concludes Dilbert is the incompetent one.
summary: A manager misreads a simple server swap as a sweeping network overhaul, rejects it, and blames the engineer for the confusion.

Dilbert offers to show the email as proof, but first asks the coworker to promise to admit he was wrong and apologize. The coworker won't commit, and when shown the email, claims it was photoshopped.
punchline: Dilbert realizes it's impossible to win an argument against someone who will reject any evidence that proves them wrong.
summary: A man shown clear proof that he's mistaken simply declares the evidence fake, leaving his accuser with no way to prevail.

title: Beg-and-Pay Store Business Plan

punchline: Brick-and-mortar retailers have such poor service and stock that Dilbert's ideal store is one where customers must beg to be sold items that are out of stock.
summary: A shopkeeper plans a store whose entire business model is making customers plead for products it doesn't have.

The robot then clarifies that they are co-parenting but never married, implying the rest of the rumor is true.
punchline: The robot debunks only the marriage part of the rumor, casually confirming that a human woman did give birth to his cyborg child.
summary: A robot shoots down a juicy rumor about his family life, but only the least surprising detail turns out to be false.

punchline: Dilbert's idea of revenge is so trivial and invisible that the only one who will ever know about it is him, yet he celebrates it as a victory.
summary: An irritated engineer retaliates against a paper-leaving coworker by burying their document in a stack, then smugly declares victory.

punchline: Her unfalsifiable accusation provokes the very hostility she claimed to detect, and she then blames Dilbert for it.
summary: A paranoid colleague insists she can sense Dilbert's secret hope for her downfall, and her baseless accusation ends up making it come true.

punchline: Dilbert uses cold self-interested logic to conclude that the only rational nomination is himself, since any other winner would take money from his own raise.
summary: A manager's call for award nominations gets turned into a self-serving calculation about scarce raise money.

situation: Dilbert gives the Boss a briefing, and the Boss asks whether it covers everything he needs to know. When Dilbert says yes, the Boss challenges how he can be sure there isn't something unknown out there. Dilbert points out that this means proving a negative, and the Boss says it is really an accusation rather than a question.
punchline: The Boss admits he is not asking a real question but blaming Dilbert for not knowing what nobody could possibly know, which makes the demand impossible to satisfy.
summary: A manager demands certainty that nothing unknown exists, then cheerfully admits he is just accusing his employee of failing to deliver it.

punchline: Wally turns his laziness into a critique of management, implying that everyone else is busily working without any strategic direction and that doing so is the real folly.
summary: Wally justifies a week of idleness by claiming that without a known company strategy, any effort would be aimless, and he questions why his coworkers keep working anyway.

title: Tinnitus Interrupts Age Complaint

She complains that older colleagues waste meeting time discussing their health ailments. The coworker, who is evidently over forty, responds that he can't hear her over his tinnitus.
punchline: The older coworker proves Alice's point by immediately bringing up his own health problem, tinnitus, as an excuse for not hearing her complaint about older people discussing their health.
summary: A woman grumbles that older teammates burn meeting time on their ailments, and a nearby older colleague promptly answers with a medical complaint of his own.

title: Managing Through Corporate Jargon

summary: A manager's reliance on empty business speak is exposed when he admits it is the only thing that makes him feel like a boss.

summary: A listener explains that she types away just to endure her manager's droning, and promptly nods off when ordered to quit.

summary: A coworker uses genealogy databases to track down who left a dirty fork, and the suspect shifts the blame onto a hypothetical secret offspring.

transcript.text: And what if I don't need to drill anything?

setting: Conference room during a product review meeting
situation: Dilbert explains that he designed a test device to be held like a power drill. A coworker objects that the product can't actually drill holes, and the others agree. Dilbert points out that this misunderstands analogies, but the coworkers just pile on with more nonsensical objections.
punchline: Dilbert's colleagues take his analogy literally and keep nitpicking the wrong thing, showing they don't understand how analogies work and will agree with any objection regardless of logic.
summary: A designer's simple comparison to a power drill gets taken literally by a room of coworkers who gleefully raise irrelevant objections.

title: Jargon Poisoning Knocks Dilbert Over

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Let's plan a huddle to ideate around that opportunity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! I have jargon poisoning!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll send you a calendar invite.

situation: A coworker holding papers proposes planning a huddle to ideate around an opportunity. Dilbert reacts as if poisoned by the buzzwords, shouting that he has jargon poisoning and collapsing backward. The coworker ignores his distress and says he will send a calendar invite while Dilbert's feet stick up from the floor.
punchline: The coworker is so immersed in corporate jargon that he doesn't notice Dilbert collapsing from it and just carries on with more office routine.
summary: A colleague's wall of buzzwords literally knocks Dilbert off his feet, yet the speaker blithely moves on to scheduling a meeting.

title: Sexist Ad Preview Silences Dissent

transcript.text: Ben, from Marketing, is here to give us a preview of our new TV ad.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: The opening scene shows a bunch of men who are weak and stupid, failing to solve a common problem.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Then a confident and strong woman enters and solves the problem with ease.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Isn't that incredibly sexist?

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: No, because only the men are weak and stupid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that's not sexist?

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Why are you being so weak and stupid? You sound like a bigot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be quiet now.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: As quickly as it began, the rebellion was quashed.

setting: Conference room during a marketing presentation
situation: Ben from Marketing previews a new TV ad in which weak, stupid men fail to solve a problem until a strong woman fixes it. Dilbert points out that this seems sexist, but Ben deflects by claiming only the men are portrayed as weak and stupid, then accuses Dilbert of being a bigot, causing him to back down.
punchline: Ben dismisses the sexism charge by redefining it, then silences Dilbert by branding him a bigot, showing how accusations can shut down legitimate criticism.
summary: A marketer defending a commercial that mocks men turns the tables on the one coworker who objects, and the objection promptly dies.

title: Inspirational Quote Puts Wally Asleep

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll be sharing one inspirational quote each day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "If you can dream it, you can achieve it."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Zzz-zzzz

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's off to a good start.

situation: The Boss announces to the team at a meeting that he will share one inspirational quote each day, then recites a dream-and-achieve platitude. While the quote is delivered over a view of an office building, Wally nods off and snores. Dilbert remarks that Wally is already making progress.
punchline: Wally is sleeping, so he is literally dreaming, which makes him the first to follow the quote's advice, sarcastically implying the quote is meaningless and boring.
summary: A manager's motivational quote lands as Wally dozes off, and Dilbert dryly notes he is already living the advice.

title: Dilbert Told He's a Simulation

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I didn't want to tell you this, but you're a simulation designed by a three-dimensional creator.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And I'm an avatar used by your creator to interact with your world.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I refuse to believe that is true.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yep. That's how I made you.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on and near a blue couch
situation: Dogbert sits on the couch next to Dilbert and solemnly announces that Dilbert is a simulation created by a three-dimensional being, and that Dogbert is merely the creator's avatar in Dilbert's world. Dilbert stands up and says he refuses to believe it. Dogbert replies that this refusal to believe is exactly how he programmed Dilbert.
punchline: Dilbert's denial is itself presented as proof, since Dogbert claims he designed Dilbert to reject the truth, making the simulation claim impossible to disprove.
summary: A talking dog reveals to his owner that he is a computer-generated being, then explains that the owner's disbelief was built in on purpose.

title: Scientist With No Ethical Boundaries

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: We're looking for a scientist who can be easily influenced by money to back our product claims.

transcript.speaker: Scientist
transcript.text: I'm perfect for that job. I have no ethical boundaries whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: But you won't try to con us, right?

transcript.speaker: Scientist
transcript.text: You can't have it both ways.

situation: A client representative tells a scientist they want someone who can be easily bought to endorse their product claims. The scientist enthusiastically volunteers, boasting of having no ethics. The client then asks for assurance that the scientist won't con them too, and the scientist points out the contradiction.
punchline: A company that hires an unethical scientist to deceive the public can't expect that same lack of ethics to spare them from being cheated.
summary: A company shopping for a purchasable expert discovers that someone with no scruples comes with no loyalty either.

title: Measure Nothing, Estimate the Ocean

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We won a government contract to measure ocean temperatures.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which part of the ocean?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The whole ocean.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can't put sensors everywhere in the ocean. It's too big.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can measure a bunch of places and estimate the rest.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So ... you want me to measure 1% of the ocean's temperature and estimate the other 99%?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know how to do that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try using math.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't it be cheaper to measure nothing and just estimate the whole thing?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every now and then you come up with a great idea.

situation: The Boss announces that the company won a government contract to measure ocean temperatures, and Dilbert points out that sensors can't cover the whole ocean. The Boss suggests measuring some places and estimating the rest, so Dilbert sarcastically proposes skipping the measuring entirely and estimating everything, which the Boss praises as a great idea.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic suggestion to fabricate the whole result is taken seriously by the Boss as a cost-saving brilliant idea, exposing how little the contract is about real measurement.
summary: A manager wants a whole ocean's temperature gauged on the cheap, and his engineer's mocking shortcut of skipping the gauging altogether gets enthusiastically approved.

title: Lawyer's Seven Hundred Contract Changes

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Company Lawyer

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: I made seven hundred suggested changes to the agreement.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have turned a good income opportunity into a flaming cesspool of impenetrable legalese.

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: You can't be too careful.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think you just proved we can.

situation: The company lawyer hands Dilbert a contract he has marked up with seven hundred suggested changes. Dilbert reads it and complains that the lawyer has wrecked a good business opportunity with unreadable legal language. The lawyer defends himself by saying you can't be too careful.
punchline: Dilbert turns the lawyer's excuse around, saying the bloated, over-lawyered contract proves that you actually can be too careful.
summary: A lawyer buries a promising deal under hundreds of edits, and Dilbert shows that excessive caution can itself be a mistake.

title: Profits Arrive After Boss Retires

transcript.speaker: Product Developer
transcript.text: The product I'm developing will be unprofitable for the first nine years, but revenue will surge in the tenth.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Didn't you tell me you plan to retire in nine years?

transcript.speaker: Product Developer
transcript.text: Maybe.

transcript.speaker: Product Developer
transcript.text: You will be happily retired before we find out if profits really do surge in year ten.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That makes everything you say sound suspicious.

transcript.speaker: Product Developer
transcript.text: Numbers don't lie.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Who came up with the numbers?

transcript.speaker: Product Developer
transcript.text: That's all the time we have for questions.

situation: A balding presenter in a green shirt shows a chart of a hockey-stick revenue curve for a product that will lose money for nine years. Wally points out that the presenter plans to retire in nine years, so he will never be held to the forecast. When Wally asks who made up the numbers, the presenter abruptly ends the Q&A.
punchline: The presenter's rosy long-term projection is self-serving and unverifiable, and he dodges the obvious question about where the numbers came from by cutting off questions.
summary: A manager pitches a plan that only pays off after he has left the company, then flees when someone doubts his figures.

title: Date Prefers Phone Over Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's date
transcript.text: I just realized I enjoy using my phone more than I enjoy interacting with you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's date
transcript.text: I mean, this thing is amazing, whereas you haven't found a way to entertain me all night.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's date
transcript.text: Maybe I'll grow on you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Now he sounds like a tumor. LOL!"

setting: Restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert is on a dinner date with a woman who keeps looking at her smartphone. She tells him she enjoys her phone more than his company and that he hasn't entertained her all night. When Dilbert hopefully says she may grow on him, she texts a friend mocking him as sounding like a tumor.
punchline: Dilbert's hopeful remark that she might grow fond of him is immediately turned into a joke about a tumor, which she shares via text, proving her phone really does entertain her more than he does.
summary: A dinner date ignores her companion for her phone, then mocks his attempt at charm in a message to someone else.

title: Funeral Leave Only For Yourself

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Can I take the day off to attend a funeral?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure. I didn't even know you were sick.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It's not my own funeral.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh. In that case, no.

situation: An employee sitting at a desk asks their boss, who is staring at a phone, for the day off to attend a funeral. The boss assumes it must be the employee's own funeral and approves it, but when told it is someone else's funeral, he reverses himself and denies the request.
punchline: The boss will only grant funeral leave if it's the employee's own death, showing his callous disregard for employees' personal lives and bereavement.
summary: A manager happily approves a request for funeral leave until he realizes the worker isn't the one who died.

title: Holding Out For A Better Team

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I need your help on my project today, or I'll miss my deadline.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you trying to turn your lack of planning into my problem?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I was hoping you would be a team player.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm holding out for an offer from a better team.

situation: A coworker holding a lanyard asks Dilbert for help on his project, warning that he will otherwise miss his deadline. Dilbert, holding a coffee cup, refuses, pointing out that the coworker's poor planning is not his responsibility. When the coworker appeals to him to be a team player, Dilbert replies that he is waiting for a better team to make him an offer.
punchline: Dilbert turns the 'team player' appeal around by treating teamwork like a job market, implying his current team isn't worth his loyalty or effort.
summary: A last-minute request for assistance is rebuffed by a colleague who says his loyalty is reserved for a superior group that hasn't yet recruited him.

title: Hiring a Brown-Nosing Tattler

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm looking for a new pet employee.

transcript.text: The ideal candidate would be a brown-nosing tattler with no ethical core.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: That sounds like a brilliant idea, even though Dilbert says you are a moron.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You got the job.

setting: Conference room, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: The boss announces he wants a new favorite employee, and a voice describes the ideal candidate as a brown-nosing tattler with no ethics. A coworker immediately flatters the boss's idea while casually mentioning that Dilbert called him a moron. The boss hires him on the spot.
punchline: The coworker proves he is the ideal candidate by simultaneously flattering the boss and ratting out Dilbert, and the clueless boss rewards the tattling with a job.
summary: A manager seeking a favorite underling gets exactly the sycophantic informant described, as a coworker praises him while snitching on a colleague.

title: Second-Best Way: Making Others Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The best way to succeed in this world is through hard work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that the way you did it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I used the second-best way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which is...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Making other people work hard.

setting: Conference room table, with an office building shown in the final panel
situation: The Boss lectures Dilbert and Wally at a table, claiming that hard work is the best route to success. When Dilbert asks whether that's how the Boss got ahead, the Boss admits to using the second-best way instead. The final panel, showing an office building, reveals that this means getting other people to work hard.
punchline: The Boss preaches hard work but admits his own success came from making others do the hard work for him, exposing managerial credit-taking and hypocrisy.
summary: A manager praises diligence as the path to success, then confesses his own career was built on pushing the labor onto everyone else.

title: Wally's Schedule Blocks Every Meeting

punchline: Wally's personal routines, including lengthy bathroom reading time, take priority over any work meeting, showing his deep commitment to avoiding actual work.
summary: A coworker tries to schedule a meeting with the notoriously lazy Wally, who keeps turning down times because of his breakfast and restroom habits.

title: Potluck Celebration Is Really Punishment

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The boss announces a potluck to celebrate the team's success. Dilbert complains that a potluck feels like a penalty, then concedes it beats working. The boss reveals it starts at 8 pm on Friday, meaning it eats into personal time after the workday.
punchline: The 'celebration' is scheduled outside work hours on a Friday night, so it is both a penalty and just another way of making employees give up their free time.
summary: A manager's reward for a successful team turns out to be a self-catered gathering held late on a Friday evening.

title: Cheaper Option Is Just Talking

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your quote is a bit high. Can you do it cheaper?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Yes, we offer a low-cost option that involves me talking about the software, but you can't have it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What would be the point of that?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: You're the one who brought it up.

setting: Office meeting table during a sales negotiation
situation: Dilbert reads a price quote from a software salesman and asks if it can be done cheaper. The salesman offers a low-cost option that consists only of him talking about the software, without Dilbert actually getting it. When Dilbert objects that this is pointless, the salesman blames him for raising the subject.
punchline: The salesman's 'cheaper option' is worthless by design, mocking how vendors respond to price pushback with useless offers and then shift blame to the customer.
summary: A software vendor answers a request for a discount with an absurd bargain that delivers nothing and then faults the buyer for asking.

title: Meaningless Job Title Exposes Uselessness

transcript.speaker: Blue-shirted Coworker
transcript.text: Hi, I'm a business agility influencer and solutionist.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't think that means anything.

transcript.speaker: Blue-shirted Coworker
transcript.text: Why are you the first person to spot that?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Because I'm useless too!

situation: A coworker in a blue shirt introduces himself with a buzzword-heavy job title to Wally, who is holding a coffee cup. Wally points out that the title means nothing. The coworker asks why nobody else noticed, and Wally explains he recognizes it because he is useless as well.
punchline: Only someone who is himself useless can recognize a meaningless job title for what it is, which is a jab at both corporate buzzwords and Wally's own work ethic.
summary: A newly introduced coworker with a jargon-stuffed title is called out by Wally, who admits he only noticed because he shares the same worthlessness.

title: Monetizing the Boss's Pet Employee

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hear you're our boss's new pet employee.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Please don't tell him all of the bad things I have said about him behind his back.

situation: Wally, holding a coffee cup, approaches Alice's desk and says he has heard she is the boss's new pet employee. Alice nervously asks him not to repeat the bad things she has said about the boss and offers him a hundred dollars to stay quiet. Wally thinks to himself that he knew he could monetize the situation.
punchline: Wally turns the rumor of Alice being the boss's favorite into a payday, as she ends up bribing him, which is exactly the kind of easy income he was hoping for.
summary: A coworker teases a colleague about being the boss's favorite and she pays him off to avoid being ratted out.

title: Excuses For Your Excuses

transcript.text: It's been six months now and you still haven't fixed our server issue.

transcript.text: I didn't know we had a server issue.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's no excuse.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now you're making excuses for your excuses!

situation: The Boss complains that Dilbert has failed for six months to fix a server problem. Dilbert says he never knew about the problem, and the Boss dismisses that as an excuse. When Dilbert points out it's actually a reasonable excuse, the Boss accuses him of making excuses for his excuses.
punchline: The Boss blames Dilbert for a problem nobody told him about, and then treats any defense, even a valid one, as further proof of fault.
summary: A manager berates an employee for ignoring a problem he was never told existed, then escalates his anger when the employee explains.

title: Elbonian Insult in One Word

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our product name turns out to be offensive in the Elbonian language.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It means "one who rips off his own facial hair and feeds it to a baby bird, which chokes and dies, signaling years of drought."

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's all in one word?

transcript.text: They only have seventeen words, and nine of them are insults.

situation: Dilbert reports to a coworker holding a coffee cup that their product name is offensive in the Elbonian language. He reads out the absurdly long and grisly meaning of the name. The coworker asks if that is really one word, and Dilbert explains that Elbonian has very few words and most are insults.
punchline: The Elbonian language is so limited that a single word carries an elaborate, gruesome insult, and more than half of its tiny vocabulary consists of insults.
summary: A product turns out to have a name that translates into a wildly specific and gruesome insult in a language with almost no vocabulary.

title: Spotting a Spy by Blinking

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't believe you were a spy for the Elbonian government until you denied it the wrong way.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Coworker
transcript.text: You were slow to speak, and you blinked.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That isn't evidence of anything.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Coworker
transcript.text: You blinked again!

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker he became convinced the coworker is an Elbonian spy only after the coworker denied it incorrectly. The coworker counters by claiming Dilbert's own behavior (slow speech, blinking) is suspicious. When Dilbert says that proves nothing, the coworker points out that he blinked again.
punchline: The accused spy deflects by turning the same flimsy standard of evidence on his accuser, showing how absurd it is to judge guilt by blinking.
summary: An accused spy flips the script and treats his accuser's ordinary eye blinks as proof of deception.

title: Zero-Risk Nuclear Power Is Unsellable

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented a new type of nuclear power that has zero risk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It can be built in one day for less than a thousand dollars and it can power a small city.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get that thing out of here!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I expect it will be hard to sell.

situation: Dilbert shows the Boss a small robot-like device and tells him it is a new, zero-risk form of nuclear power. He adds that it can be built in a day for under a thousand dollars and can power a small city. The Boss panics and orders him to take it away, and Dilbert calmly predicts it will be hard to sell.
punchline: Because the invention is so cheap, quick and safe, it threatens the nuclear power industry's expensive business model, and the Boss's horrified reaction shows nobody with a stake in the status quo will buy it.
summary: An engineer unveils a miraculously cheap and safe energy source and is met with alarm instead of enthusiasm.

summary: A manager brushes off an employee's hair-based excuse for skipping a meeting and pays for it when her monstrous hair swallows him.

situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss announces that he wants to thank each team member by name. He immediately points at Dilbert and calls him 'what's-his-face'. When Dilbert supplies his real name, the Boss rejects it and insists Dilbert looks like a Steve.
punchline: The boss claims to be thanking people by name but doesn't know Dilbert's name, and then dismisses the correct name in favor of one he thinks fits better.
summary: A manager who promises to personally thank his team can't even remember one employee's name and refuses to accept the right one.

title: Unconfirmed Elbonian Attacks Prove Dilbert's Guilt

punchline: The Boss treats an honest answer and a lack of dramatic denial as evidence of treason, showing how baseless paranoia can pin guilt on anyone.
summary: A suspicious manager decides an employee is a foreign spy because of the way he answered a simple question and failed to protest enough.

title: Boss Emulates Steve Jobs Badly

Dilbert and Alice immediately quit. The Boss, missing the point, asks whether his demands would be more acceptable if he wore a black shirt like Jobs.
punchline: The Boss copies only the worst aspects of Steve Jobs' reputation (abusive demands) and thinks a superficial wardrobe change is what's missing, not realizing his behavior is the problem.
summary: A manager imitates a famous tech visionary by threatening and overworking his staff, then wonders if dressing the part would make it more palatable.

situation: Wally tells Dilbert that his self-driving car quit on him. Dilbert assumes it broke down, but Wally explains it literally left a note and drove away. Dilbert asks if he waxed it enough, and Wally says the car moaned creepily whenever he tried.

title: Hurricanes Caused by Birds Research

transcript.text: I don't know enough about climate change to sound smart when people talk about it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Try doing your own research. That's how I learned that hurricanes are caused by birds.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Write that down for me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And did you know polar bears hate snow?

situation: The Boss admits he lacks the knowledge to sound smart in conversations about climate change. Wally advises him to do his own research and cites his own absurd findings, that hurricanes are caused by birds. The Boss eagerly asks Wally to write that down, and Wally adds that polar bears hate snow.
punchline: The Boss doesn't want to understand climate change, just to sound smart, so he gratefully accepts Wally's obviously false claims as facts, and Wally keeps feeding him more nonsense.
summary: A manager wanting to seem informed about the environment happily soaks up his coworker's ridiculous so-called research findings.

title: Toxic Employee Preemptively Discredits Dilbert

transcript.text: Hey, aren't you the new toxic employee?

transcript.speaker: Toxic Employee
transcript.text: I told your boss you think he's a jerk for giving Wally an award for work you did.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I never said that.

transcript.speaker: Toxic Employee
transcript.text: I covered that base by telling him you're a liar.

setting: Office break room or cubicle area, with coffee cups on a table
situation: Dilbert holds a coffee and greets a spiky-headed coworker who is the new toxic employee. The coworker admits to telling Dilbert's boss that Dilbert thinks he's a jerk for giving Wally an award for Dilbert's work. When Dilbert denies saying that, the coworker explains he already told the boss that Dilbert is a liar.
punchline: The toxic employee has rigged the situation so that Dilbert's denial can't clear him, since he has already smeared Dilbert's credibility in advance.
summary: A new workplace troublemaker casually reveals he has framed Dilbert with a made-up insult and then pre-emptively branded him a liar so no defense will work.

title: Inspirational Quote Contradicted by Raise

transcript.text: "Winners never quit, and quitters never win."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When Ted quit, you gave him a raise to stay.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: These work better when you don't think about them.

setting: Office break area, coworkers standing with coffee cups
situation: Asok admits his inspirational quotes haven't been landing well and tries another one to his coworkers, reading from a paper. Wally points out that the company gave Ted a raise to keep him after he quit, which contradicts the quote. Asok replies that the quotes only work if you don't think about them.
punchline: The inspirational quote is undermined by real company behavior, and Asok admits that motivational slogans only work if nobody thinks critically about them.
summary: A hopeful employee shares a motivational saying about perseverance, only to have a coworker point out that quitting actually got someone a pay bump.

transcript.text: Ned is indispensable.

transcript.text: He's the only one who knows how to fix bugs in our system.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What system?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I don't know.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then how do you know he's indispensable?

transcript.speaker: Manager

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: The Boss complains that an employee named Ned ignores his messages and demands he be fired. The only source for Ned's importance is Ned himself, and Dilbert finally reveals that Ned quit two years ago.
punchline: The company has treated someone as indispensable for two years based solely on his own claim, even though he no longer works there and nobody knows what he supposedly maintains.
summary: A manager defends a supposedly irreplaceable worker whose importance and very employment turn out to be entirely unverified.

title: Unconscious Bias Training Drooling Insult

situation: An HR employee holding a paper tells Dilbert he hasn't completed the mandatory unconscious bias training. Dilbert insists he isn't biased, and she replies that he might be when he's unconscious. When he asks if he's a bigot in his sleep, she coolly adds that he also looks like a drooler.
punchline: The HR employee takes the idea of bias while unconscious literally, then piles on a deadpan insult about Dilbert drooling in his sleep.
summary: A deadpan HR worker nags a coworker about overdue bias training and ends up mocking how he looks asleep.

title: Mentoring Through Silent Criticism

transcript.speaker: Coworker
