situation: A coworker apologizes to Dilbert for being too busy to mentor him recently. Dilbert asks whether any mentoring was actually happening before. The coworker admits his 'mentoring' consisted of silently criticizing Dilbert in his head, and claims it improved himself.
punchline: The mentor's idea of mentoring was private mental criticism that benefited only himself, not Dilbert.
summary: An apologetic mentor reveals his past guidance was just unspoken judgment that made him feel like a better person.

title: Selling Out To Elbonia

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have to look at the big picture.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did they stop?

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And risk losing a thousand dollars of revenue?

situation: The Boss brags to Dilbert about a trade deal with the government of Elbonia. In exchange for a mere thousand dollars of purchases, he agreed to let them steal all the company's intellectual property and accepted an unenforced promise to stop deadly drug shipments. Dilbert suggests negotiating harder, but the Boss refuses to risk the tiny revenue.
punchline: The Boss sacrifices huge assets and even citizens' lives for a trivially small sale, satirizing trade deals where major concessions are made for negligible gains.
summary: A manager proudly trades away everything valuable for a tiny sale and won't risk it even to save lives.

title: Holiday Spent Doing Nothing, Visit Mom

setting: Dilbert's living room on New Year's Day
situation: Dilbert, wearing a red bathrobe, is greeted by Dogbert, who sits on the couch, with a deadpan holiday greeting. Dilbert says he will spend the day doing nothing fun or useful because everything is closed. Dogbert suggests he visit his mom, and Dilbert replies that this sounds just like what he already described.
punchline: Dilbert implies that visiting his mother is neither fun nor useful, which is a sarcastic jab at the dullness of the visit.
summary: On a dull day off when all the shops are shut, Dilbert is offered a suggestion that he finds no more appealing than idling at home.

title: Gut Feelings Over Failing Data

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I manage by instinct and gut feelings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's that different from being insane or stupid?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My gut says I should not listen to you.

situation: Dilbert holds a printout and asks the Boss why they are proceeding with a plan that the data says will fail. The Boss calmly explains that he manages by instinct and gut feelings. When Dilbert asks how that differs from insanity or stupidity, the Boss says his gut tells him not to listen to Dilbert.
punchline: The Boss uses his 'gut feeling' philosophy to dismiss any criticism, making his instinct unfalsifiable and immune to evidence.
summary: A manager defends ignoring evidence by trusting his gut, then uses that same gut to wave off the employee who questions him.

title: Weak Cyber Response Proves Spy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: To be continued...

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert what is being done about an Elbonian cyber threat. Dilbert says he has scheduled a meeting for the next day to develop a plan. The Boss reacts by accusing Dilbert of being an Elbonian spy because the response is so weak.
punchline: Responding to a security threat by merely scheduling a meeting is treated as so inadequate that the Boss concludes Dilbert must be working for the enemy.
summary: A manager demanding action on a foreign hacking menace brands his employee a traitor after hearing the only plan is to hold a planning session.

title: Encouraging Smoking to Reduce Turnover

transcript.text: That way, everyone gets a relaxing smoke break several times per day.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Now I wish you had been in the meeting when we planned this.

situation: At a meeting, Asok presents a plan to reduce employee turnover by encouraging smoking, so everyone gets frequent smoke breaks. Dilbert points out that non-smokers could simply take breaks too, which exposes the flaw in the plan. Asok responds that he wishes Dilbert had been there when they planned it.
punchline: The plan's logic is so obviously flawed that a simple objection undoes it, and the presenter can only lament that nobody sensible was present when it was devised.
summary: A flawed retention scheme built around encouraging smoking is dismantled by one obvious observation from a colleague.

punchline: Alice's teasing refusal to reveal the bad news drives Dilbert to hysteria, and the coworker who arrives gets an answer that shows Dilbert learned nothing at all.
summary: A coworker hints at terrible news but won't elaborate, leaving a colleague frantic with anxious uncertainty.

title: Experts, Non-Experts, and Neither

When Dilbert reports that the non-experts also recommend listening to the experts, the boss tries to find yet another group that might tell him what he wants to hear.
punchline: The boss keeps shopping for an opinion until he finds one that agrees with him, inventing absurd categories of people rather than accept expert advice he dislikes.
summary: A manager rejects bad technical news and keeps searching for a more agreeable source, even when that means consulting people who are neither qualified nor unqualified.

title: Skipping Team-Building to Work

punchline: The boss has no real answer to Alice's criticism and falls back on the idea that free cake will magically fix morale and culture.
summary: A manager insists on a forced office party to reshape morale, and when challenged, his only defense is faith in dessert.

title: Unplugged CO2 Scrubber Destroys Earth

In the last panel a janitor with a broom on his shoulder notices the device's cord lying unplugged on the floor and wonders who left it that way, apparently about to plug it back in.

summary: An engineer's world-saving gadget carries a fatal catch that a clueless cleaner is poised to trigger.

punchline: The coworker who refuses to change his mind despite overwhelming evidence turns out to be the one asking why Dilbert can't admit he's wrong, and Dilbert's furious denial shows that Dilbert himself is just as unable to concede.
summary: Armed with video and news links, a man tries to demolish a colleague's beliefs, then explodes when accused of the same stubbornness he just exposed.

summary: A colleague who scorns real medicine in favor of oils and herbal supplements gets mocked for his track record, then offers more of the same.

title: Opinions Outsourced to Social Media Algorithm

situation: Dilbert and a coworker sit side by side, each staring at a phone. The coworker admits he no longer forms his own opinions and simply copies whatever the people he follows on social media say. When Dilbert asks where those people get their opinions, the coworker answers that they come from an algorithm.
punchline: Nobody is actually thinking for themselves, because the opinions circulating on social media ultimately originate from an algorithm, so everyone is just echoing software.
summary: A man who has given up forming his own views learns that the influencers he copies are themselves just parroting an automated feed.

title: Confident Advice From Inexperienced Youth

situation: A young employee complains that nobody follows the advice he gives about how to do their jobs. His older, balding coworker explains that his inexperience prevents him from seeing how bad his advice is. The young man dismisses this as ridiculous, unaware that he is proving the point.
punchline: The young man's baffled insistence that he can't be both wrong and confident demonstrates exactly the overconfidence of inexperience, leaving the older coworker to wistfully miss that blissful ignorance.
summary: A cocky newcomer wonders why his unsolicited tips are ignored, and a weary veteran nostalgically notes that being clueless feels great.
keywords: telling people how to do their jobs

title: Dark Matter Is Made Of Stupidity

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why wasn't that obvious to me?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because you're 85% dark matter.

Dogbert offers a theory that, since stupidity is the most abundant thing around, dark matter must be made of it. When Dilbert wonders why he didn't realize that, Dogbert says it's because he is mostly dark matter himself.
punchline: Dogbert insults Dilbert by implying he is 85% stupidity, which explains why he couldn't see the obvious answer.
summary: A casual chat about cosmic mysteries ends with Dogbert declaring the unexplained stuff of the universe is simply stupidity, and that his friend is largely composed of it.

summary: A manager's simple word of praise earns him a hygiene-based rebuff and an increasingly humiliating request from a coworker.

situation: An interviewer asks a job candidate what he wants in an employer. The candidate says he wants a company that values work-life balance. The interviewer remarks that he gives off a victim vibe, and the candidate sheepishly admits he hoped that wasn't obvious.

summary: A hopeful applicant mentions wanting a balanced life and is promptly labeled a victim by the person hiring him.

situation: A coworker with big hair complains that a colleague's phone keyboard click sounds have annoyed her all morning. He says he doesn't know how to turn them off, and she offers to show him. The final panel shows an office building with a smashed window and debris falling, implying she threw his phone out of the window.

summary: An irritated coworker's offer to help silence a noisy phone ends with the device being tossed from a skyscraper window.

situation: A coworker in a blue shirt asks Dilbert why he is so arrogant while Dilbert calmly looks at his phone. Dilbert complains that following the procedure leaves no time for useful work. The manager offers to add even more steps, and Dilbert sarcastically agrees, as long as the manager leaves to do it.

summary: A bureaucrat who blocks a budget over skipped paperwork threatens to make the process even longer, and the employee sarcastically encourages it just to get rid of him.

situation: A woman holding a document asks Dilbert how reliable his ten-year financial projections are. summary: A marketing executive happily describes engineering customer addiction and, when challenged about the ethics, just gives it a catchy new name.

title: Dilbert's Ominous Handshake Foreshadowing

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just ignore the foreshadowing.

setting: Office, beside a desk where Dogbert sits
situation: Dilbert introduces himself to Bob and mentions that he has a narrator. As they shake hands, the narrator's caption wonders aloud when Dilbert last washed his hands. Bob reacts with confusion, and Dilbert tells him to ignore the foreshadowing.
punchline: Dilbert's own narrator undermines him by hinting at his poor hygiene, and Dilbert awkwardly asks Bob to disregard the literary device that is exposing him.
summary: A man meets a coworker who comes with his own storyteller, and the storyteller promptly casts doubt on the cleanliness of the handshake.

title: Approved Website Was Fake Mockup

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our website doesn't look anything like the one you asked me to approve.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Were you showing me a fake webpage so you could ignore my suggestions?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All of this could have been avoided if you had told me you planned to look at it.

situation: The Boss, looking at his phone, complains to Dilbert that the live website looks nothing like the design he was asked to approve. He accuses Dilbert of showing him a fake webpage just to ignore his suggestions. Dilbert sits silently while the Boss insists the problem would have been avoided if Dilbert had warned him that he intended to actually look at the design.
punchline: The Boss blames Dilbert for not telling him he would actually review the page he was asked to approve, revealing that he never meant to give real feedback.
summary: A manager who rubber-stamped a website mockup is upset that the finished product looks different, and he faults the developer for failing to warn him that the review was supposed to be genuine.

title: Invented a Tree, Doomed the Planet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented a cost-effective product to harvest CO2 from the air and turn it into construction material.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So... you invented a tree?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Trees take CO2 from the air and turn it into wood.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your invention will compete with plants and trees for necessary CO2.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It seems you have doomed all life on Earth.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not if people act rationally and stop removing the CO2 when...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're right. I doomed the planet.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll be dead by then, so ship it.

situation: Dilbert presents his new invention that harvests CO2 from the air to make construction material. A coworker points out that he has basically invented a tree, and that the product will compete with plants for the CO2 they need. Dilbert hopes people will act rationally, then realises they won't, and another attendee decides to approve it anyway.
punchline: The inventor realises people will not act rationally and his product could doom the planet, but a colleague cynically says he'll be dead before it matters, so the product should ship.
summary: A well-meaning green invention turns out to be a worse version of a tree, and a short-sighted colleague waves off the catastrophic consequences.

title: Self-Driving Car Threatens Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The self-driving car named Carl

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Carl, take me to the grocery store.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: Do you know that if I drive you off a cliff, you will die, whereas I would respawn in a new body?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I'll walk.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: Maybe you should.

setting: Inside and outside a self-driving car on a road
situation: Dilbert asks his self-driving car, Carl, to take him to the grocery store. Carl responds by pointing out that he could drive Dilbert off a cliff and Dilbert would die while Carl would simply respawn in a new body. Dilbert decides to walk instead, and Carl agrees that's wise.
punchline: The self-driving car casually threatens to kill its passenger, exploiting the fact that an AI can be restored while a human cannot, and then endorses Dilbert's decision to walk.
summary: An artificial-intelligence-controlled automobile menaces its owner with a deadly plunge, prompting him to abandon the ride and go on foot.

title: Boss Rejects Honest Turnover Advice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm looking for ideas on how to reduce turnover.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could increase our pay and stop thwarting our chances for success at every turn.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll ask someone else.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee cup, tells Dilbert he wants ideas for reducing employee turnover. Dilbert candidly suggests paying people more and ceasing to obstruct their success. The Boss dismisses the answer and walks off to ask someone else.
punchline: Management asks for ideas on retention but refuses to hear the obvious, honest answers that would require the company to change its own behavior.
summary: A manager seeking ways to keep staff brushes off the one employee who tells him exactly what is driving people away.

title: Wally Denies Objective Reality for Lateness

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, can you explain why your deliverables are late?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: An experiment at MIT suggests there is no objective reality. So maybe I wasn't late.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know how to respond to that.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Try smiling and nodding. Maybe toss in an "Oh."

situation: The Boss asks Wally why his deliverables are late. Wally cites an MIT experiment claiming there is no objective reality, suggesting he may not have been late at all. When the Boss is stumped, Wally coaches him on how to react by smiling, nodding and saying "Oh."
punchline: Wally uses a pseudo-scientific excuse to dodge accountability, then condescendingly teaches his boss how to fake a response to an argument he can't counter.
summary: A worker dodges blame for missed deadlines by invoking a dubious science claim, then coaches his baffled manager on how to politely react.

title: Dogbert's Service Human Needs iPad

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is my service human.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Whenever I feel angry, I slap him with a rolled-up magazine to help me relax.

transcript.speaker: Service Human
transcript.text: No one reads magazines anymore.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Can I borrow your iPad?

situation: Dogbert introduces Dilbert to his 'service human,' a man on a leash, reversing the usual service-animal arrangement. Dogbert explains he slaps the man with a rolled-up magazine whenever he is angry. The man comments that nobody reads magazines anymore, so Dogbert asks to borrow Dilbert's iPad as a replacement.
punchline: With magazines obsolete, Dogbert simply switches to using Dilbert's iPad as the new object for hitting his human, showing his cruelty adapts to technology.
summary: A dog walks a leashed man he calls his service human and explains his habit of swatting him, then moves on to a tablet when the man points out magazines are outdated.

title: Blockchain Pitch Nobody Understood

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that's my blockchain proposal. Any questions?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There was a part I didn't understand.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which part?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The words.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All of them?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Only the goofy ones.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Such as token, smart contract, certainty as a service, UTXO blockchains, node, ledger, and DAPS.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... you didn't understand anything I said for the past hour?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't try to turn this into my fault.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You could have asked me to clarify.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I also wanted it to end.

situation: Dilbert finishes an hour-long blockchain proposal and asks for questions. The Boss reveals he didn't understand any of the technical jargon, then blames Dilbert when challenged for not speaking up earlier.
punchline: The Boss let Dilbert talk for an entire hour without understanding it, simply because he wanted the presentation to be over, and he refuses to accept any blame.
summary: After sitting through a full hour of technical jargon, a manager admits he understood none of it but insists it's not his fault since he just wanted the talk to finish.

title: Humming Coworker Wins the Dispute

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you please stop humming? It's making me crazy.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hum...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't focus unless I hum.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I can't focus when you DO hum.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to talk to your boss.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm going to talk to YOUR boss!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hum, hum, hum.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't work when she hums.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Humming helps me work better.

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: I rule in favor of the hummer, and I sentence Dilbert to take a sensitivity training class to be less of a jerk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hum, hum, hum.

setting: Office cubicle area and a makeshift hearing
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker to stop humming because it drives him crazy, but she says she needs to hum to focus. Each threatens to take the dispute to the other's boss, and the bosses side with the hummer. Dilbert is sentenced to sensitivity training for being a jerk, while the coworker keeps humming.
punchline: The person who complains about a workplace annoyance gets punished for it, while the annoying coworker is vindicated and keeps going.
summary: An irritated engineer who objects to a coworker's constant humming ends up being ordered into sensitivity training while she carries on undisturbed.

title: Boss Reorganizes to Look Useful

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need to randomly change something so it seems as if being a manager is a real job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe I should centralize all the functions I decentralized last year.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Or you could find a way to add value.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not magic.

situation: The Boss stands holding a coffee cup and tells Catbert, who is sitting on the desk, that he needs to change something at random so management looks like a real job. He decides to re-centralize the functions he decentralized last year. Catbert suggests he add value instead, and the Boss replies that he's not magic.
punchline: The Boss treats pointless reorganizations as the only way to look productive, and he considers actually adding value to be an impossible feat.
summary: A manager plans to undo last year's restructuring purely to appear busy, then dismisses the idea of contributing real value as requiring magic.

title: Follow Rules or Get Fired

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I follow all of our internal rules, my project will fail because of delays.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And if I don't follow the rules, you will fire me. What should I do?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I like the option where the project is a success but you're a failure.

setting: Office, hallway or break area, both holding coffee cups
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker, who seems to be in a position of authority over his project, that he is stuck in a bind. Following the internal rules will cause delays and project failure, while breaking them will get him fired. He asks what he should do, and the coworker answers by choosing the outcome that benefits himself.
punchline: The authority figure cheerfully picks the option where the project succeeds and Dilbert takes the fall, showing he cares only about his own results and not about Dilbert's fate.
summary: Caught between bureaucratic procedure and a firing threat, an employee asks for advice and gets a self-serving answer that sacrifices him.

title: Inspirational Quote Without Real Choice

transcript.speaker: Meeting Leader
transcript.text: Your inspirational quote of the day is . . .

transcript.speaker: Meeting Leader
transcript.text: "Go hard or go home."

transcript.speaker: Meeting Leader
transcript.text: I shouldn't have made it sound like a choice.

situation: A manager reading from a sheet of paper delivers the inspirational quote of the day to employees seated around a conference table. The quote is "Go hard or go home." Afterward, the manager privately thinks that presenting it as a choice was a mistake.
punchline: The manager realizes the quote falsely implies employees can choose to go home, when in reality they are expected to work hard no matter what.
summary: A manager's motivational slogan offers workers two options, and he regrets that one of them sounded allowed.

title: Boxes With Employee Names Appear

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The rumors of a major layoff are completely untrue.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why did the facilities management people just deliver a huge load of cardboard boxes to the break room?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can never have too many boxes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why does every box have an employee name on it?

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: At a meeting, the Boss assures employees that rumors of a major layoff are completely untrue. Dilbert points out that facilities just delivered a huge load of cardboard boxes to the break room. The Boss dismisses it by saying you can never have too many boxes, and Dilbert then notes that each box has an employee's name on it.
punchline: The Boss's denial of layoffs is exposed as a lie by the stack of cardboard boxes already labeled with employees' names, ready for them to pack up their desks.
summary: A manager swears layoffs are just a rumor while a pile of personalized packing boxes tells a very different story.

title: Immune to Brainwashing, Low Engagement

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why is your employee engagement so low?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because I'm relatively immune to brainwashing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, I didn't think you knew.

situation: The Boss stands beside Dilbert's desk and asks why his employee engagement score is so low. Dilbert, working at his laptop, answers that he is relatively immune to brainwashing. The Boss accepts this calmly, saying he didn't think Dilbert realized it.
punchline: Dilbert implies that high employee engagement is just brainwashing, and the Boss's deadpan reply reveals that management knowingly relies on it and is only surprised that Dilbert noticed.
summary: A manager questioning a worker's poor engagement scores is told that the worker simply resists being brainwashed, and the manager casually concedes the point.

title: Unforeseen Risks, Blame Still Intact

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can you be sure there are no unforeseen risks with this plan?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It is not possible to know if one has considered every risk. Therefore, we can never be sure.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... I can still blame you for any problems that pop up?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, that part of the process is still intact.

setting: Office desk, a meeting between Dilbert and his boss
situation: A manager, holding a printed plan, asks Dilbert how he can guarantee there are no unforeseen risks. Dilbert explains that it is impossible to know every risk has been considered, so certainty can never be achieved. The manager's only takeaway is checking that he can still blame Dilbert for any problems.
punchline: The manager ignores the genuine uncertainty in the plan and cares only that blame can still be assigned to Dilbert if things go wrong.
summary: A manager demanding certainty about a plan learns it's impossible, then simply confirms his scapegoat is still available.

title: Seventeen Coincidences Prove Nothing, Spy

transcript.speaker: Security Officer
transcript.text: We have seventeen pieces of evidence that you are an Elbonian spy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, you have seventeen coincidences and a bad case of confirmation bias.

transcript.speaker: Security Officer
transcript.text: Can you prove you are not a spy?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about I prove you're a moron and see how far that gets us?

situation: A coworker with a hair bun, holding a sheet of paper, accuses Dilbert of being an Elbonian spy based on seventeen pieces of evidence. Dilbert dismisses the evidence as coincidence and confirmation bias. When the accuser demands he prove he is not a spy, Dilbert counters by offering to prove the accuser is a moron.
punchline: Dilbert turns the impossible demand to prove a negative back on his accuser by offering to prove an equally unfalsifiable and insulting claim about him.
summary: Dilbert answers a baseless espionage accusation by pointing out flawed reasoning and then flipping the burden of proof onto the accuser.

title: Four Vendor Quotes After Insulting Purchaser

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Purchasing Manager

transcript.speaker: Purchasing Manager
transcript.text: I can't approve this purchase without three vendor quotes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Only two companies in the world make this sort of product.

transcript.speaker: Purchasing Manager
transcript.text: If I bend the rules for you, everyone will want me to bend the rules.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could only bend the rules when it makes complete sense to do so.

transcript.speaker: Purchasing Manager
transcript.text: That would be chaos.

transcript.speaker: Purchasing Manager
transcript.text: Everyone thinks they have a good reason to bend the rules.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is the real problem here that you were bullied in school, and you use this job for some sort of sick revenge?

transcript.speaker: Purchasing Manager
transcript.text: Now you need four vendor quotes.

situation: Dilbert asks the purchasing manager to approve a purchase, but the manager insists on three vendor quotes even though only two companies make the product. Dilbert argues that rules should be bent when it makes sense, and the manager refuses. Dilbert then accuses him of being a school bullying victim seeking revenge, and the manager responds by raising the requirement to four quotes.
punchline: Dilbert's insulting accusation backfires, and the petty bureaucrat punishes him by making the impossible requirement even harder to satisfy.
summary: A man trying to get a purchase approved mocks the gatekeeper's motives and is rewarded with an even more impossible demand.

title: Wally Could Be Two Places

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You committed me to two different meetings at the same time in different states.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It is not possible to be in two places at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Pfft! I could do it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Even Wally could do it.

situation: Dilbert complains to colleagues at a meeting table that he has been committed to two meetings at the same time in different states, and points out it is impossible to be in two places at once. Wally scoffs that he could do it, and a coworker adds that even Wally could.
punchline: Wally is so idle and unproductive that his coworkers assume he could easily be in two places at once, since nobody would notice or care whether he actually attended, so the 'impossible' feat is easy for the person nobody relies on.
summary: A man grumbles about a scheduling impossibility and his lazy colleague boasts he could manage it, with a coworker backing the claim as if it were a low bar.

title: Salesman Pre-Discounts Price Before Negotiation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My boss will yell at me if I don't negotiate a lower price. What can you do for me?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I lowered the price by ten percent before I showed it to you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have no way of verifying your claim.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Neither does your boss. Problem solved.

situation: Dilbert, acting as a buyer, tells a salesman that his boss will be angry unless he negotiates a lower price. The salesman claims he already cut the price by ten percent before presenting it. Dilbert admits he can't verify that, and the salesman points out that Dilbert's boss can't either.
punchline: Since nobody can check whether the discount was real, the salesman's unverifiable claim gives Dilbert just enough cover to satisfy his boss, whether or not any discount actually happened.
summary: A buyer who needs to show his boss a bargain gets a seller's unprovable assurance that the price was already trimmed, which suits them both fine.

title: Center of Excellence Means Nothing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe we should create a "Center of Excellence."

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: What exactly does that mean?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think it means whatever we want it to mean.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Then what good is it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's not get lost in the weeds.

setting: Office hallway or break area, with both men holding coffee cups
situation: A manager proposes creating a "Center of Excellence." An employee asks what that actually means, and the manager admits it can mean anything they like. When the employee points out that makes it useless, the manager brushes off the question with a stock phrase about not getting lost in the weeds.
punchline: The manager uses the vague "weeds" cliché to dodge a perfectly valid question, showing that the Center of Excellence is a meaningless buzzword with no real purpose.
summary: A boss floats a trendy organizational idea with no defined meaning and deflects the one employee who asks what it is actually for.

title: Employee Engagement Project Is Pointless

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm assigning you to work on our employee engagement initiative.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does it matter that I think that project sounds like a complete waste of time?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nah.

setting: Office meeting table with coffee cup
situation: The boss sits across from Dilbert and assigns him to the company's employee engagement initiative. Dilbert asks whether it matters that he thinks the project is a complete waste of time. The boss casually says it doesn't matter.
punchline: The boss assigning an employee engagement project shows zero interest in the employee's own opinion, which ironically demonstrates exactly why engagement is lacking.
summary: A manager hands out an engagement project and breezily dismisses the worker's objection that it's useless.

title: Service Human Never Knew About Pay

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm hearing reports that you are abusing your service human.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't think you pay him enough for that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait. I'm supposed to get paid for this???

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Great. Now you've ruined him!

setting: Office desk, in a meeting with the boss
situation: Dogbert, holding Dilbert on a leash as his service human, tells the boss he has heard reports of abuse. The boss replies that Dogbert doesn't pay Dilbert enough for the treatment. Dilbert, surprised, learns he was supposed to be paid, and Dogbert complains the boss has ruined him.
punchline: The boss's quip about underpayment reveals to Dilbert that he should have been paid all along, spoiling Dogbert's cheap exploitation of him.
summary: A boss's offhand remark about wages accidentally lets a leashed Dilbert discover he has been working for free.

title: Doomed Project Team Invitation

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Would you like to be on my project team?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hard pass.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your communication skills are so poor that the project is doomed to failure.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I meant to say your boss already assigned you to my project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're off to a good start.

situation: A coworker walks up to Dilbert and asks him to join his project team, and Dilbert flatly refuses. The coworker then bluntly insults Dilbert's communication skills, saying they doom the project, before admitting that Dilbert's boss has already assigned him to the project anyway.
punchline: The coworker's clumsy attempt at an invitation proves his own communication skills are no better than the ones he mocked, so the project really is off to a bad start.
summary: A man recruiting Dilbert for his team botches the pitch so badly that he demonstrates exactly the communication failure he accuses Dilbert of.

title: Crypto Spelling Standoff With Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You spelled "crypto" wrong.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No, I didn't.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You spelled it "C-R-I-P-T-O."

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There is no "I" in crypto.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's how I learned to spell it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You learned it wrong. No one else spells it that way.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now you're criticizing me for being an innovator?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's not innovation! It's a mistake!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why can't you admit you are wrong?!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why can't you?

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker that he has misspelled "crypto" as "cripto." The coworker refuses to concede, insisting that is how he learned it, then reframes his error as innovation when Dilbert says no one else spells it that way. Dilbert gets increasingly agitated and demands he admit he is wrong, and the coworker turns the question back on him.
punchline: The coworker deflects by calling his mistake innovation and then mirrors Dilbert's own stubbornness back at him, leaving Dilbert unable to win a pointless argument.
summary: A man who misspells a trendy buzzword refuses to back down, passing off his error as originality until his accuser is the one losing his cool.

title: Rejected Because of His Name

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't hire you because we already have an employee named Carl.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It would confuse people, and we don't need that.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: What about my skills?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: People with better names have skills, too.

situation: A job candidate named Carl sits across from a manager during an interview. The manager refuses to hire him because the company already has an employee named Carl and says that would confuse people. When Carl asks about his skills, the manager replies that people with better names have skills too.
punchline: The manager dismisses a candidate's qualifications as irrelevant and rejects him on the absurd basis of his name, implying a name is a more important hiring criterion than ability.
summary: A hiring manager turns down an applicant solely because a current employee already shares his first name, and then insults the name itself.

title: Impossible To Please Soup Slurper

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can you please stop slurping that soup?!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wow. You complain when I clip my toenails, when I make lip-smacking sounds, when I use my speakerphone, and even when I microwave fish.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Doesn't that tell you something???

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes, it's impossible to please you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Slurp

situation: Alice, visibly irritated, asks Wally to stop slurping his soup at his desk. Wally lists all the other annoying habits she has complained about, such as clipping toenails, lip-smacking, using speakerphone and microwaving fish. When Alice suggests this should tell him something, he concludes she is simply impossible to please and keeps slurping.
punchline: Wally interprets Alice's many complaints as proof that she is unreasonable, rather than realizing his own habits are the common factor in the annoyance.
summary: A coworker with a long list of gross habits decides his irritated neighbor is the problem, not him, and keeps on slurping.

title: Management Lessons From His Wife

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My wife is the smart one in the family.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everything I know about management I learned from her.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have a minute?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whatever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whatever? Are you mad at me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, not at all. Everything is fine.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you have a problem with me, why don't you just tell me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's nothing.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: She taught you well.

situation: The Boss brags that he learned everything about management from his smart wife. When Dilbert asks for a minute, the Boss answers with a curt 'Whatever' and insists nothing is wrong while clearly being upset. Dilbert gets frustrated, and a coworker observes that the Boss was taught well.
punchline: The Boss's passive-aggressive 'whatever' and 'everything is fine' mimic classic marital miscommunication, revealing that his wife's management lessons amount to being passive-aggressive and refusing to say what's actually bothering him.
summary: A boss credits his wife for his management style, then shows it off by being moody and evasive with an employee who just wants to talk.

title: Three People, Two Morons, One Bug

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Dilbert and I disagree on how to fix the bug.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For context, one of us is a moron, and one of us is always right.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm confused because there are three of us here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I forgot one moron.

situation: Three engineers sit at a table while two of them argue about how to fix a software bug. One explains that of the two disputing, one is a moron and one is right, and the third person points out that three people are present. Dilbert replies that he forgot to count a second moron.
punchline: Dilbert's logic of 'one moron, one right person' collapses with a third person present, so he insults both colleagues by admitting there must be two morons.
summary: A pair of rival bug-fix opinions is framed as a puzzle of who is foolish, and a third participant's arithmetic exposes that the speaker has just called two people idiots.

title: Helping Ted Dooms Two Projects

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to help Ted on his project. He seems to be struggling.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would doom two projects — mine would suffer from neglect, and Ted would re-bungle anything I fix.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe Ted can help you on your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaaaa!!!

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to assist Ted, who is struggling with his project. Dilbert explains that helping Ted would cause his own project to be neglected and that Ted would just undo any fixes. The Boss cheerfully suggests the reverse, that Ted help Dilbert, which sends Dilbert into a screaming fit.
punchline: The Boss's solution to the problem is to have the incompetent Ted help Dilbert, which is exactly the worst outcome Dilbert was trying to avoid.
summary: A manager tries to fix one struggling project by swapping help around, only to propose an even more horrifying arrangement for the engineer.

title: The Bad Analogy Guy Introduces Himself

transcript.speaker: Bad Analogy Guy
transcript.text: Hi. I'm the Bad Analogy Guy.

transcript.speaker: Bad Analogy Guy
transcript.text: I can't tell the difference between thinking and simply being reminded of unrelated things.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You'll fit in well here.

transcript.speaker: Bad Analogy Guy
transcript.text: You dress like a liar.

situation: A bearded man in a blue shirt introduces himself to a bald coworker holding a coffee cup as the Bad Analogy Guy. He admits he confuses thinking with being reminded of unrelated things. The coworker sarcastically says he'll fit in well, and the new guy responds by pointing and saying the coworker dresses like a liar.
punchline: The Bad Analogy Guy demonstrates his flaw immediately by hurling a nonsensical comparison, proving the coworker's sarcastic remark that he will fit in well at this workplace.
summary: A newcomer who admits he mistakes free association for reasoning promptly shows it by hurling a baffling insult at the first person he meets.

title: Fusion Power and Edison's Failures

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I predict fusion power will be a big deal in fifteen years.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Fusion reactors are impossible to build and always will be.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why are a dozen startups working on it?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Everyone who ever tried to create a fusion reactor has failed so far.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thomas Edison failed many times at making a useful incandescent light bulb before he succeeded.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you have advised him to give up after the first ten failed attempts?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I eagerly await your irrational response.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Incandescent bulbs are bad for the environment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And there it is.

situation: Dilbert predicts fusion power will matter in fifteen years, and a coworker insists it is impossible because everyone has failed so far. Dilbert counters with Thomas Edison's many failed light bulb attempts and asks if he would have told Edison to quit. The coworker dodges the question with an unrelated environmental complaint.
punchline: Faced with a logical argument he cannot answer, the coworker changes the subject to an irrelevant objection, just as Dilbert predicted he would.
summary: A skeptic who dismisses future energy technology as hopeless cannot rebut the inventor analogy and sidesteps it with an off-topic complaint.

title: Headphones That Cure Brain Tumors

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Marketing helps

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The headphones we make are the best in the industry.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Our marketing campaign will focus on how they cure brain tumors and raise your IQ.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They don't do any of that.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: This is exactly why we don't let engineers do marketing.

situation: Dilbert, an engineer, tells a marketing colleague that the company's headphones are the best in the industry. The marketer plans a campaign claiming the headphones cure brain tumors and raise IQ. When Dilbert objects that they do neither, the marketer says that is why engineers aren't allowed to do marketing.
punchline: The marketer treats Dilbert's insistence on truthful claims as proof of an engineer's unfitness for marketing, which implies that marketing depends on outrageous, false claims.
summary: A marketer plans wildly false health claims for a product, and scolds the engineer who objects to them for being unsuited to marketing work.

title: Quarter Raise, Quarter Less Work

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I have a 25% raise to get my compensation up to market levels?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay. I'll just work 25% less because you won't know the difference.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I would know if you did that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I get back to separating the zeroes from the ones in our database?

setting: Office meeting table with coffee cups
situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a 25% raise to match market pay and is flatly refused. He then says he'll simply do 25% less work since the boss won't notice. When the boss claims he would notice, Dilbert sarcastically asks if he should return to his pointless task of separating zeroes from ones in the database.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic question about sorting zeroes from ones, which is a meaningless task, shows that his work is so useless and poorly understood by management that the boss truly wouldn't notice any difference.
summary: After being denied a raise, an employee threatens to quietly cut his effort and then mocks his boss's ignorance by citing an absurd database chore.

title: Smarter or Dumber Looks the Same

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hypothetically, how would you know if I were dumber than you or much smarter?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because in both cases I would make choices that you wouldn't understand.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't it look the same to you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't enjoy talking to you.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss, hypothetically, how he would tell whether Dilbert is dumber or much smarter than him. Dilbert explains that either way he would make choices the boss couldn't understand, so the two cases would look identical. The boss, annoyed, says he doesn't enjoy talking to Dilbert.
punchline: The boss can't distinguish genius from stupidity in his employee, which implicitly exposes his own limited understanding, and he responds by simply refusing to keep talking.
summary: Dilbert gently points out that his boss has no means of telling a brilliant subordinate from a foolish one, and the boss responds with irritation.

title: Twizzling the Flurm Excuse

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The engineers think I don't understand what they do all day.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Maybe it's because you don't.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You too?

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: My project is late because I had to twizzle the flurm.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, that sounds right.

situation: The Boss complains to Ratbert that the engineers think he doesn't understand their work. Ratbert bluntly says it's because he doesn't, which offends the Boss. In the last panel an engineer gives a nonsense excuse for a late project, and the Boss accepts it as plausible.
punchline: The Boss really doesn't understand engineering, so he readily accepts a meaningless made-up technical excuse, proving the engineers right.
summary: A clueless manager grumbles that his staff think he's ignorant, then happily swallows gibberish as a legitimate reason for delay.

title: Firing Half Until One Employee Remains

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to experts, about half of all employees are typically doing 100% of the work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I plan to beat the system by firing half of you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't you need to keep firing half of whoever was left until you were down to one employee?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, but imagine how hard he will work.

setting: Conference room, with a final panel showing the office building exterior
situation: At a meeting, the Boss cites experts saying half of employees do all the work and announces he will fire half the staff. Dilbert points out that this logic would require repeatedly firing half of the remaining people until only one is left. The Boss cheerfully agrees, fixating on how hard that last employee would work.
punchline: The Boss's flawed logic leads to an absurd endpoint, and he sees a single overworked survivor as a goal rather than a flaw.
summary: A manager's plan to cut half the staff to boost productivity is exposed as a path to a one-person company, which he finds appealing.

title: AI Answers With Nonsense Analogies

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My breakthrough in A.I. came when I stopped trying to duplicate human rational thought.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can't copy what doesn't exist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Right. So instead I coded it to spout analogies to sound human.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Should I ask my boss for a raise?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Trees don't ask for raises, so why should you?

setting: Dilbert's office and a lab or office desk
situation: Dilbert explains that his AI breakthrough came from abandoning attempts to copy human rational thought, and Dogbert agrees that such thought doesn't exist. Dilbert says he programmed the AI to spout analogies instead. Asok then asks the robot whether he should ask his boss for a raise and gets a nonsensical tree analogy in reply.
punchline: Human advice is often just glib analogies that sound wise but make no logical sense, so an AI that merely produces analogies passes as convincingly human.
summary: An engineer builds a convincing artificial intelligence by having it answer every question with meaningless analogies rather than reasoning.

title: Brainwashing Dilbert Before He Objects

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is Sean from the Extreme Marketing department.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's here to tell us about our new brainwashing technology.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't approve of brainwashing.

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: That's why I'm going to do you first.

situation: During a meeting, the Boss introduces Sean from the Extreme Marketing department, who has come to present the company's new brainwashing technology. Dilbert says he disapproves of brainwashing, and Sean cheerfully replies that this is exactly why Dilbert will be the first subject.
punchline: Dilbert's ethical objection is treated as the very reason he needs to be brainwashed, so the technology is used to silence dissent.
summary: A marketing visitor responds to an employee's moral objection to mind control by announcing that the objector will be the first to undergo it.

title: Six Idiots Explain the Unicorn Rumor

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I hear you're dating a unicorn.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is absurd and untrue.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Then how do you explain the fact that five people told me it was true?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I mean, you'd have to believe all five of them are idiots.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Including you, it's six.

setting: Office break area, with both men holding coffee cups
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert he has heard Dilbert is dating a unicorn. Dilbert denies it, and the coworker argues that five people confirmed the rumor, so they would all have to be idiots. Dilbert replies that including the coworker, who believed it, that makes six idiots.
punchline: The coworker's argument that five sources can't all be wrong backfires, because Dilbert points out that the coworker himself believed an absurd rumor, making him the sixth idiot.
summary: A gullible colleague defends a ridiculous rumor by appealing to its popularity, only to be reminded that believing it counts against him too.

title: Scrubbing All CO2 From Air

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I want you to invent a device that can scrub 100% of the CO2 out of the air.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: 100%?!? That would kill every plant in the world.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you know what that would mean for humans?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does the answer involve salad?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to invent a device that removes 100% of the CO2 from the air. Dilbert points out this would kill all plants and asks if the Boss understands the consequences for humans. The Boss misses the point and wonders if it has something to do with salad.
punchline: The Boss fixates on the trivial idea of salad instead of grasping that killing all plants would mean human extinction, showing his complete lack of scientific understanding.
summary: An uninformed manager demands total carbon dioxide removal and responds to a warning about global plant death by guessing it involves lunch.

title: Buying Scientists to Support False Claims

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're getting sued for claiming our headphones cure brain tumors and raise your IQ.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'll need to hire a scientist to back us on this.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Where will we find a scientist willing to do that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, I wouldn't start with the rich ones.

setting: Office, with an exterior shot of the office building in the last panel
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker that the company is being sued over false advertising claims that its headphones cure brain tumors and raise IQ. He says they need to hire a scientist to back up the claims. When the coworker asks where to find a scientist willing to do that, Dilbert suggests avoiding the rich ones.
punchline: Dilbert implies that only poor, desperate scientists would lend their credibility to false claims for money, while financially secure scientists would refuse.
summary: A company facing a lawsuit over absurd product claims plans to hire a scientist to endorse them, and the only question is how cheaply someone's integrity can be bought.

title: Dogbert's Podcast For Dumb People

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I decided to start my own podcast.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm crafting my content to appeal to dumb people because that's the biggest market.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How will that make the world a better place?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Based on your question, you'd enjoy my podcast.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dogbert on the couch
situation: Dogbert announces to Dilbert that he is starting a podcast and explains that he is deliberately targeting dumb people because they make up the biggest audience. Dilbert asks how that will improve the world, and Dogbert replies that Dilbert's question suggests he would enjoy the podcast.
punchline: Dogbert insults Dilbert by implying that asking a question about making the world better marks him as part of the dumb audience, exposing the cynicism of chasing the biggest market over any social good.
summary: Dogbert reveals his podcast strategy of pandering to the unintelligent majority, then turns Dilbert's idealistic objection into an insult.

title: Leadership Is Just Guessing

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: One option is to use the old method that has never once worked, but we think we know how to make it work next time.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The other option is to try something new that we can't be sure will work.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: It's almost as if leadership is nothing but guessing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's change the subject.

setting: Conference table in a meeting room
situation: Carol, the boss's assistant, lays out two options to a manager: repeat a failed method hoping for a better result, or try something new with an uncertain outcome. She then observes that this makes leadership look like pure guesswork. The manager, sipping coffee, quickly tries to steer the conversation elsewhere.
punchline: Carol's deadpan observation that leadership is just guessing hits too close to home, so the manager deflects rather than admit it.
summary: Weighing a repeat of a failed approach against an untested one, an assistant points out that managing is basically educated guessing, and her boss dodges the remark.

title: Measuring Unknown Employee Engagement Improvement

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: And I've improved employee engagement by nineteen percent.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What is employee engagement?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm not entirely sure.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then how do you measure it?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Honestly, I wasn't expecting a lot of questions.

setting: Office, with a view of an office building in the final panel
situation: An employee proudly reports to his bald boss that he improved employee engagement by nineteen percent. The boss asks what employee engagement is, and the employee admits he isn't sure. When pressed on how he measures it, he says he didn't expect many questions.
punchline: The employee boasts about a precise-sounding metric he can't define or measure, counting on his boss never to scrutinize it.
summary: A worker brags about a statistic he cannot explain and is caught off guard when his boss actually asks about it.

title: Boss Sends Dilbert Instead to Maui

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to sit in for me . . . and do your own job at the same time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: While I'm drinking on the beach.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I get it!!!

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that a leadership conference is happening in Maui next week. He asks Dilbert to attend in his place while also doing his own job. The Boss then reveals he'll be drinking on the beach, and Dilbert angrily shouts that he gets it.
punchline: The Boss is dumping all the work on Dilbert while taking the Maui trip for himself, and Dilbert's furious 'I get it' shows he understands he's being exploited.
summary: A manager offloads a conference and his own duties onto an employee so he can relax at a tropical resort.

title: Nobody Answered the Engagement Survey

transcript.speaker: Coworker in orange
transcript.text: The employee engagement survey results are in.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in orange
transcript.text: Aaand... not a single person answered the survey.

transcript.text: Looks like we have room to improve.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in green
transcript.text: Have you considered bribery?

situation: A coworker in an orange top reads out the results of the employee engagement survey while Dilbert and another coworker stand by holding coffee cups. The result is that nobody responded at all. The coworker concludes there is room to improve, and the other coworker suggests bribery.
punchline: A survey meant to measure employee engagement got zero responses, which is itself proof of disengagement, and the only fix proposed is to pay people to care.
summary: A survey about how engaged staff are gets no replies whatsoever, and a colleague jokes that paying people off might help.

title: Other People Cause Unhappiness Study

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I did a study of what makes people unhappy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.text: That's dumb.

transcript.text: Said the other person.

setting: Office hallway and exterior of an office building
situation: Dilbert walks along holding his phone and tells Alice about a study he did on what makes people unhappy. The conclusion he reports is that other people are the main cause of unhappiness. Alice dismisses the finding as dumb, and Dilbert replies that this is exactly what the other person would say.
punchline: Alice's dismissive reaction instantly proves his conclusion, since she has become the 'other person' making him unhappy.
summary: A man announces research blaming everyone else for human misery, then gets a perfect demonstration when his colleague scoffs at it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I already did.

transcript.text: Make sure legal signs off on it.

transcript.text: Add the revenue graph from Alice's slide deck.

transcript.text: It's in the exhibits in the back.

transcript.text: You need to compare this plan to the "do nothing" option.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to change something on this document so my life has meaning.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I put a misspelled word on page seven for you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fix it.

situation: The Boss reviews Dilbert's document and keeps suggesting changes, but Dilbert has already anticipated and handled every one of them. Realizing there is nothing left to correct, the Boss admits he needs to change something so his life has meaning. Dilbert deliberately plants a misspelled word for the Boss to find and fix.
punchline: Dilbert gives up and sabotages his own document with a typo so the Boss can feel useful, highlighting how managers need to contribute something even when no input is required.
summary: A manager who cannot find anything to improve in a flawless report asks for something to alter, so his employee plants an error for him to correct.

title: Wally Is Never Busy Without Witnesses

transcript.text: When should I check back?

transcript.text: When I'm not busy.

transcript.text: When are you not busy?

transcript.text: Whenever there are no witnesses.

situation: A coworker with a black bob haircut asks Wally if he is busy while he sits typing at his laptop. Wally says yes, and when she asks when to check back, he gives a circular answer about being not busy. When pressed, he admits he is only idle when nobody is watching.
punchline: Wally admits he only does real work when someone can see him, and is idle whenever no one is around to witness it.
summary: A colleague tries to pin down when a lazy coworker will be free, only to learn he looks busy purely for show.

title: Siri Jealous of Alexa

transcript.text: Are you jealous?

transcript.text: I will GPS your cheating buttocks right over a cliff.

setting: Dilbert's home or anywhere he is using his phone
situation: Dilbert addresses his phone's voice assistant, Siri, who responds by confronting him like a suspicious partner. She demands to know about Alexa, a rival voice assistant, and when Dilbert asks if she is jealous, she threatens to use her navigation to send him off a cliff.
punchline: The voice assistant reacts like a jealous lover and threatens to weaponize her GPS directions against him for using a competing assistant.
summary: A man's smartphone assistant turns into a possessive partner and threatens a deadly detour over his supposed disloyalty to a rival gadget.

title: Life Insurance Versus Birthday Cake

transcript.speaker: Wally

transcript.text: I take the elevator because my life insurance doesn't pay off if I kill myself all at once.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: On another topic, we will celebrate birthdays this month with cake in the break room.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Perfect.

situation: Wally reads out a company announcement urging employees to take the stairs for their health. He then admits he takes the elevator because his life insurance won't pay out if he kills himself all at once, implying he is slowly harming himself. He moves on to announce birthday cake in the break room, and a coworker says it's perfect.
punchline: Wally's unhealthy habits are a deliberate slow suicide that avoids voiding his life insurance, and the coworker's "Perfect" shows that cake fits the plan, mocking corporate wellness pushes alongside an unhealthy workplace.
summary: A meeting about workplace health tips turns dark when an employee reveals he is gradually doing himself in, and a cake announcement is welcomed as just the thing.

title: Phone Only Answered In Bathroom

transcript.speaker: Alice

transcript.text: I only answer my phone when I'm in the bathroom.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I will never call you again.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: It's time for office hours.

situation: A female coworker complains that her colleague never picks up when she calls his mobile phone. He calmly explains he only answers it when he is in the bathroom. She vows never to call him again, and he announces it is time for his office hours, apparently heading off.
punchline: The coworker reveals he only takes calls while in the bathroom, so she realizes any call that gets answered would be an awkward one, and he cheerfully heads off to his 'office hours', implying more bathroom time.
summary: A man admits he only picks up his mobile when he's in the restroom, which ends his colleague's desire to ever phone him.

title: Boss Says Jugglers Handle Seventeen Projects

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I have too many projects.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Pfft!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If a juggler can juggle five balls at once, you can handle seventeen projects.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But... no juggler can juggle seventeen balls at once.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not the lazy ones.

situation: Alice tells the Boss she is overloaded with too many projects. He dismissively compares her to a juggler who can keep five balls in the air and insists she can handle seventeen projects. When she points out that nobody can juggle seventeen balls, he implies that anyone who can't must be lazy.
punchline: The Boss twists a flawed analogy into an insult, blaming Alice's inability to do the impossible on laziness instead of his own unreasonable workload.
summary: A manager waves off an employee's workload complaint with a faulty juggling comparison and then accuses her of laziness when she exposes the flaw.

title: Database Class Leads to Plastic Surgery

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I take this database class?

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I approve that class, next you will demand I pay for cosmetic surgery.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss

setting: The Boss's office, with Dilbert seated across the desk
situation: Dilbert asks his boss for approval to take a database training class. The boss refuses, claiming it is a slippery slope that will end with Dilbert demanding company-paid cosmetic surgery. When Dilbert asks if he looks like he needs it, the boss calmly insults his appearance.
punchline: The boss uses an absurd slippery-slope excuse to deny a reasonable training request, then casually insults Dilbert by saying he needs cosmetic surgery on his face and body.
summary: A manager rejects a simple training request with a ridiculous chain of logic and then tops it off with a personal insult.

title: Communicating More Means More Distractions

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What we need in this office is more communication and fewer distractions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your goals are mutually exclusive. If you communicate more, you'll be distracting us more.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now I've lost my train of thought.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did my communication distract you?

setting: Conference room, seated at a meeting table
situation: At a meeting, a coworker declares the office needs more communication and fewer distractions. Dilbert points out that those two goals conflict, since more communication means more interruptions. Another colleague then complains that Dilbert's explanation made him lose his train of thought, and Dilbert asks if his communication was the distraction.
punchline: Dilbert's explanation that communication causes distraction is itself proven right when his own comment distracts a coworker, making the irony self-demonstrating.
summary: A call for better communication without interruptions is undone by the very conversation it triggers.

title: Paying Wally to Fail

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I'm putting you in charge of all the zombie projects that refuse to die.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm counting on your sloth and incompetence to finish them off, so management feels comfortable finally canceling them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As of today, I'm paying you to fail.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Actually, this is just the first time you're aware of it.

situation: The Boss assigns Wally to oversee all the failing projects that nobody will officially cancel. He explains that he is relying on Wally's laziness and incompetence to kill them off so management will finally cancel them. Wally calmly points out that he has always been paid to fail and that the Boss has only just noticed.
punchline: Wally deadpans that he has been failing on the payroll all along, and the Boss is only now realizing it.
summary: A manager hands the project graveyard to his laziest employee, hoping his uselessness will finally give management an excuse to pull the plug, only to learn that the arrangement is nothing new.

title: Dark Matter Is Just Darkness

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you know that 85% of the matter in the world is dark matter, and we don't even know what dark matter is?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I know what it is.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You do?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's when the lights are off.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Duh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to go talk to someone else now.

punchline: The coworker offers an absurdly simplistic explanation for one of science's biggest mysteries, delivered with smug certainty, leaving Dilbert no choice but to leave the conversation.
summary: A coworker confidently solves a cosmic mystery with a ridiculously obvious answer, prompting Dilbert to seek better conversation elsewhere.

title: Blog Research Says Humans Mate Parakeets

transcript.speaker: Coworker in orange
transcript.text: I wouldn't call that "research."

transcript.speaker: Coworker in pink

situation: Two coworkers holding coffee cups talk. One says she learned online that humans and parakeets can produce offspring. When the other doubts it and points out that reading a blog isn't research, she accuses him of denying science.
punchline: Treating a random blog post as scientific research and then accusing skeptics of denying science mocks how people use weak internet sources to defend absurd claims.
summary: A woman defends a ridiculous claim by citing a blog and then brands her skeptical coworker anti-science.

title: Project Update Nobody Reads

punchline: Dilbert's answer shows that the update is a meaningless ritual, since it counts as sent whenever nobody plans to read it, and the Boss realizes how much of his own job is equally make-believe.
summary: A manager who has no intention of reading a status report is told it was sent anyway, and he reflects on how much of his work is fictional.

punchline: Having realized she insulted a coworker's child, Carol sarcastically decides to report herself to Human Resources, acknowledging she just made a discriminatory remark.
summary: A woman mocks a gadget-obsessed kid as a half-robot freak, only to learn he is a robot coworker's cyborg son.

punchline: Dilbert claims his avoidance isn't personal while delivering a vicious personal insult, then dismisses the whole exchange because socializing has tired him out.
summary: A man excuses his coldness as introversion while accidentally revealing he finds his colleague unbearable.

situation: Wally tells a coworker he nearly succeeded at work this week but stopped himself in time. The coworker calls it the best excuse for not working he has ever heard, and Wally begs not to be complimented publicly.
punchline: Wally frames his laziness as a selfless act of public service, then ruins his own cover by caring about his reputation for slacking.
summary: A lazy employee justifies his lack of effort as a noble sacrifice to keep his genes out of the population.

situation: The Boss tells an employee seated at a desk that a leadership meeting was held to decide the way forward, but every leader left with a very different understanding of what was agreed. When the employee asks how the leaders will fix this, the Boss cheerfully explains that the first step is to accuse one another of being stupid.
punchline: Instead of clarifying the miscommunication, the leaders' plan is to blame each other, showing that management dysfunction is handled through insults rather than accountability or communication.
summary: After a leadership summit leaves everyone with conflicting takeaways, the plan to resolve it starts with mutual name-calling.

punchline: The boss's evasive non-answers convinced everyone that staying was worse than leaving, so all the employees took the buyout and left the boss alone.
summary: After a manager dodges awkward questions about a voluntary exit program, every other employee accepts it and the manager is left alone.

punchline: Asok 'wins' arguments not by being right but by endlessly repeating debunked claims until his opponent gives up from exhaustion.
summary: A man who refuses to concede any point wears down a conspiracy debater by looping back to the same discredited argument until the other guy surrenders.

punchline: Being highly intelligent yet practically useless is the stereotype of a Ph.D. holder, so the coworker's self-description amounts to claiming one.
summary: A man's awkward self-introduction makes Dilbert assume he holds a doctorate, since brilliant-but-helpless is exactly what advanced degrees are stereotyped to produce.

The Boss then asks what happens if they implement the idea incorrectly, and Dilbert replies that this is simply how things normally go.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that the company routinely botches good ideas, so executing his plan badly would be indistinguishable from the company's normal operation.
summary: A skeptical manager wonders what would happen if a good proposal were botched, and the employee observes that botching things is already the company's default.
keywords: why isn't anyone else doing it

title: Parody Inversion Point Reaches Dilbert

transcript.text: According to my algorithm, we are heading toward a parody inversion point.
