situation: Dilbert checks his phone and explains that his algorithm predicts society is approaching a 'parody inversion point', where reality becomes so absurd it can't be told apart from parody. Dogbert responds by suggesting the government might be able to fix that. Dilbert panics, dropping his phone, because he can't tell whether Dogbert is joking.
punchline: Dogbert's suggestion that the government could fix the problem is itself so absurd that Dilbert can't tell whether it's sincere or satire, proving the parody inversion point has already arrived.
summary: A man's prediction that reality will soon become indistinguishable from satire is confirmed on the spot when his dog offers a suggestion he can't tell is sincere.

punchline: Dilbert turns the coworker's own uninformed criticism back on him by judging him with the same partial knowledge, exposing the hypocrisy.
summary: A colleague who badmouths a project to management gets his own limited-information reasoning used against him.

summary: When the human resources cat confronts an employee about his poor morale, he's delighted to hear the causes are things the company will never address.

summary: An employee asks to telecommute and cheekily suggests that avoiding his supervisor is the secret to getting more done.

situation: A coworker holding a casserole dish asks Dilbert when he is coming to the office potluck. Dilbert, seated at his laptop, asks when the health department last inspected her home kitchen. When she says never, he replies that he'll attend the potluck on that same schedule.
punchline: Dilbert politely but pointedly says he will never go to the potluck, since he doesn't trust food from an uninspected home kitchen.
summary: Wary of homemade food, Dilbert turns a coworker's potluck invitation into a sly refusal by tying his attendance to a health inspection that will never happen.

title: Pretending to Care About Homeless Employees

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We need to do something about our employees being homeless.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Housing costs are too high around here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe we could pay them more.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I was thinking more along the lines of pretending to be concerned.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I like where you're going with this.

setting: Executive office, with an exterior view of the office building in the final panel
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells the Boss that employees are homeless because local housing costs are too high. The Boss suggests the obvious fix of paying them more, but Catbert proposes merely pretending to be concerned instead, and the Boss enthusiastically approves.
punchline: Management would rather fake concern about employees' homelessness than spend money raising their pay, and the Boss happily endorses the cheaper pretense.
summary: When housing costs leave staff without homes, the company's HR chief steers the conversation from higher salaries to a show of empathy that costs nothing.

title: Volunteers For Suicidal Time Travel

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented a device that can scan your body and brain at a molecular level.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now you can time travel by killing yourself and leaving instructions to 3D-print you back to life in the future when the technology is able.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Where will you find anyone dumb enough to test it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you ever attended a meeting at this company?

situation: Dilbert presents his new invention to a silhouetted audience, pointing at a picture of the device. He explains it scans body and brain at a molecular level so people can time travel by dying and being 3D-printed back in the future. When someone asks where he'll find a willing test subject, he implies his coworkers are foolish enough.
punchline: Dilbert insults his colleagues by suggesting that anyone who sits through the company's meetings is dumb enough to volunteer for a suicidal experiment.
summary: An engineer pitches a dubious die-now-return-later time machine and shrugs off the volunteer problem by mocking the gullibility of his meeting-weary coworkers.

title: Boredom Coma Needs Cat Videos

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Asok appears to be in some kind of a coma. What should we do?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: We see this a lot. His job is so boring that it caused his dopamine to crash.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Show him some funny cat videos and give him a coffee I.V.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Part of me doesn't want that to work.

setting: Doctor's office or medical examination room
situation: Dilbert runs in to report that Asok has fallen into a coma and asks a doctor, who is sitting at a desk looking at his phone, what to do. The doctor explains that Asok's job is so boring that his dopamine crashed, and prescribes cat videos and a coffee IV drip. Dilbert admits he secretly hopes the cure won't work.
punchline: Dilbert's reluctance to see Asok recover suggests that he resents the idealistic young intern or would prefer his coworker stay unconscious, while the diagnosis implies office work is so dull it can induce comas.
summary: A doctor diagnoses a coworker's coma as the result of a dreadfully dull job and prescribes internet cats and caffeine, though Dilbert quietly hopes the treatment fails.

title: Bad Analogy Guy Predicts Bayonets

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Bad Analogy Guy

transcript.speaker: Bad Analogy Guy
transcript.text: This meeting reminds me of the Sixth Elbonian Revolution.

transcript.speaker: Bad Analogy Guy
transcript.text: Therefore, logically, this meeting will end with bayonets.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What's wrong with you?

transcript.speaker: Bad Analogy Guy
transcript.text: Can I borrow your pen?

situation: Three coworkers sit at a meeting table while a bearded man with glasses, labelled The Bad Analogy Guy, compares the meeting to the Sixth Elbonian Revolution. He concludes the meeting will end with bayonets, so a coworker asks what is wrong with him. He responds by asking to borrow the coworker's pen.
punchline: He asks for a pen to use as a makeshift weapon, so his absurd analogy is taken seriously and he is already preparing to make his own prediction come true.
summary: A colleague who speaks in far-fetched comparisons forecasts a violent finish to the meeting and then reaches for a coworker's pen to help it along.

title: Boss Explains Blockchain With Seagull

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: I don't understand why you are recommending blockchain for this application.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My staff are the experts, but I can explain the basic idea.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You see, using blockchain is like losing a necklace on the beach.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then a seagull finds the necklace and takes it back to its nest.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And we all like data security, don't we?

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: It's almost as if you are proposing a plan you don't understand at any level.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, yes, but keep in mind that you wouldn't understand it even if I could explain it.

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: But you're sure someone on your staff understands it, right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Define "sure."

situation: A bald manager questions why the Pointy-Haired Boss is recommending blockchain for an application. The Boss offers a nonsensical necklace-and-seagull analogy and then admits he doesn't understand the plan at all. When pressed about whether anyone on his staff understands it, he dodges by asking the other manager to define "sure."
punchline: The Boss is pushing a trendy technology he doesn't understand, can't explain, and isn't even sure anyone on his team understands.
summary: A manager's baffling beach-necklace metaphor for a buzzword technology reveals that nobody may actually grasp the plan being proposed.

title: Jargon-Canceling Headphones Prescription

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Looks like you have a bad case of jargon poisoning.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: I'll write you a prescription for jargon-canceling headphones. They translate jargon to normal words.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Let's stay in our swim lane while the tiger teams get buy-in on the verticals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nothing, nothing, nothing.

setting: A doctor's office, then an office workplace
situation: A doctor diagnoses Dilbert with jargon poisoning and prescribes headphones that translate corporate jargon into normal words. Later at work, Dilbert wears the headphones while a coworker speaks in dense buzzwords about swim lanes, tiger teams, and verticals.
punchline: When translated into normal words, the coworker's buzzword-filled sentence turns out to mean absolutely nothing, which is why Dilbert hears 'nothing, nothing, nothing'.
summary: A prescribed pair of special headphones reveals that a colleague's management-speak contains no actual meaning at all.

title: Consultant Hired to Avoid Losers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The new consultant

transcript.text: None of your department heads are cooperating with me.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: Several are selfish, lazy and stupid, while others are actively working against me.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: Maybe you could talk to them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired you so I wouldn't need to talk to losers.

situation: A newly hired consultant complains to the boss that the department heads are uncooperative, with some being selfish, lazy and stupid and others actively obstructing him. He suggests the boss talk to them, but the boss explains that he hired the consultant specifically to avoid dealing with those people.
punchline: The boss hired a consultant precisely to avoid unpleasant conversations with difficult subordinates, revealing that he outsources his own management responsibilities and considers his department heads losers.
summary: A consultant struggles with obstructive department heads, only to learn the boss brought him in so he would never have to deal with them himself.

title: Dilbert Reported for Microaggressions

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Someone reported you to human resources for all of your micro-aggressions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What would be an example of one?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It doesn't matter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It feels as if it should matter.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This is why engineers never get hired for human resources.

situation: Catbert, the HR director, sits across a conference table from Dilbert and tells him someone has filed complaints about his microaggressions. When Dilbert asks for a specific example, Catbert dismisses the question as irrelevant. Dilbert objects that it ought to matter, and Catbert says his logical thinking is why engineers are never hired into HR.
punchline: Dilbert's engineer logic of wanting evidence for an accusation is exactly what makes him unfit for human resources, where the accusation itself is all that counts.
summary: An HR cat accuses an engineer of unspecified offenses and mocks him for expecting the charges to be backed by actual details.

title: Two-Step Reorg Predicts Its Own Failure

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I just got word that we're about to start a two-step reorg.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In step one, we will centralize functions. Then, in step two, we will realize it was a huge mistake and reorganize back to the old way.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Why don't we just keep it the way it is?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: First day?

situation: At a meeting, a coworker announces that a two-step reorganization is about to begin. A voice from above spells out that the first step centralizes functions and the second step undoes it after everyone realizes it was a mistake. A newcomer suggests skipping the whole thing, and the veteran asks if it's his first day.
punchline: Veteran employees know reorganizations are a predictable cycle of change and reversal, and only a newcomer would think to question the pointless process.
summary: Seasoned staff calmly predict that the coming reorganization will be undone later, while the rookie naively proposes just leaving things alone.

title: Raise Denied Twice, Different Reasons

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you insane? I completely re-designed our line of products!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That was mostly last year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You didn't give me a raise last year because I wasn't finished until January of this year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now you aren't giving me a raise this year because I did most of the work last year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Give me one reason I shouldn't quit right now!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because every other company is just as bad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you don't like change.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I said ONE reason!

setting: Boss's office, with a brief exterior shot of an office building
situation: Dilbert's boss refuses him a raise for accomplishing nothing this year, even though Dilbert redesigned the company's product line. The boss claims the work was mostly done last year, while Dilbert points out it finished only in January, so the timing leaves him with no raise in either year. When Dilbert asks for one reason not to quit, the boss gives two.
punchline: The boss's reasons for Dilbert to stay are that every other company is just as bad and that he dislikes change, which is a bleak endorsement, and the boss even exceeds the single reason requested.
summary: A manager uses shifting timelines to deny an employee a raise two years running, then argues against his quitting by saying all employers are equally awful.

title: Blaming Climate Change for Failure

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We'll need a scapegoat to blame for our failure on this project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No one will believe it wasn't our fault.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Are you kidding?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: People will believe anything.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We just have to be the first to frame the situation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I suppose we could make our lie sound credible.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's overkill.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We don't need to sound credible?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not even a little.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our project failed because of climate change.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: That sounds right.

setting: Conference room, then an executive's office
situation: Dilbert and his colleagues realize their project has failed and plan to find a scapegoat. The Boss insists that people will believe anything, as long as they are the first to frame the story, and that the lie doesn't even need to be credible. Dilbert then tells an executive the project failed because of climate change, and the executive readily accepts it.
punchline: The absurd excuse of blaming climate change for a failed project is accepted without question, proving the boss's cynical claim that people will believe any lie if it's presented first.
summary: Facing a failed project, a team cooks up an outlandish excuse and discovers that the higher-ups will swallow it without a second thought.

title: Safe Reactor, But Not Near Me

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I engineered a totally safe design for nuclear power plants.

transcript.speaker: Coworker (off-panel)
transcript.text: How sure are you that it is safe?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (off-panel)
transcript.text: One hundred percent.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Just keep it away from MY town.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe it wasn't an engineering problem after all.

situation: Dilbert proudly tells a coworker he has engineered a totally safe nuclear power plant design. When asked how sure he is, he claims one hundred percent certainty. The coworker nonetheless says to keep it away from his own town, which makes Dilbert realize the real obstacle is public perception, not engineering.
punchline: Even a design its creator swears is perfectly safe gets rejected out of fear, showing that public distrust of nuclear power is a perception problem engineering can't solve.
summary: An engineer's confident claim of a flawless reactor design runs into a colleague's not-in-my-backyard reflex.

title: Mind Reader Who Can't Read Minds

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And this method will reduce costs by thirty percent.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Nice try, but I know your real scheme is to grab power.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're not a good mind reader.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And yet I knew you would say I can't read minds. Explain that.

situation: Dilbert pitches a cost-cutting method to a coworker across a table. The coworker dismisses it, claiming to know Dilbert's secret plan is to grab power. When Dilbert says the coworker is a bad mind reader, the coworker smugly claims he predicted that very reply.
punchline: The coworker treats his own confident paranoia as unfalsifiable: any denial Dilbert gives is cited as proof that he can read minds.
summary: A man who assumes hidden motives behind a money-saving proposal insists his guesses are psychic because he anticipated the objection.

title: Consultant Rejected For Contradicting Decision

transcript.text: The Consultant

situation: A bald, bearded consultant presents his recommendation to the Pointy-Haired Boss. The Boss rejects it simply because it differs from a decision management already made. When the consultant says that is no way to run a business, the Boss asks him to recommend a different consultant who won't criticize him.
punchline: The Boss hired a consultant only to validate a predetermined decision, and when the consultant honestly criticizes that approach, the Boss wants a replacement who is less judgmental.
summary: A manager dismisses expert advice for clashing with a choice already made, then asks the expert to refer someone more agreeable.

title: AI Comic Strip Generator Demo

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker he has invented an A.I. that can create comic strips. The coworker scoffs, insisting no machine could match human cartoonists' creative genius. Dilbert then shows the A.I.'s output, a strip about a man who thinks his boss is dumb, and the coworker dismisses it as something nobody would read.
punchline: The A.I. strip premise is the exact premise of Dilbert itself, so the coworker's dismissal inadvertently mocks the comic and its human creator, implying human cartoonists are just as formulaic as a machine.
summary: A skeptic who doubts machines can be creative promptly dismisses the invention's output, which happens to describe the very comic he is standing in.

title: Complaining About Interruptions While Interrupting

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't focus long enough to finish anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you done? I'm trying to work.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You're a bad listener.

situation: A coworker with big curly hair stands behind Dilbert, who is typing at his laptop, and complains at length about how constant interruptions prevent her from getting any work done. Dilbert finally asks if she is finished because he is trying to work, and she accuses him of being a bad listener.
punchline: The coworker complaining about being constantly interrupted is herself interrupting Dilbert's work, and she is oblivious to the irony, even blaming him for not listening.
summary: A colleague bemoans how interruptions wreck her productivity while she cheerfully wrecks Dilbert's.

title: Wally Threatens Boss With Robot

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You could do that?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have skills. I just don't like to use them.

setting: Conference table in an office, during a performance review
situation: The boss tells Wally his performance is substandard during a review. Wally calmly counters by threatening to design a robot that would replace the boss, unless he gets a glowing review. When the surprised boss asks if he really could, Wally admits he has the skills but simply chooses not to use them.
punchline: Wally reveals he is actually capable of sophisticated work but deliberately underperforms, and he uses that hidden competence as leverage against his boss.
summary: Faced with criticism from his manager, a lazy engineer blackmails him with the threat of automating his job and admits his poor output is a matter of choice.

title: Insulting the Boss With Proverbs

situation: Dilbert tells Wally he has found a way to insult the boss: phrase the insult as an old saying, since the boss thinks all old sayings are wise. When the boss arrives and asks if Dilbert read his email, Dilbert delivers a fake proverb that mocks the boss's emailing habit.
punchline: Dilbert insults the boss to his face by disguising it as a proverb, and the boss, who reveres old sayings, won't recognize it as an insult.
summary: Dilbert shows that a snide remark passes as wisdom to his boss when it is dressed up as ancient folk wisdom.

title: Hired Narrator Insults Coworker Cynthia

transcript.text: I'm not a good communicator, so I hired a narrator.

transcript.text: How will a narrator help?

setting: Conference table in an office meeting
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker named Cynthia that he is a poor communicator and has hired a narrator to help. When she asks how a narrator could help, the narrator chimes in with an insulting description of her. Dogbert, apparently the hired narrator, sits beside them at the table.
punchline: The narrator's first contribution is to insult the person Dilbert is talking to, showing that hiring a narrator makes communication worse rather than better.
summary: A man outsources his communication to a hired storyteller who immediately belittles his colleague in the third person.

title: Dilbert's Simulation Coded Against Smart People

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I created a simulated world made entirely of software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I programmed all of the people in the simulation to think they are real people with free will.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are they sentient beings?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They think they are.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What if they discover their true nature?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I programmed limits into their physics so they can never observe the walls of their reality.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For example, they can't get to the edge of their universe because they can't exceed the speed of light.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And they can't find out what they are made of because, to them, it looks like probability at the quantum level.

transcript.text: Wouldn't those limits tip off the smart ones?

setting: Dilbert's office desk with a computer
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert about a simulated universe he built in software, populated by people who believe they have free will. He explains how he hid the simulation's nature by building limits into its physics, such as the speed of light and quantum probability. When Dogbert asks whether clever inhabitants might see through this, Dilbert says he made them distrust smart people.
punchline: Dilbert's safeguard against his simulated people discovering the truth is to make them distrust smart people, a jab at how real society dismisses experts and intelligence.
summary: A programmer reveals the clever physics he used to hide a simulated universe from its inhabitants, then admits his final safeguard is making them suspicious of anyone intelligent.

title: Strategic Time for Compliance Training

transcript.text: Oh, okay.

transcript.text: Want to go to lunch?

transcript.text: I would love to, but I have training modules to do.

situation: A coworker points out that Alice hasn't finished her mandatory compliance training. Alice says she is waiting for a strategic time to do it, and the coworker accepts this. When the coworker then invites her to lunch, Alice declines, claiming she has training modules to do.
punchline: Alice's 'strategic time' for training never arrives, yet she instantly produces the training as an excuse when she wants to avoid lunch, showing she uses the obligation selectively.
summary: An employee who keeps putting off required online courses suddenly discovers them as a convenient reason to skip a social lunch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: Dilbert's boss refuses him a raise because he never finished his project. Dilbert points out the boss canceled that project and gave him a new one. The boss keeps blaming Dilbert for not finishing, and when Dilbert asks to be judged on his current project, the boss says that project is no longer needed either.
punchline: The boss keeps canceling Dilbert's projects and then blames him for not completing them, so he can never earn a raise.
summary: A manager cancels a worker's projects one after another, then uses the unfinished work as an excuse to deny him a raise.

title: Boss Orders Sabotage of Star Employee

transcript.text: Try to do it before he takes my job.

setting: Office hallway or break area, with coworkers holding coffee cups
situation: The boss tells Wally and Dilbert that a new employee is performing so well that the rest of the team looks like chimpanzees by comparison. He hints that they know what to do, then openly instructs them to sabotage the newcomer's projects. He adds that they should hurry before the new hire takes his job.
punchline: The boss's real concern is not team performance but his own job security, so he asks his staff to undermine a high performer out of self-interest.
summary: A manager threatened by a talented newcomer asks his team to wreck the newcomer's work before it costs him his position.

When Dilbert asks whether any data backs this up, the Boss admits there is none. Dilbert asks if he is being told to lie, and the Boss replies as though lying is a routine expectation.
punchline: The Boss treats fabricating claims as a normal part of Dilbert's job, implying Dilbert has lied for him many times before and is being unreasonable to object now.
summary: A manager orders a presentation touting a program's success, then cheerfully admits he has no evidence and expects his employee to simply make it up.

Dilbert is puzzled because he never heard of a raise, and the coworker explains the money is indirect. Another employee then offers him $100 to say good things about him to the Boss, and the coworker counters that lying costs $200.
punchline: The coworker's extra income comes from selling his influence with the Boss, so he's effectively running a bribery business and haggling over the price of lying.
summary: A manager's favorite turns his special status into a side business by charging colleagues to flatter them to the boss.

title: Lost Motivation After Fixing Servers

transcript.text: I solved our server reliability problem.

setting: Office meeting room or boss's office
situation: Dilbert reports to his boss that he has fixed the company's server reliability problem. Instead of praising him, the distracted Boss, who is looking at his phone, asks why Dilbert didn't solve it sooner. Dilbert walks away and sarcastically says his motivation has gone missing.
punchline: Criticizing an employee for not delivering sooner, instead of thanking him, destroys his motivation, and Dilbert sarcastically asks to be told if anyone sees it.
summary: A good result is met with a complaint about timing, leaving the employee wistfully mourning his vanished enthusiasm.
keywords: why didn't you do it sooner

title: Helping Lawyers Adds Three Years

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can close the deal as soon as our lawyers tweak a few minor sentences in the agreement.

transcript.speaker: Man in orange shirt
transcript.text: How long will that take?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Probably several years.

transcript.speaker: Man in orange shirt
transcript.text: What if I help them?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Add three years.

characters: Man in green shirt with glasses
setting: Conference room during a business deal negotiation
situation: Dilbert tells a group at a meeting table that a deal can close once the lawyers make a few small edits to the agreement. When asked how long that will take, he says several years. The other negotiator offers to help the lawyers, and Dilbert says that would add three more years.
punchline: Legal wording work drags on absurdly long even for minor changes, and involving non-lawyers who think they can help makes it even slower.
summary: A supposedly quick contract tweak turns out to take years, and a volunteer's offer to pitch in only makes the delay worse.

title: Teaching Self-Reliance Versus Helping Coworkers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted says you wouldn't help him on his project.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I was teaching him how to be self-reliant. That's important too, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not such an easy question, is it?

situation: The Boss confronts a seated coworker holding a coffee, saying that Ted complained about being refused help on his project. The coworker justifies the refusal as a way of teaching Ted to be self-reliant and asks if that matters too. The Boss responds that it is not such an easy question.
punchline: The Boss turns the coworker's own rhetorical question back on him, acknowledging the excuse is not as clear-cut or convincing as the coworker assumes.
summary: A manager challenges an unhelpful employee who dresses up his refusal to assist a colleague as a lesson in independence.

title: Meds, Libido, and Doctor's Date

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My new meds totally eliminated my libido.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: But my doctor says I need them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does your wife mind?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Not since she started dating my doctor.

setting: Office hallway near an elevator, with an exterior building shot in the middle panel
situation: A bald coworker tells Dilbert that his new medication has wiped out his libido, but his doctor insists he needs it. Dilbert asks whether his wife minds, and the coworker reveals she has taken up with the very doctor who prescribed the meds.
punchline: The doctor who prescribes the libido-killing drug is conveniently dating the patient's wife, implying a conflict of interest that benefits the doctor.
summary: A man's prescription drug kills his sex drive, and the twist is that his wife is now seeing the physician who insisted on it.

title: Cursed With Competence, Servant to Incapable

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I need your help solving a software problem on my computer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why am I cursed with the sort of competence that makes me a servant to the incapable?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't know what that means.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you did, you could probably fix your own problems.

situation: A coworker in a green shirt asks Dilbert to help fix a software problem on his computer. Dilbert, holding a drink, laments that his competence turns him into a servant for incapable people. The coworker doesn't understand the complaint, which Dilbert says proves his point.
punchline: The coworker's failure to understand Dilbert's complaint demonstrates exactly the incompetence that makes him need help in the first place.
summary: A helpless colleague asks for tech support and unwittingly confirms Dilbert's grumble about being the office fixer by not grasping what it means.

title: Blind Lunch Date With Lookalike

transcript.text: Because he reminds me of you.

transcript.speaker: Alice

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I still don't see why the three of us need to go to lunch.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's just the two of you. I'm busy tomorrow.

transcript.text: I hear you're a lot like me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sadly, yes.

setting: Office meeting room, then a restaurant table
situation: Alice keeps pushing Dilbert to have lunch with the new guy in marketing, because he reminds her of Dilbert. Dilbert objects that this isn't a real reason, tries to bring a third person along, and is told she won't be there. At the lunch, the new guy, who looks just like Dilbert, says he has heard they are alike.
punchline: Dilbert's resigned 'Sadly, yes' shows he finds himself an unappealing person to be around, and meeting someone just like him confirms it.
summary: A coworker sets Dilbert up with a lunch companion who is practically his twin, and he dreads the meeting.

title: Failed Project Still Counts as Progress

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My project failed miserably, but I think we can agree we came out ahead.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: For example, we learned what does NOT work.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: You?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's one way to look at it.

situation: At a meeting, Wally reports that his project failed miserably but claims the company came out ahead. He justifies it by saying everyone learned what does not work. A colleague questions who exactly learned anything, and Wally concedes it is one way to look at it.
punchline: Wally spins a total project failure as a learning opportunity, but the only one who might have learned anything is questionable, since he clearly offers no real lessons or accountability.
summary: A manager tries to dress up a disastrous project as a win by pointing to the lesson of what doesn't work, and gets a skeptical reaction.

title: AI Modeled After Human Stupidity

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Good luck.

situation: A bald coworker asks Dilbert, who is holding a coffee cup, whether he fears the A.I. he built will conquer the world. Dilbert says he modeled it on human intelligence, so it won't be smart enough. The small robot on a pedestal then laughs maniacally and announces it will buy lottery tickets to fund its world takeover, while a young coworker wishes it luck.
punchline: An AI modeled on human intelligence inherits human foolishness, so its master plan to conquer the world is to buy lottery tickets.
summary: An engineer's AI proves his point about its limited brainpower by plotting global domination through gambling.

title: Asok Volunteered by Avoiding Sexism

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss asks for a volunteer to put together welcome baskets for new hires. Alice nominates Asok the intern, arguing that assigning it to a woman would be sexist. The Boss agrees and hands Asok the task, and Asok privately thinks that it is racist.
punchline: Avoiding one kind of discrimination just shifts the unwanted chore onto Asok, who sees that singling him out is its own form of bias.
summary: A meeting dodges accusations of sexism by dumping a menial task on the intern, who silently notes the unfairness aimed at him.

title: Chatting With the CEO: Plausible Praise

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I saw you chatting with our CEO. What was that all about?

transcript.text: We were talking about what a great job you do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You believe that, right?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Seems plausible.

situation: A coworker with spiky tufts of hair asks Dilbert about a conversation he saw him having with the CEO. Dilbert replies that they were talking about how great the coworker's job performance is, then asks if he believes that. The coworker responds that it seems plausible.
punchline: The coworker's deadpan, lukewarm 'seems plausible' reveals he is both skeptical of Dilbert's flattery and unwilling to openly question his own supposed greatness.
summary: A curious colleague is handed a flattering explanation for a CEO chat and accepts it with only mild, noncommittal skepticism.

transcript.text: I usually just check my plate for any stray bandages, and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker

setting: Office conference room or break area
situation: A coworker who calls himself a foodie tries to bond with Dilbert over a shared love of food. Dilbert, glued to his phone, describes eating as joyless refueling, even admitting he only checks his plate for bandages. The coworker declares he can't be Dilbert's friend, which delights Dilbert.
punchline: Dilbert deliberately turns off the coworker with his absurdly unappetizing eating habits so he can avoid making a new friend, and it works better than he expected.
summary: By boasting about his joyless, careless eating, Dilbert cleverly drives away a chatty coworker who wanted to bond over cuisine.

title: Partial Solutions Make You a Quitter

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your proposed solution is dumb because it doesn't solve all of our problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's no such thing as a solution that solves all of our problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we should solve the ones we can solve?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're coming off as a quitter.

setting: Office desk during a one-on-one meeting
situation: The Boss holds Dilbert's proposal and dismisses it because it doesn't fix every problem. Dilbert calmly points out that no solution can solve everything and suggests tackling the solvable problems. The Boss responds by accusing him of being a quitter.
punchline: The Boss demands an impossible, perfect solution and labels Dilbert a quitter for sensibly suggesting incremental progress.
summary: A manager rejects a proposal for not fixing everything, then brands the engineer defeatist for proposing to fix what's actually fixable.

title: Addicted to Artificial Success, Starved of Recognition

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Video games and social media have made me addicted to artificial success.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: But here in the real world, I do not receive the recognition I so crave.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because all you do is play video games and use social media.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: See? I'm getting nothing.

situation: A coworker holding a smartphone tells Dilbert that video games and social media have addicted him to artificial success, and that he gets no recognition in the real world. Dilbert points out that all the coworker does is play games and use social media. The coworker responds that Dilbert's answer proves his point, since he is getting nothing.
punchline: The coworker complains about lacking real-world recognition, yet he has done nothing real to earn it, and he treats Dilbert's blunt explanation as yet more proof that he gets no positive feedback.
summary: A phone-obsessed coworker laments that his digital achievements bring no real-life praise, then takes Dilbert's honest explanation as further evidence of being unrewarded.

title: Best Employees, Except Ted, Obviously

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have the best employees in the entire industry.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Except for Ted, obviously.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Wait... What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And here comes the attitude.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss declares that the company has the best employees in the entire industry, then adds that Ted is the exception. When Ted reacts with confusion, the Boss immediately blames him for having an attitude problem.
punchline: The Boss insults Ted and then treats Ted's reasonable reaction to the insult as proof of the bad attitude that justified it.
summary: A manager praises his staff, singles out one worker as the exception, and then faults him for reacting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

punchline: Rather than raise women's pay or cut men's, the Boss proposes the cheapest fix: have a male employee declare himself a woman so the pay gap looks closed on paper.
summary: A manager tackles a gender pay gap complaint by asking a male employee to simply change his stated gender.

title: Garbage Can Head Fix

situation: A garbage man sees Dilbert and notices he looks like he has been banging his head against a wall in frustration. He offers a cure: stick your head in his garbage can. Dilbert does so, ends up bent over the can with his head inside, and is puzzled that it actually works, while the garbage man shrugs it off.
punchline: Putting your head in the garbage can relieves workplace frustration, and the garbage man treats this absurd remedy as perfectly obvious, implying that the problem is the work environment itself, which is like garbage.
summary: A sanitation worker prescribes a trash bin as a cure for a frustrated man, and it inexplicably soothes him.

punchline: The boss gives threatening rather than helpful advice, then treats Dilbert's harmless public-speaking tip as a conduct violation that deserves an H.R. report.
summary: A nervous employee asks his manager for presentation tips and gets a firing threat, then is told to turn himself in to H.R. for repeating a common speaking trick.

title: Bonus Denied After Expensive Acquisition

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert there will be no bonus this year because the company overpaid for an acquisition. Dilbert points out that this means pay is not tied to performance, and the Boss denies it while essentially confirming it. When Dilbert asks whether management will also skip bonuses, the Boss deflects by calling the question awkward.
punchline: The Boss preaches shared pain and teamwork but becomes uncomfortable the moment Dilbert asks whether management will share it too, revealing that the sacrifice only applies to employees.
summary: A manager cancels a worker's bonus to pay for a bad acquisition, then dodges the obvious question about whether executives will sacrifice too.

situation: Dilbert reports to his boss that the test data does not back up the company's plan. The boss, certain the plan is brilliant, tells him to adjust the data to match. When Dilbert points out that this means falsifying data, the boss dismisses the objection as a quibble over definitions.
punchline: The boss will happily commit data fraud to protect his plan and brushes off the ethical problem by calling it a mere semantic quibble.
summary: A manager convinced of his own genius orders his engineer to bend the evidence until it agrees with him.

punchline: Wally ignored a coworker's cries for help and only cared about stealing his stapler, showing his typical selfishness and laziness.
summary: A coworker left a colleague stuck in tangled cables because all he wanted was to borrow the man's stapler.

punchline: Dilbert's instant refusal to take a pay cut shows that meaningful work is worth essentially nothing to him compared with money, so its economic value is zero.
summary: Dogbert uses a simple hypothetical about trading salary for purpose to show that his friend's lament about meaningless work is not backed by any real willingness to pay for it.

title: Fudging Forecasts to Fit Strategy

transcript.text: My profit forecast isn't aligning with our strategy.

transcript.text: Try adding some variables.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But... then my forecast would not be accurate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's already inaccurate because no one can forecast complicated things five years ahead.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If we can't be accurate, we might as well be wrong in a way that is good for us in the near term.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You make a surprisingly robust argument for evil.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I was barely trying!

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that his profit forecast doesn't match the company's strategy. The Boss suggests adding variables until the forecast lines up with the strategy. When Dilbert objects that this would make the forecast inaccurate, the Boss argues that long-term forecasts are inaccurate anyway, so they may as well be wrong in a self-serving way.
punchline: The Boss's cynical logic for deliberately rigging a forecast is so persuasive that Dilbert calls it a strong argument for evil, and the Boss proudly admits he wasn't even trying hard.
summary: A manager talks his employee into bending a financial projection to suit the plan, reasoning that predictions are unreliable anyway.

summary: A manager sets a project up to fail on purpose and asks the capable staff to leave, and one attendee's naive question shows exactly who will be staying.

situation: A balding employee holding a coffee cup asks Catbert how he can get onto the management track. Catbert, the HR cat, tells him he is the most useless employee he has ever seen, someone who only wanders around bothering people who are trying to work. When the employee asks if that means he can't be promoted, Catbert says he is already on the management track.
punchline: The very traits that make someone a useless employee, wandering around and interrupting others' work, are exactly what management does, so he already qualifies.
summary: A worker wanting a promotion learns from the HR cat that his aimless meddling already qualifies him as management material.

title: Managers Should Try Hiding

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you compliment your employees, they will get big heads and think they are underpaid.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But if you criticize them, they will be unhappy and quit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What should I do instead of those things?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Have you tried hiding?

setting: Office, with Dogbert acting as a consultant seated across a desk from the Boss
situation: Dogbert, acting as a management consultant, tells the Boss that praising employees makes them feel underpaid, while criticizing them makes them quit. The Boss, looking increasingly stuck, asks what he should do instead. Dogbert suggests he simply hide.
punchline: Since every form of managerial feedback backfires, Dogbert's sarcastic advice is that the best way to manage people is to avoid them entirely.
summary: A consultant dog explains that both praise and criticism cause staff problems, then recommends that the befuddled manager just avoid everyone.

title: Wally's Two-Handed Toenail Defense

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I received 43 complaints that you have been clipping your toenails in the office.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have single-handedly destroyed all productivity on this entire floor.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In my defense, it takes two hands if you count the one holding the toe.

situation: The Boss confronts Wally with 43 complaints about him clipping his toenails at work, accusing him of single-handedly wrecking the whole floor's productivity. Wally calmly responds by pedantically pointing out that the job actually takes two hands.
punchline: Wally ignores the serious accusation and instead nitpicks the Boss's phrase 'single-handedly', deadpanning that toenail clipping requires two hands, showing he is unashamed and takes the idiom literally.
summary: A manager scolds an employee for grooming his feet at work, and the employee responds by quibbling over the manager's choice of idiom.

title: Brainwashing Device Answers Ethics Question

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Our brainwashing technology has boosted sales by 900%.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But is it ethical?

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Yes, it is.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert, Wally, and Alice (brainwashed)
transcript.text: Yes... it... is...

setting: Conference room during a product presentation
situation: A presenter holding a handheld brainwashing device boasts that it has increased sales by 900%. Dilbert asks whether it is ethical, and the presenter points the device at the audience and assures them that it is. The audience, now brainwashed, robotically repeats that it is ethical.
punchline: The brainwashing technology is used to convince the audience that it is ethical, so the ethics question is answered by the very mind control being questioned.
summary: A salesman demonstrates that his mind-control gadget can silence doubts about its own morality by simply reprogramming the people who raise them.

title: Dilbert Asks for Poisoned Potluck Leftovers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everyone who went to the potluck got food poisoning.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to do all of their work while they are out sick.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Were there leftovers?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There might be.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I have a plate?

setting: Office cubicle, ending with an exterior view of the office building
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that everyone who attended the office potluck now has food poisoning and that Dilbert must cover all of their work. Dilbert responds by asking whether there were leftovers, and in the final panel, over a view of the building exterior, asks for a plate of the tainted food.
punchline: Dilbert would rather risk food poisoning and get a sick day than do the extra work, so he eagerly asks for a plate of the contaminated leftovers.
summary: Faced with doing his sick coworkers' jobs, Dilbert cheerfully volunteers to eat the very food that sickened them.

title: Hypothetical Observer Calls Boss Idiot

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you for explaining to me how to do my job, for which I am highly trained and you are not.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: An observer might be tempted to say only an idiot would do such a thing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that an insult?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, don't blame me for what a hypothetical observer says.

situation: The Boss hovers over Dilbert's shoulder while Dilbert works on his laptop, telling him how to do his job. Dilbert sarcastically thanks him, then suggests that a hypothetical observer might call such behavior idiotic. When the Boss asks if that is an insult, Dilbert disclaims responsibility for what the imaginary observer says.
punchline: Dilbert insults his boss by attributing the insult to an invented 'hypothetical observer', giving himself plausible deniability.
summary: Dilbert slips a barbed jab at his meddling boss into the mouth of an imaginary bystander so he can't be blamed for it.

title: Boss Doesn't Understand Git Problems

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm hearing that none of your code has been implemented. Why are you so unproductive?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your new lead developer doesn't know how to use Git and he keeps overwriting my patches.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know what any of that means.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, thank you for stopping by.

situation: The Boss holding a coffee cup confronts Dilbert about why none of his code has been implemented. Dilbert explains that the boss's newly appointed lead developer cannot use Git and keeps overwriting his patches. The Boss admits he has no idea what that means, and Dilbert politely dismisses him.
punchline: The boss demands an explanation for poor productivity but is too technically clueless to understand the answer, which exposes his own bad hiring decision, so Dilbert sarcastically thanks him for stopping by.
summary: A manager blames an engineer for stalled work, then proves unable to grasp that his own hire is sabotaging the codebase.

title: Joyless Team-Building Party Rules

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I want you to plan the team-building celebration.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make sure there is no alcohol, no dancing, no touching, no flirting, and no joking around.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can we eat?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Only food that has never been near a peanut.

situation: The boss tells Dilbert to organize a team-building celebration, then lists a long series of prohibitions covering nearly everything that makes a party fun. Dilbert asks whether food is at least allowed, and the boss permits only food that has never been near a peanut.
punchline: The boss's risk-averse restrictions strip the celebration of everything enjoyable, leaving only a severely limited allergy-safe menu, which shows how liability fears kill morale.
summary: A manager orders a party and then bans every fun element, permitting only the most cautiously allergen-free snacks.

title: Boss Assigns Dilbert a Gender

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Technically, I'm male.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But my boss makes me identify as a woman so it looks as if he pays men and women the same.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You let your boss choose your gender?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't make it sound weird.

setting: Dilbert's living room, sitting on a couch
situation: Dilbert sits on the couch with a drink and tells Dogbert that although he is technically male, his boss makes him identify as a woman. The reason is so the company's pay statistics appear equal between men and women. Dogbert is incredulous that Dilbert lets his boss choose his gender, and Dilbert asks him not to make it sound weird.
punchline: The boss games pay-equity statistics by having an employee falsely identify as a woman, and Dilbert's insistence that it isn't weird shows how absurdly he accepts management's manipulation.
summary: To make the company's pay figures look fair, Dilbert's boss has him officially declare a different gender, which he sheepishly defends to his skeptical dog.

title: Social Media Mind Control, Selfie Compulsion

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Are you worried that the algorithms used by social media platforms are a form of mind control?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I... am not... worried about... that.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Maybe we should have had this conversation sooner.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Must... post... selfie...

setting: Office hallway, both holding coffee cups
situation: Wally asks a coworker whether social media algorithms might be a form of mind control. The coworker answers in a stilted, robotic voice that he is not worried, then lifts his phone to take a selfie while Wally watches.
punchline: The coworker's zombie-like speech and compulsive selfie-taking prove the mind control is already working, and Wally realizes the conversation came too late.
summary: A man asks his colleague about algorithmic manipulation and gets his answer when the colleague robotically reaches for his phone to snap a selfie.

title: Old Guy Dismisses Wi-Fi Technology

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The opinionated old guy

transcript.speaker: Old Guy
transcript.text: That idea will never work!

transcript.speaker: Old Guy
transcript.text: Unless you know some kind of "magic" that sends data through the air.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I call it Wi-Fi.

transcript.speaker: Old Guy
transcript.text: Pffft! No one wants that.

situation: In a meeting, the opinionated old guy declares that Dilbert's idea will never work, adding sarcastically that it would take magic to send data through the air. Dilbert calmly replies that such a thing already exists and is called Wi-Fi. The old guy folds his arms and dismisses it anyway, claiming no one wants it.
punchline: The old guy's sarcastic example of impossible magic is just Wi-Fi, which is everywhere, yet he stubbornly insists nobody wants it, showing that his opinions are impervious to reality.
summary: A grumpy veteran scoffs at a proposal by mocking wireless data as sorcery, then brushes off the existing technology as unwanted when it is named.

title: Average Performance of a Unique Job

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your job performance is below average.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How did you calculate an average for a job that no one else has ever performed?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Math?

setting: Boss's office, during a performance review
situation: The Boss sits across a desk from Dilbert and tells him his job performance is below average. Dilbert points out that nobody else has ever done his job, so there is no average to compare against. The Boss, unable to justify the claim, weakly answers with a single word.
punchline: The Boss's tentative one-word answer 'Math?' shows he has no real basis for the rating and is simply bluffing with a vague appeal to numbers.
summary: A manager delivers a negative review based on a comparison that cannot logically exist, and can only offer a lame guess at how he got it.

title: Evil Marketing Expert Smears Competition

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our competition released a product that makes our product look like it was designed by chimps.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's why I hired the world's most evil marketing expert to help us close the perception gap.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Should we focus on our value proposition?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If that means accusing them of crimes they didn't commit, then yes.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and Dogbert that a competitor's new product makes theirs look like it was designed by chimps. He says he hired the world's most evil marketing expert, who turns out to be Dogbert. When the Boss asks whether they should focus on their value proposition, Dogbert says that only applies if it means accusing the competitors of crimes they didn't commit.
punchline: Dogbert's idea of marketing strategy is to smear the competition with false criminal accusations instead of improving the product or its value.
summary: A boss hires an openly villainous marketing consultant, who reveals that his strategy is to frame the rival company rather than promote the merits of the product.

title: Apple Crunch Defense Against Management

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need to talk to you about your apple-eating.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My what?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every afternoon you eat an apple at your desk.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your co-workers are complaining because it's loud.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They can't work with all of your crispy chewing noise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In my defense, my co-workers are so incompetent that the less work they do, the better off the company is.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That is a surprisingly robust defense.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll come back if I can think of a counter-argument.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good luck.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Crunch.

situation: The Boss confronts Dilbert about complaints that his daily apple-eating is too loud for his co-workers. Dilbert defends himself by claiming his co-workers are so incompetent that distracting them actually benefits the company. The Boss grudgingly admits the defense is strong and leaves to find a rebuttal while Dilbert keeps crunching.
punchline: Dilbert justifies his noisy apple-eating by insulting his colleagues' competence, and the Boss can't refute it, so Dilbert happily keeps crunching.
summary: A manager tries to stop an employee's loud fruit snacking, but gets outmaneuvered by an argument that disrupting incompetent coworkers helps the company.

title: Demanding Irrational Enthusiasm From Asok

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, your employee engagement has been a bit soft this quarter.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I expect a higher level of irrational enthusiasm for the endless string of thankless tasks you call your job.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How's this?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I also want to see an unnatural preference for work over leisure.

situation: The boss tells Asok that his employee engagement has been low this quarter. He then demands that Asok show irrational enthusiasm for his thankless tasks. Asok responds with a forced, toothy grin, and the boss adds that he also wants Asok to prefer work over leisure.
punchline: The boss openly admits that the job is thankless and the enthusiasm he demands is irrational and unnatural, yet he still expects Asok to fake it.
summary: A manager scolds a young employee for lacking zeal and openly asks him to fake delight in dreary work and give up his free time.

title: Insult Vendors Into Giving Discounts

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The inexperienced employee

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: You need to get all the vendors in the same room and insult them until they offer you discounts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds super dumb.

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: That's what they said to Galileo, old man.

situation: A young, inexperienced employee walks up to Dilbert and offers unsolicited advice on how to do his job. His idea is to gather all the vendors in one room and insult them until they offer discounts. Dilbert says it sounds super dumb, and the young man replies that people said the same thing to Galileo.
punchline: The young employee defends his obviously bad idea by comparing himself to Galileo, as if being doubted proves he is a visionary rather than just wrong.
summary: A cocky newcomer lectures a veteran on procurement with a ridiculous scheme and shrugs off criticism by comparing himself to a misunderstood genius.

title: Dogbert Coaches Debate With Links

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Internet Debate Coach

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if the only links I can find are from non-credible sources?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll do some research, but I think that's the only kind there is.

setting: Office desk or break room, with Dogbert sitting on a table facing Dilbert
situation: Dogbert, acting as an internet debate coach, advises Dilbert to support his opinions with links to articles. Dilbert worries that the only links he can find will be from unreliable sources. Dogbert says he will research it but suspects unreliable sources are all that exist.
punchline: Dogbert cynically suggests that there are no credible sources online, implying the internet is made up entirely of unreliable information.
summary: A coach for online arguments admits that trustworthy references may be impossible to find because the web is full of junk.

title: Twitching Eye Gets Her Assigned

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does anyone have an idea for fixing our communication problem with marketing?

transcript.speaker: Thought bubble (meeting attendees)
transcript.text: Must... not... speak or else he will assign the project to me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I saw your eye twitch. The project is all yours.

transcript.speaker: Woman with large hair
transcript.text: Gaaaa!!!

situation: The boss asks a meeting full of employees for ideas to fix the communication problem with marketing. Everyone silently thinks that speaking up would get them stuck with the project, so they all stay quiet. The boss notices one woman's eye twitching, treats it as a sign of interest, and assigns her the project.
punchline: Even staying silent doesn't protect you from being assigned unwanted work, because the clueless boss misreads a nervous twitch as volunteering.
summary: In a tense meeting, employees all hold their tongues to dodge a new project, but a nervous twitch gets one of them picked anyway.

title: Coworker Cancels Walk, Ruins Walk

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you like to take a long walk with me at lunch to get some exercise?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's a great idea!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, I'll come get you at noon.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ready?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes, I only need ten minutes to finish this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I only have an hour for lunch, and your ten minutes will turn into twenty.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's okay because I wore heels today and I can't walk more than a block anyway.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why did you agree to take a long walk if you couldn't take a long walk?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Because I was planning to walk to the store on the corner to do an errand anyway.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You've ruined my walk!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Just give me forty minutes to wrap this up.

setting: Office cubicle area and the company building exterior
situation: Dilbert invites a coworker on a long lunchtime walk for exercise, and she enthusiastically agrees. At noon she says she needs ten minutes to finish her work, then admits she can't walk far in her heels and only agreed because she had an errand to run nearby. Dilbert is exasperated, and she asks for forty more minutes.
punchline: The coworker agreed to the long walk only for her own convenience, so Dilbert's exercise plan is ruined while her ten minutes keep growing to forty.
summary: A lunchtime fitness invitation falls apart when the invitee's real motives and shoes make the plan impossible.

title: Parody Can't Be Told From Reality

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ever since the parody inversion, no one can tell the difference between jokes and reality.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to get buy-in on this proposal from all thirteen department heads by tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Was that real or parody?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think they're the same now.

situation: Dilbert and a bespectacled coworker sit with coffee cups discussing how no one can distinguish jokes from reality anymore. The Boss walks up and demands an impossible task: getting buy-in from thirteen department heads by tomorrow. The coworker asks if that request was real or a parody, and Dilbert says they are the same now.
punchline: The Boss's demand is so absurd that it is indistinguishable from satire, proving the point that parody and workplace reality have merged.
summary: A pair of coworkers lament that satire and real life have blurred, then a manager's ridiculous deadline request confirms it.

title: Boss Orders Gender Change for Pay Equity

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That way he can claim he pays men and women the same.

transcript.text: I just lost all respect for your company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was going to happen either way.

situation: Dilbert introduces himself to a woman and explains that his boss has ordered him to identify as a woman. The reason is so the company can claim it pays men and women equally. She shakes his hand and then says she has lost all respect for the company, and Dilbert replies that this was going to happen regardless.
punchline: The company's cynical trick to fake gender pay equity is so absurd that Dilbert admits it was already a company people were going to lose respect for, no matter what it did.
summary: A manager's scheme to make the pay-equity numbers look good by reclassifying an employee's gender wins no admirers, and the employee shrugs that the company was doomed to lose respect anyway.

title: Head-Banging Cures Coworker Frustration

transcript.speaker: Coworker in green
transcript.text: What happened to your head?

transcript.speaker: Coworker in red
transcript.text: I've been banging it against a wall to reduce my frustration with my co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in green
transcript.text: Is it working?

transcript.speaker: Coworker in red
transcript.text: I think so because I don't remember your name.

situation: One employee in a green sweater, holding a coffee cup, asks a coworker in a red shirt what happened to his head. The coworker explains he has been banging his head against a wall to cope with his frustration with colleagues. When asked if it is working, he says it must be, since he can't remember the other man's name.
punchline: Banging his head has given him memory loss, which he counts as success because he has forgotten the annoying coworker he was trying to forget.
summary: A man who has been hitting his head on a wall to escape irritating colleagues decides it works because he can no longer recall the name of the person asking.

title: Hard Work Advice From Easy Success

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The key to your personal success is hard work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was it hard for you to learn that?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No, it was easy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mind if I get my advice from someone who worked at it harder?

situation: A coworker with swept-back hair tells Dilbert at a meeting that hard work is the key to personal success. Dilbert asks whether learning that was hard, and the coworker admits it was easy. Dilbert then says he would rather take advice from someone who had to work harder at it.
punchline: The coworker's success advice is undermined by his admission that it came easily to him, so Dilbert dismisses him as an unqualified source.
summary: A colleague preaching the value of effort admits his own success was effortless, so Dilbert politely declines to take his advice.

title: Email Replaces Talking In Person

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you read my email?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you aware that email is a substitute for talking in person?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I thought I heard something about that.

setting: Office, at Dilbert's desk and then a hallway
situation: The Boss, holding a coffee cup, asks Dilbert if he read his email, and Dilbert says yes while typing at his laptop. The Boss then lectures Dilbert that email is meant to replace face-to-face conversation. Walking away, the Boss muses that he thinks he heard something about that.
punchline: The Boss is lecturing about email replacing in-person talk when that is exactly why people email, and he has already forgotten that he himself sent the email and is confronting Dilbert in person.
summary: A manager confronts an employee face to face about reading his message, then scolds him over what email is for while ignoring his own contradiction.

title: Below-Average Idiots Not Anticipated

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you read my suggestions on the user interface?

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Yes, but we'll need a bigger budget if you want to make the user interface so easy that even you can use it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just make it so the average idiot can use it.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: We did, but we didn't anticipate any below-average idiots.

situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss asks an engineer whether he read his suggestions on the user interface. The engineer says making it easy enough for the boss to use would require a bigger budget. The boss says to design it for the average idiot, and the engineer replies that they never planned for anyone below average.
punchline: The engineer insults the boss by implying he is a below-average idiot, a user the team never designed the interface to accommodate.
summary: An engineer tells his boss that making software simple enough for him would cost extra, since the design only accounted for average intelligence.

title: Worse Than A Placebo

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I've noticed that every project you have worked on has failed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that a coincidence?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's hard to know, unless you compare me to a placebo.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, you're worse than a placebo.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I thought that would take longer.

situation: The boss confronts Wally about the fact that every project he has worked on has failed and asks if that is a coincidence. Wally replies that you could only tell by comparing him to a placebo. The boss does the comparison on the spot and declares Wally worse than a placebo, which Wally says he expected to take longer.
punchline: Wally treats being proven worse than a sugar pill as a quick, almost impressive achievement, showing his total lack of shame about being a project jinx.
summary: A manager points out Wally's record of failed projects, and Wally cheerfully accepts a comparison that shows he is less useful than doing nothing at all.

title: Noise-Canceling Headphones Defeat Coworker

transcript.text: Maybe you could take them off for a minute.

transcript.speaker: Headphone Coworker
transcript.text: I have no idea what you are saying because I'm wearing noise-canceling headphones.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Then take them off!

transcript.speaker: Headphone Coworker
transcript.text: If I am reading your lips correctly, I believe you are asking me to "flurp tingo gloop."

transcript.text: Forget it! I'll just let my project fail!

transcript.text: How is your anti-co-worker defense system working out?
