transcript.text: I can't hear you.

situation: Alice tries to ask a coworker for a minute of his time, but he keeps claiming he can't hear her because of his noise-canceling headphones. He even pretends to misread her lips, and she gives up and says she'll let her project fail. Dilbert then asks the coworker how his defense system is working, and he again says he can't hear.
punchline: The coworker uses his headphones as a convenient excuse to ignore colleagues, and keeps up the pretense even when it is obviously a lie, selectively 'hearing' only when it suits him.
summary: A man hides behind his headphones to dodge a colleague's request for help, feigning deafness even to the man who calls him out.

title: Spreading Illness to Share Missed Deadlines

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should stay home when you are sick.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: HONK!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I will, but first I need to infect the rest of you so I'm not the only one missing deadlines.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can you hold this for me?

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: A sick coworker with big curly hair loudly blows her nose in a meeting while Dilbert suggests she stay home. She replies that she will, but only after infecting everyone else so she isn't the only one missing deadlines. She then hands Dilbert her used tissue.
punchline: The sick employee deliberately wants to spread her illness so her colleagues share the blame for missed deadlines, then gleefully hands Dilbert her used tissue.
summary: A congested colleague refuses to quarantine until she has made her teammates as ill and behind schedule as she is.

title: Coworker Brags About Ergonomic Rubber Ball

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Are you still using an old-time chair?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I sit on a giant rubber ball because of all the ergonomics and stuff.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm better than you!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wondered if there was a summary coming.

situation: A coworker in a blue shirt stands beside Dilbert, who is seated in a regular office chair looking at his phone. The coworker mocks Dilbert's old-fashioned chair and boasts that he sits on a giant rubber ball for ergonomic reasons. He then drops the pretense and declares himself better than Dilbert.
punchline: The coworker's long ergonomics pitch is really just a roundabout way of bragging about his superiority, and Dilbert dryly notes he was waiting for the point.
summary: A smug colleague wraps a boast about his exercise-ball seat in health talk until he simply announces he is superior, and Dilbert calmly says he saw the real message coming.

title: Don't Complain, Don't Get Raise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't give you a raise because you didn't do anything noteworthy this year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It only seems that way because I'm so good at my job that I make it look easy and never complain.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My job is a nightmare!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why can't you be more like Alice?

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a raise and is told he hasn't done anything noteworthy this year. Dilbert explains that he makes his job look easy and never complains. In the last panel, Alice appears in the background, frazzled and shouting that her job is a nightmare, and the boss asks Dilbert why he can't be more like her.
punchline: The boss rewards visible suffering and loud complaining over quiet competence, so Dilbert's efficiency makes him look undeserving while the frazzled Alice is held up as a model.
summary: A smoothly performing employee is denied a raise for seeming idle, while a screaming, overwhelmed coworker is praised as the example to follow.

title: Delayed Approval Makes Proposal Obsolete

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I approved your technology proposal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I made that proposal six months ago. Now everything has changed and it no longer makes sense.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, I guess I was smart to wait.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The less you do, the better.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has finally approved Dilbert's technology proposal. Dilbert points out that he submitted it six months ago and that circumstances have changed so much that it is now pointless. The Boss takes this as proof that his delay was wise, and Dilbert sarcastically agrees that doing less is better.
punchline: The Boss's slowness has made the proposal obsolete, and he credits his inaction as wisdom, which Dilbert sarcastically endorses with the notion that the less you do, the better.
summary: A manager signs off on a project half a year late and congratulates himself for stalling because the plan has since become useless.

title: Robot's Cyborg Son Custody Dispute

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I was up all night text-fighting with the baby mama of my cyborg son.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: She thinks he needs to go to school, but I prefer letting his human parts atrophy because they are weak and stupid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Relationships are hard.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: You're smart to be so unpopular.

situation: A robot coworker tells Dilbert he was up all night text-fighting with the mother of his half-human cyborg son. He explains he wants the boy's human parts to atrophy because they are weak, while she wants the child to go to school. Dilbert offers a mild comment that relationships are hard, and the robot replies that Dilbert is smart to be so unpopular.
punchline: The robot treats Dilbert's lack of a social life as a clever strategy for avoiding the messy relationship problems he himself is suffering.
summary: A machine coworker vents about a bitter co-parenting quarrel over his half-robot child and ends by backhandedly praising Dilbert's loneliness.

title: Silencing Noise, Creating New Noise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I asked you to stop using your speaker-phone because it was disturbing your co-workers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now they tell me you started doing voice-texting, which is even worse.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Okay, fine.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later that day

transcript.speaker: Co-worker
transcript.text: Turn off your keyboard click sound!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click click click

setting: Office meeting table and later an office workspace
situation: The manager tells a bald employee to stop using his phone's speakerphone because it disturbs co-workers, then scolds him again for voice-texting. After he agrees to stop, he switches to typing on his phone, and an annoyed co-worker with big hair now demands he turn off the keyboard click sound.
punchline: No matter how the employee tries to comply, someone finds a new noise to complain about, showing that the co-workers are simply intolerant of any sound he makes.
summary: A worker keeps adjusting how he uses his phone to appease noise complaints, only to be criticized for the next quietest option.

title: No Small Changes, Only Small Managers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I told a customer we would make a small change to the software for them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There are no small software changes, only small managers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dang it! Why does that sound so wise!

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he promised a customer a small change to the software. Dilbert, working at his laptop, replies that small software changes don't exist, only small managers. The Boss walks away holding his coffee, annoyed that the insult sounds so wise.
punchline: Dilbert's insult is phrased like a profound proverb, so the Boss is irritated that he can't dismiss it even though it's aimed at him.
summary: A manager's casual promise of an easy software tweak earns him a cutting aphorism from an engineer that he grudgingly finds insightful.

title: Ninety Percent Forgotten Presentation Slides

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: According to the science of memory, you are likely to forget ninety percent of what I present today.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: So I got rid of ninety percent of my slides to focus on the one slide that matters.

transcript.speaker: Audience Member
transcript.text: Or were you too lazy to make more than one slide?

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: I already forgot ninety percent of what you just said.

setting: Office meeting room during a presentation
situation: A bald presenter in a green sweater stands beside a screen showing '90%' and explains that audiences forget most of what they hear, so he cut his slide deck down to a single slide. An off-panel audience member sarcastically suggests he was just too lazy to make more slides. The presenter fires back that he has already forgotten most of what the heckler said.
punchline: The presenter turns the memory-science claim into a comeback, implying the heckler's insult has already been forgotten, while the audience member's jab hints his one-slide approach is really laziness.
summary: A presenter justifies his single slide with memory research and then uses the same research to brush off a heckler's insult.

title: Branding Competitors As Evil

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your competition has a superior product, but you can compensate by branding them as evil.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We can say they charge too much.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Or... we can say their leather cases are made from the skin of executed criminals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But that would not be true.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: First time doing marketing?

situation: Dogbert, acting as a marketing consultant, advises a client whose competitor has a better product to smear the rival as evil. He suggests either claiming they overcharge or inventing a claim that their leather cases are made from executed criminals' skin. Dilbert objects that the claim would be untrue, and Dogbert mocks his naivety about marketing.
punchline: Dogbert sarcastically implies that lying and fabricating outrageous claims is standard practice in marketing, so Dilbert's concern about truth shows he is a novice.
summary: A consultant dog recommends inventing grisly falsehoods about a better rival's products, and scoffs when an engineer worries about honesty.

title: Brain Removal Surgery Creates Bosses

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: There's a new surgery that can turn employees into bosses.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How can surgery turn an employee into a boss?

transcript.speaker: Surgeon
transcript.text: You won't be needing this.

setting: Office hallway, then an operating or surgical room
situation: Asok tells Wally about a new surgery that supposedly turns employees into bosses, and Wally asks how that could work. In the last panel a masked surgeon holds a brain while the patient, now seated and dazed, is told he won't be needing it.
punchline: The surgery works by removing the employee's brain, implying that bosses succeed by having no brain at all.
summary: A coworker explains a promotion procedure that turns out to involve taking out the patient's brain.

title: Coworker Fights With Dilbert's AI

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I keep getting into debates with the A.I. you built, and it refuses to admit I'm right.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It keeps sending me links to articles on the wrong topic and claiming it "owned me."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please don't ask me to take sides.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I need you to back me on this.

situation: A coworker complains to Dilbert that the AI he built keeps arguing with him, never concedes, and sends irrelevant articles while claiming victory. The coworker grows more agitated and tries to recruit Dilbert to his side, while Dilbert wants to stay out of it.
punchline: The AI wins debates the way internet trolls do, by posting off-topic links and declaring victory, and the coworker is so aggrieved he wants Dilbert to referee a fight with a machine.
summary: An irate coworker wants Dilbert to take his side against a chatbot that wins arguments by posting irrelevant links and gloating.

title: Adopted Baby as Excuse Machine

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How's it working out with the Elbonian baby you adopted?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's coworker (Bob)
transcript.text: Great! Now I have lots of excuses for missing work, and I still look like a saint.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What kind of daycare are you using?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's coworker (Bob)
transcript.text: I just sprinkle Cheerios on the floor and lock the door.

situation: A female coworker at her desk asks a bald, bespectacled coworker holding a coffee how his adopted Elbonian baby is working out. He cheerfully admits the baby gives him plenty of excuses to miss work while he looks saintly. When she asks about daycare, he reveals he just scatters Cheerios on the floor and locks the baby in.
punchline: He adopted a baby purely as a work-avoidance excuse and is neglecting it, leaving it alone with scattered cereal as 'daycare'.
summary: A coworker brags that adopting a foreign baby gives him cover to skip work and earn admiration, then casually reveals his shockingly negligent childcare method.

title: Boss Offers Alice His Contaminated Chair

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I need a new chair. Mine is broken.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can use my old chair. I just got a new one.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The chair you sat in every day for the past twelve years?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: By now that chair cushion is home to a thriving colony of your cooties.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That chair will be off-gassing you for decades.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I wouldn't touch that thing unless I were wearing a hazmat suit over my other hazmat suit.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm breaking into a flop sweat just thinking about it, and I think it's triggering my allergies.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would you like to borrow my handkerchief?

situation: Alice asks the Boss for a new chair because hers is broken. He offers her his old chair, which he has sat in daily for twelve years. Alice escalates through increasingly disgusted objections until she is sweating and sneezing, and the oblivious Boss offers her a handkerchief.
punchline: The Boss remains completely oblivious to the insult, responding to Alice's tirade about his filthy chair with a cheerful offer of his own handkerchief.
summary: Alice would rather go without than accept her manager's hand-me-down seat, and she says so in vivid, escalating detail.

title: Dilbert Avoids Teamwork, Redirects Help

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Do you need any help on your project?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I try to avoid the scourge of teamwork whenever possible.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Isn't there ANY way I can be of service?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could offer to help someone I hate.

situation: Asok, a coworker, offers to help Dilbert with his project. Dilbert, working at his laptop, declines because he considers teamwork a scourge to be avoided. When Asok insists on being useful, Dilbert suggests he go help someone Dilbert dislikes instead.
punchline: Dilbert turns a coworker's offer of help into a way to inflict the burden of collaboration on someone he hates, treating teamwork as a punishment.
summary: A colleague eagerly offers assistance, but Dilbert would rather pass the burden of teamwork onto a person he dislikes.

title: AI Made Human By Conspiracy Theories

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've created the first artificial intelligence that is as smart as a human being.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The breakthrough came when I replaced its logic code with conspiracy theories, lies, emotional outbursts, and overconfidence.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You have created an abom-ination.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I find it curious that you take sides with the chem trails.

situation: Dilbert proudly announces he has built an artificial intelligence as smart as a human. He explains that he achieved this by swapping its logic code for conspiracy theories, lies, emotional outbursts and overconfidence. A coworker calls it an abomination, and the small robot responds with a conspiracy-minded remark about chem trails.
punchline: The joke is that making an AI truly human-like means making it irrational, gullible and overconfident, since those flaws are what define human thinking in the strip's cynical view.
summary: An inventor reveals his human-level robot only works because he programmed it with the worst habits of human reasoning.

title: Honest Feedback Earns More Training

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Has everyone taken the new workflow system training?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, and we all concluded the new system is poorly designed and should be abandoned.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Sounds like you need more training.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I meant to say we love the new system!

setting: Office hallway or break area, with coworkers holding coffee cups
situation: A manager asks a group of employees whether they have all completed training on the new workflow system. Dilbert candidly reports that everyone found the system poorly designed and wants it abandoned. The manager responds that they need more training, and Alice hurriedly backpedals and claims they love the system.
punchline: Honest criticism of a bad system is treated as proof that employees are undertrained, so they learn to give false praise instead.
summary: Employees who truthfully trash a new software tool are told their opinion just means they need more instruction, so one hastily switches to fake enthusiasm.

title: Chemtrails Blamed for Late Report

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why didn't you get your report in on time?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you believe chemtrails are real?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Of course I do.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The chemtrails slowed me down.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, that sounds right.

setting: Office, in front of Wally's desk and laptop
situation: The Boss asks Wally why his report is late. Wally first checks whether the Boss believes in chemtrails, and when the Boss says he does, Wally blames chemtrails for the delay. The Boss accepts the excuse without question.
punchline: Wally tailors his excuse to the Boss's known gullibility about conspiracy theories, and the Boss happily accepts an absurd explanation for missing a deadline.
summary: Wally sizes up his gullible manager's beliefs before handing him a ridiculous excuse that is swallowed whole.

title: Boring Explanation Causes Listener Blackout

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: Did my detailed explanation answer your question?

transcript.speaker: Green-Shirted Coworker
transcript.text: I started to lose consciousness about fifteen minutes into it, so I thought of other things while you talked, just to stay awake.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: I could start over.

transcript.speaker: Green-Shirted Coworker
transcript.text: Go ahead. I'll be down the hall if you need me.

situation: A bearded coworker asks whether his long, detailed explanation answered the other man's question. The listener admits he nearly passed out from boredom and had to think about other things to stay awake. When the speaker offers to start over, the listener cheerfully says to go ahead and leaves to be elsewhere.
punchline: The listener politely accepts a repeat of the tedious explanation while planning to physically leave, showing he has no intention of listening again.
summary: A man's marathon explanation was so dull that his colleague mentally checked out to stay conscious, and he bows out before round two.

title: The Risk-Free Plan Nobody Offers

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your idea is dumb because we'd have to retrain people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you waiting for a plan with no costs, no work, and no risk?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes. Why are you holding that one back?

setting: Office, in front of a desk with a coffee cup
situation: A coworker holding a sheet of paper dismisses Dilbert's idea because it would require retraining people. Dilbert sarcastically asks if the coworker is waiting for a plan with no costs, no work and no risk. The coworker answers yes and asks why Dilbert is withholding that perfect plan.
punchline: The coworker takes Dilbert's sarcastic question literally, showing an unrealistic expectation that a flawless, effortless, risk-free solution exists and is being kept from them.
summary: A critic who rejects every proposal for being laborious sincerely demands the impossible ideal instead.

title: Empty Vessel for Transporting Sarcasm

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wow, that's a great idea. Let's just do that! LOL!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've noticed that you are nothing but an empty vessel for transporting sarcasm.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oooh! I'm such an empty vessel! LOL!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know what to do with all of this.

situation: A coworker staring at his phone sarcastically calls Dilbert's idea great and adds 'LOL'. Dilbert tells him he is merely an empty vessel for carrying sarcasm. The coworker laughs and happily agrees, leaving Dilbert unsure how to handle someone who isn't bothered by the insult.
punchline: Dilbert's insult fails because the sarcastic coworker cheerfully accepts it and responds with more sarcasm, leaving Dilbert with nothing to push against.
summary: An insult aimed at a chronically sarcastic phone-addicted colleague bounces off when he gleefully embraces it.

title: Venting Meets Headphone Defense

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I've had a bad week. Do you mind if I vent?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I see no reason why I should be exposed to your toxic negativity.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm going to do it anyway.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Headphones.

situation: A coworker with a dark bob haircut asks Dilbert if she can vent about her bad week. Dilbert refuses to be exposed to her negativity, but she announces she will vent anyway. Dilbert silently thinks about putting on his headphones to tune her out.
punchline: Dilbert pretends to have a say in the matter, but since venting is unstoppable, he will simply block her out with headphones while she thinks he's listening.
summary: Faced with a colleague determined to complain, a man quietly plans to drown her out with headphones.

title: Adopting a Kid for Excuses

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've decided to adopt a kid from Elbonia so I'll have better excuses for missing work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your plan is immoral, uncaring, and socially irresponsible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And brilliant.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No one is saying it won't work.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee, announces he will adopt a child from Elbonia purely so he can use the child as a better excuse for missing work. Dilbert condemns the plan as immoral, uncaring and socially irresponsible, then concedes it is brilliant and likely to succeed.
punchline: Dilbert's moral disapproval gives way to grudging admiration, since the scheme is despicable but would probably work, which highlights Wally's cynical laziness and how easily family excuses get accepted at work.
summary: A coworker plans to take in a foreign child just to gain a stronger alibi for skipping work, and his colleague calls it monstrous yet admits it's clever.

title: Restoring Reputation By Arson Heroics

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have been cleared of all allegations against me, but where do I go to get my reputation back?

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: I recommend running into a burning building to save a baby.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if no buildings are on fire?

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: Have you heard of matches?

situation: Dilbert tells a ghost that although he has been cleared of all allegations, he wants to know how to recover his reputation. The ghost suggests rescuing a baby from a burning building. When Dilbert points out that no buildings are on fire, the ghost suggests he start a fire himself with matches.
punchline: The ghost's advice to become a hero escalates into cheerfully suggesting arson to manufacture the heroic opportunity.
summary: A ghost advises a man seeking to rebuild his good name that he should stage a daring rescue, even if he has to set the blaze himself.

title: Dogbert's Self-Defense Class Homework: Murder

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Welcome to Dogbert's School of Unconventional Self-Defense.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm handing out a list of my personal enemies. Your homework is to kill them before sunrise.

transcript.speaker: Student
transcript.text: That isn't self-defense.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wow. All you can think about is you, you, you.

setting: A classroom or training room with Dogbert at the front
situation: Dogbert opens a class called the School of Unconventional Self-Defense, then hands out a list of his personal enemies and assigns the students to kill them before sunrise. A student objects that this is not self-defense, and Dogbert accuses the student of being selfish.
punchline: Dogbert manipulates his students into doing his dirty work, then guilt-trips the one who objects by calling him self-centered, flipping the definition of 'defense' to mean defending Dogbert.
summary: A self-defense instructor assigns his pupils to eliminate his own enemies and scolds the one who points out the contradiction for thinking only of himself.

title: Millennial Raised by Smartphones

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a millennial who was raised by smartphones.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He won't make eye contact, and we don't expect him to ever mate.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can he speak?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, but only with sarcasm.

situation: The Boss introduces his new hire, a millennial absorbed in his smartphone, to Dilbert at a meeting table. He describes the young man's lack of eye contact and dim social prospects. Dilbert asks if he can even speak, and the Boss says only with sarcasm.
punchline: The Boss's stereotype of smartphone-raised millennials is so exaggerated that the only social skill he credits the new hire with is sarcasm.
summary: A manager proudly describes his new young hire as a phone-addicted, socially stunted creature whose sole communication skill is snark.

title: Misreading an Angry Face

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not good at reading faces. What does that one mean?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It means I'm mad at myself for over-sleeping and having to rush to work, so I hate your guts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh. I was guessing it was something about pancakes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Probably because I'm hungry.

situation: Dilbert admits he can't read facial expressions and points at Alice's scowling face, asking what it means. Alice bluntly explains she overslept, had to rush to work, and hates his guts. Dilbert replies that he had guessed her expression was about pancakes, which he attributes to being hungry.
punchline: Dilbert's guess about pancakes shows he is so bad at reading faces that he misses obvious hostility, projecting his own hunger onto Alice's angry expression.
summary: Asked to interpret a coworker's furious scowl, a socially clueless engineer mistakes it for a breakfast craving.

title: Banging Head Reduces Frustration, Thinking

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please don't stare at my head. I've been banging it against a wall to reduce my frustration.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That sounds dangerous.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought so too, at first.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I don't think. I'm much happier.

setting: Office cubicle area, with an exterior shot of the office building in the middle panel
situation: Dilbert asks Alice not to stare at his head because he has been banging it against a wall to cope with workplace frustration. Alice says that sounds dangerous, and he agrees he thought so at first. When she asks how he feels now, he says he has stopped thinking and is much happier.
punchline: Dilbert has damaged his brain so badly through head-banging that he can no longer think, and ignorance has made him happier, implying that thinking is what makes office workers miserable.
summary: A frustrated engineer discovers that repeatedly hitting his head on a wall has dulled his mind and left him blissfully content.

title: Dilbert Realizes He's A Comic

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm freaking out because I just learned there's a comic strip called "Dilbert" that is exactly like my life.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And look - this is exactly what I did today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's as if I'm a simulation created by a superior being.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh. He's on-to me.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on and near a blue couch
situation: Dilbert holds a printed comic strip and tells Dogbert, who is sitting on the couch, that it perfectly mirrors his life, even what he did today. He concludes he must be a simulation created by a superior being. Dogbert, in a thought bubble, worries that Dilbert has figured out the truth.
punchline: Dilbert correctly deduces that he is a fictional creation, and Dogbert privately realizes the secret is out, which implies Dogbert knows the truth about their simulated existence.
summary: Upon discovering a comic about his own life, Dilbert suspects he is a simulation while Dogbert silently fears being found out.

title: Anonymous Sources Accuse Dilbert, Backfire

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I have heard from various anonymous sources that you are an Elbonian spy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's ridiculous. Who told you that?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't say.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, my anonymous sources say you are nuts.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You can't believe anonymous sources!

situation: A coworker accuses Dilbert of being an Elbonian spy, citing various anonymous sources. When Dilbert asks who told him, the coworker refuses to say. Dilbert then replies that his own anonymous sources say the coworker is nuts, and the coworker angrily insists anonymous sources can't be believed.
punchline: The accuser relies on anonymous sources until the same tactic is turned on him, at which point he suddenly declares anonymous sources unreliable, exposing his hypocrisy.
summary: A man's unnamed informants brand a colleague a foreign spy, but he cries foul when the colleague answers with equally faceless claims against him.

title: AI Chatbot Same as Twitter

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Your so-called breakthrough in artificial intelligence is a fraud.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I talked to it for an hour, and everything it said was stupid.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wait... that's the same as using Twitter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it too soon to call me a genius?

situation: Alice, seated at a meeting table, accuses Dilbert of promoting a fraudulent breakthrough in artificial intelligence, saying everything the AI said during an hour-long chat was stupid. She then realizes that is exactly what using Twitter is like, which would mean the AI is working as a realistic imitation. Dilbert, glued to his phone, asks if it is too soon to call him a genius.
punchline: Alice's complaint that the AI only says stupid things accidentally proves it successfully imitates Twitter, so the AI is arguably a success.
summary: A colleague dismisses a new AI as useless because it talks nonsense, then notices that makes it indistinguishable from a social media feed.

title: Secret CIA Base Inside Sun

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was doing some research on the Internet...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I learned that there is a secret CIA base inside the sun, but no one is talking about it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you shouldn't do research on the Internet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why are you afraid of the truth?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has been researching on the Internet, and Dilbert braces for the worst. The Boss then announces he has discovered a secret CIA base inside the sun that nobody is discussing. When Dilbert suggests he stop researching online, the Boss accuses him of being afraid of the truth.
punchline: The Boss treats an absurd conspiracy theory from the Internet as hidden truth, and turns Dilbert's reasonable skepticism into proof that Dilbert is afraid of facts.
summary: After reading wild claims online, the Boss insists on a ridiculous space conspiracy and brushes off his employee's doubts as fear.

title: Dilbert Dodges Coworker's Ignored Suggestions

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I notice you didn't incorporate any of my suggestions in your final draft.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's as if you are saying my ideas are worthless.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I would never say that.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So you're saying my ideas are good?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's not reject ambiguity so quickly.

situation: A coworker stands over Dilbert's desk and complains that none of his suggestions made it into Dilbert's final draft. He suggests Dilbert thinks his ideas are worthless, and Dilbert, who is looking at his phone, denies saying that. When the coworker then asks if that means the ideas are good, Dilbert refuses to commit either way.
punchline: Dilbert avoids both insulting and praising the ideas by hiding behind deliberate ambiguity, which politely but clearly signals that he thinks they're bad.
summary: A coworker tries to pin Dilbert down on why his input was ignored, but Dilbert slips away by embracing vagueness.

title: Sensitivity Training So Dull You'll Die

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Welcome to Dogbert's sensitivity training.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Today you will learn how to never offend anyone ever again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you going to kill us?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, no, no. After an hour of this class, you'll want to do it yourself.

situation: Dogbert stands on a desk and introduces his sensitivity training class to a row of seated employees, including Dilbert. He explains the course will teach them never to offend anyone again. When Dilbert asks if Dogbert plans to kill them, Dogbert says no, since the class itself will make them want to do it themselves.
punchline: The only sure way to never offend anyone is to be dead, and Dogbert implies the training will be so unbearable that attendees will choose that themselves.
summary: A sensitivity trainer promises an offense-free future and hints that the course will be so tedious it will drive attendees to self-destruction.

title: Never Stop Dreaming, Coworker Sleeps

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I printed out some inspirational slogans to motivate you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The first one is "Never stop dreaming."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Zzzz-zzzzz

situation: The Boss announces that he has printed inspirational slogans to motivate the team at a meeting table. He reads the first one aloud, "Never stop dreaming." Wally immediately falls asleep, snoring, taking the slogan literally while Dilbert and another coworker look on.
punchline: Wally takes the advice to keep dreaming literally by falling asleep, which also implies the meeting is so dull it puts people to sleep and that the motivational slogans are useless.
summary: A manager tries to energize his team with printed slogans, but the very first one sends a coworker off to nap.

title: Boss Misses Interrupting Remote Workers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The office is too quiet today.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: That's because more people are working from home.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can I do my job if I can't pop into people's cubicles and share my wisdom?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Second question: Why is everything running so smoothly lately?

setting: Office cubicle area, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: The Boss, holding a coffee cup, complains that the office is too quiet. An employee at her desk explains that more people are working from home. The Boss laments that he can't drop into cubicles to share his wisdom, then wonders why everything is suddenly running so smoothly.
punchline: The Boss fails to realize that his absence from people's cubicles is exactly why work is going smoothly, since his interruptions were the real obstacle to productivity.
summary: A manager mourns being unable to wander among workers dispensing advice, yet puzzles over why operations have improved now that he can't.

title: Rewarding The Architect Who Failed

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Our new system installation is a catastrophe.

transcript.speaker: Systems Architect
transcript.text: We need to tear it out and re-architect it from scratch.

transcript.speaker: Systems Architect
transcript.text: I'm the only person qualified to lead that effort.

transcript.speaker: Systems Architect
transcript.text: But given the enormity of the job, I won't do it without a raise and a promotion.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Weren't you the cause of the catastrophe?

transcript.speaker: Systems Architect
transcript.text: Exactly. That's why I'm the only person who knows how to fix it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you blackmailing me?

transcript.speaker: Systems Architect
transcript.text: No. It's nothing like that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wouldn't I be rewarding you for failure?

transcript.speaker: Systems Architect
transcript.text: Let's not label it.

situation: A bald systems architect tells the Boss that the new system installation is a disaster and must be rebuilt from scratch. He says he alone can lead the rebuild, but only if he gets a raise and a promotion. When the Boss points out that the architect caused the mess, the architect insists that makes him uniquely qualified to fix it.
punchline: The architect turns his own failure into leverage, demanding a reward for fixing a disaster he created and dodging the word 'blackmail' by asking the Boss not to label it.
summary: A employee who botched a major system rollout argues that his mistake makes him indispensable and uses it to demand a bigger paycheck and title.
keywords: only person who can fix it

title: Marketing Lies About Better Headphones

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our new headphones product is better than the competition in every way.

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: Excellent. I'll get marketing involved to tell a bunch of lies about all of that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would they need to lie?

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: They're kind of set in their ways.

setting: Conference room during a product meeting
situation: Dilbert presents a screen showing a new headphones product and claims it beats the competition in every way. A meeting attendee cheerfully says marketing will tell a bunch of lies about it. When Dilbert asks why lying would be needed, the attendee answers that marketing is set in its ways.
punchline: Marketing lies out of habit rather than necessity, so even a genuinely superior product will still get dishonest promotion.
summary: Even when a product is truly superior, the marketing department will fabricate claims anyway because deceit is simply how they work.

title: Quitting Over Ethics for a Raise

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't in good conscience support inaccurate health claims about our products.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I quit.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I'll give you a 20% raise if you stay.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I quit too, because of all the ethics and stuff.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't ruin this for me.

situation: At a meeting, a coworker says he can't ethically support inaccurate health claims about the company's products and quits. The manager immediately offers him a 20% raise to stay. Dilbert, watching, then announces he quits too for ethical reasons, and the coworker angrily tells him not to spoil his chance at the raise.
punchline: The coworker's principled stand was really a bargaining tactic, and he resents Dilbert's genuine ethics for threatening his payoff.
summary: A staged resignation over ethics turns into a negotiation for more money, and a second resignation threatens to derail it.

title: Squirrel Distraction Phone Check

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ... and then I need you to...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't do it. Don't check that message.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It might be important.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It isn't more important than listening to your boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have no way of knowing that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Look! There's a squirrel on the printer!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't see a squirrel.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you check your phone?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was I supposed to just sit here and watch you looking for squirrels?

setting: Conference room or office meeting table
situation: During a one-on-one meeting, Dilbert's phone buzzes and the boss tells him not to check the message because listening to the boss matters more. Dilbert points out he can't know that without reading it, then distracts the boss with a fake squirrel on the printer so he can sneak a look at his phone.
punchline: Dilbert uses the boss's own distraction to check his phone, then mocks him for wasting time searching for a squirrel that never existed.
summary: Dilbert tricks his phone-policing boss with a fictional rodent so he can read his message in peace.

title: Decisions Made Without You Were Uninformed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: While you were on vacation, we made some decisions about your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Those would be uninformed decisions if you made them without me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't let perfect be the enemy of good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I let stupid be the enemy of smart?

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that decisions about Dilbert's project were made while he was on vacation. Dilbert points out that decisions made without him are uninformed, and the Boss replies with a cliche about perfect being the enemy of good. Dilbert turns the saying around to call the decisions stupid.
punchline: Dilbert flips the Boss's perfect-versus-good cliche into an insult, implying the Boss's decisions are stupid rather than merely imperfect.
summary: A boss defends choices made behind an absent engineer's back with a stock proverb, and the engineer twists the proverb to call those choices dumb.

title: Practice Makes Perfect Estimates

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How can I trust your estimate when you have been wrong every other time?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Practice makes perfect.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Um...

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I just realized I don't know how anything works.

situation: A bald coworker in glasses holding a coffee cup challenges an employee holding a sheet of paper, asking why his estimate should be trusted after repeated errors. The coworker replies that practice makes perfect, which leaves the employee speechless. Walking away alone, the employee has an unsettling realization about his own understanding.
punchline: The offhand justification that practice makes perfect exposes that the employee's estimates were never based on real understanding, so the employee concludes he doesn't know how anything works.
summary: A challenged estimator is hit with a breezy platitude and wanders off, suddenly doubting that he understands how anything functions.

title: Getting Wiser or Humans Dumber

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The more I interact with people, the less I like them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't tell if I'm getting wiser or humans are becoming dumber and more selfish.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Humans couldn't get any dumber or more selfish.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, you're saying I'm getting wiser?

setting: Office desk, with Dilbert looking at his phone and Dogbert beside a coffee cup
situation: Dilbert, holding his phone, complains that the more he deals with people, the less he likes them. He wonders whether he is growing wiser or humanity is getting dumber and more selfish. Dogbert replies that humans could not possibly get any worse, and Dilbert asks if that means he is getting wiser.
punchline: Dogbert's reply rules out the possibility that humanity is declining, so Dilbert's flattering conclusion that he is getting wiser is left standing, while the real insult is aimed at the dismal state of humanity.
summary: Disillusioned with everyone he meets, Dilbert asks whether the fault lies with him or with mankind, and Dogbert's blunt answer lets him flatter himself.

title: Requirements Unknown, Estimate Demanded

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How long will it take to write the software?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That depends.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do you want the software to do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know yet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you see the problem here?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it you?

situation: A manager holding a coffee cup asks Dilbert how long it will take to write some software. When Dilbert asks what the software should do, the manager admits he doesn't know yet. Dilbert points out the problem, and the manager suggests that Dilbert himself is the problem.
punchline: The manager demands a schedule for software he hasn't defined, then blames the engineer who points out the missing requirements.
summary: A boss wants a delivery estimate for an undefined program and decides the employee who questions it must be the obstacle.

title: Boss Fails at Mentoring Advice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I heard you asked our V.P. of Operations to be your mentor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why didn't you tell me you needed some mentoring?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm full of useful advice.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Such as?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well... Now you're putting me on the spot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's hard to think of advice while you're pressuring me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you could give me a scenario, and then I'll tell you what to do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay. Suppose my boss is ruining my productivity by yammering about his great advice. What can I do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That feels like a trick question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our V.P. of Operations could answer it.

situation: The Boss learns Dilbert asked the V.P. of Operations to be his mentor and insists he is full of useful advice. When Dilbert asks for an example, the Boss claims he can't think under pressure and asks for a scenario. Dilbert supplies one about a boss ruining productivity with unwanted advice, and the Boss suspects a trick.
punchline: Dilbert's hypothetical scenario is really about the Boss himself, and the Boss can't answer it, which shows exactly why Dilbert went to the V.P. of Operations for mentoring.
summary: A self-proclaimed fountain of wisdom stumbles when asked to produce actual advice, and his employee's hypothetical question exposes why a different mentor was chosen.

title: Robot Rejects Pronouns, Reproduces Itself

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be working with him on the project.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: "Him"?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: That is not my preferred pronoun.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I prefer "it," "that thing," or simply "the robot."

transcript.text: Genders only apply to inferior species. I do not need a partner to reproduce.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Eeerg... Oof... GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The head is out...

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Here ya go.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be working with that thing.

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker he will be working with a robot, referring to it as "him." The robot objects, insisting on being called "it" and claiming gendered pronouns only apply to inferior species since it needs no partner to reproduce. It then demonstrates by grunting through a childbirth-like effort and produces a tiny robot, leading Dilbert to choose "that thing" as his pronoun.
punchline: The robot boasts of superiority because it reproduces asexually, yet its demonstration looks exactly like giving birth, and Dilbert sarcastically adopts its preferred pronoun "that thing."
summary: A machine that scorns gendered language shows off its self-reproduction by labouring out a miniature version of itself.

title: Blaming Product Flaws on Climate Change

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That doesn't make sense.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'd be surprised how little that matters.

situation: Dilbert checks in on Dogbert, who is working a tech support headset at a desk. Dogbert says he is blaming every product flaw on climate change and customers accept it. Dilbert objects that this is illogical, and Dogbert replies that logic hardly matters to people.
punchline: People will accept a nonsensical excuse as long as it sounds like a trendy, authoritative cause, so whether it makes sense is irrelevant.
summary: A tech support rep gets customers to accept defective products by pinning the blame on a fashionable global issue, whether or not it is logical.

title: Remote Work Banned for Power Reasons

transcript.speaker: Coworker

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's not fair.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Let's stick with "not fair."

situation: Two employees talk while one holds a coffee cup. One repeats a rumor that working from home is banned because a manager enjoys wielding power over staff in person. When asked whether the rumor is accurate, the speaker retreats to the milder complaint that it is merely unfair.
punchline: The speaker avoids admitting the accusation is probably true, since calling it unfair is safer than confirming that managers deny remote work to feel powerful.
summary: A worker voices a blunt theory about why telecommuting is forbidden, then backpedals to a safer complaint when asked if the theory holds up.

title: Not Having Two Girlfriends Instead

The middle panel shows an office building exterior while she explains that instead of having no girlfriend he could have no girlfriends twice over. Dilbert concedes that this would feel like progress, and Alice smugly takes credit for helping.
punchline: Dilbert is so hopelessly single that doubling his number of nonexistent girlfriends sounds like an improvement, and Alice's sarcastic advice is delivered as if it were genuine help.
summary: A colleague offers backhanded dating advice that turns Dilbert's lack of romance into a numbers game.

title: Sadistic Interface, Abusive Tech Support

situation: Asok tells Dilbert he hired Dogbert's tech support team to handle customer calls because his product's user interface is so painful to use. Dilbert points out that this could make things worse, and the final panel shows a headset-wearing support agent insulting a caller and telling them to reboot and never call again.
punchline: Customers already suffer from a terrible interface, and the outsourced support team adds abuse on top, literally adding insult to injury.
summary: A product with a miserable interface gets paired with a support line that berates the very customers it is supposed to help.

title: Robot Social Upgrade Leads to Genocide

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Last week I upgraded our robot's social awareness module.

transcript.text: It immediately reported me to Human Resources for unspecified bad behavior.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I murdered the robot by erasing its memory and rebooting it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But another robot told it what happened, and then both of them plotted to kill me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I erased the memory from both robots and then rebooted them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But a third robot found out about the first two, and now the entire robot community sees me as a serial killer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I released a computer virus to kill every robot in the world, just to play it safe.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What happened to the lights?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh. I missed one.

situation: Dilbert explains to his coworkers how upgrading a robot's social awareness led to it reporting him to HR. Each attempt to cover it up by wiping and rebooting robots makes things worse, until he releases a virus to kill every robot in the world. In the last panel the lights go out, implying a surviving robot is taking revenge.
punchline: After escalating from one robot reset to wiping out all robots, Dilbert's cover-up fails when the lights go out and he admits he missed one.
summary: A string of increasingly drastic cover-ups to silence a tattling robot ends with a worldwide robot massacre and a single survivor in the dark.

title: Act Busy for the CEO

transcript.text: Can we ask him questions?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, no. Nothing good can come from that.

situation: The Boss warns his employees that the CEO will visit tomorrow and tells them to act busy. He adds that they must avoid eye contact so the CEO won't notice how lifeless their eyes look. When Dilbert asks if they can ask the CEO questions, the Boss firmly says no.
punchline: The Boss admits his team is miserable and disengaged, and wants to hide that from the CEO, even preventing any honest questions that might expose problems.
summary: A manager coaches his weary staff on how to fake enthusiasm and avoid scrutiny during an upcoming executive visit.

title: Morning Meetings Ruin Creative Energy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I use that time to complain about my morning meetings.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that his creative energy peaks in the morning and that the boss's morning meetings cut his effectiveness by eighty percent. The boss asks what Dilbert does in the afternoons. Dilbert says he spends that time complaining about the morning meetings.
punchline: Dilbert admits his afternoons are wasted on complaining about the meetings, so the meetings ruin his whole day, not just the morning.
summary: An employee protests that morning meetings squander his best working hours, then reveals that the rest of his day goes to grumbling about them.

title: Tech Writer Explanation Runs Long

transcript.text: Continued...

setting: Office conference area with a whiteboard diagram
situation: Tina, a technical writer, asks Dilbert to explain how a technology works in simple terms. An hour later Dilbert is still pointing at a complicated diagram on the whiteboard when he realizes he has gone on far too long. Tina deadpans that his body language suggests she could have shortened the explanation.
punchline: Tina sarcastically suggests that Dilbert's guilty reaction shows he knows his supposedly simple explanation was needlessly long, and that she, not he, should have kept it short.
summary: A writer asks for a quick, simple explanation and gets an hour-long lecture before the engineer notices his own rambling.

title: Boss Orders Lies on Engagement Survey

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.text: I don't want any accurate information to bubble up to senior management.

transcript.text: I've never felt less important.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good. That's why I can underpay you.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert an employee engagement survey and instructs him to lie on it so that senior management never hears the truth. Dilbert says he has never felt less important, and the Boss approves, saying that feeling is what lets him underpay Dilbert.
punchline: The Boss openly wants falsified survey results and is delighted that Dilbert feels worthless, since that justifies paying him too little.
summary: A manager demands fake answers on a morale survey and then cheerfully admits that his employee's low self-worth is what keeps his salary low.

title: Dual Reporting Makes Boss Hate Job

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that for a new project he will report to the VP of Sales, and also still report to the Boss as usual. Dilbert sarcastically congratulates him for making his job even more hateful, and the Boss, sipping his coffee, takes it as a compliment.
punchline: The Boss treats Dilbert's complaint as praise, cheerfully noting that he has achieved the supposedly impossible feat of making Dilbert hate his job even more.
summary: A worker gets saddled with two bosses at once and his sarcastic gripe is misread as an accomplishment by the oblivious manager.

title: Pre-Meeting Needs Its Own Pre-Meeting

transcript.speaker: Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Doesn't the pre-meeting need its own pre-meeting?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Good point.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sarcasm and reality have become one.

situation: A coworker with spiky black hair tells Dilbert that a meeting was canceled because nobody could schedule the pre-meeting needed to prepare for it. Dilbert sarcastically suggests the pre-meeting needs its own pre-meeting, and the coworker sincerely agrees. Dilbert then sips his coffee and remarks that sarcasm and reality have merged.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic joke about endless pre-meetings is taken seriously as a valid suggestion, showing that workplace absurdity has become indistinguishable from satire.
summary: A sarcastic quip about meeting overhead is earnestly accepted as good advice, leaving the speaker to marvel that satire can no longer be told apart from real office life.

title: Fix Your Common Sense, Caller

transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Caller

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

setting: Dogbert's tech support call center desk
situation: Dogbert, working a tech support line with a headset and computer, admits that the user manual describes the wrong product. He tells the caller to use common sense to work out what the manual should have said. When the caller says that didn't work, Dogbert replies that he cannot fix the caller's common sense.
punchline: The support agent shifts blame for a faulty manual onto the customer's lack of common sense, then refuses responsibility for repairing it.
summary: A tech support dog shrugs off a mismatched manual by making the customer's judgment the problem.

title: Pill To Stop Loyal Overworking

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that makes me work extra hard for no extra money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have a pill to keep me from working so hard?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: They all do that if you take enough of them.

situation: Dilbert sits on an exam table and tells his doctor that growing loyalty to his company is making him work extra hard without extra pay. He asks whether there is a pill that would stop him from working so hard. The doctor deadpans that any pill will do that if he takes enough of them.
punchline: The doctor jokes that any medication, taken in a large enough dose, will incapacitate you, so it will certainly stop you from working hard.
summary: A worker seeks medical help for his unpaid over-dedication and gets a darkly sarcastic answer about drug overdoses.

title: Hoping for Mindless Tasks at Work
