transcript.text: Looks like it will be another full day of interacting with people I wouldn't pull out of a burning car even if I were made of asbestos.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My only hope is to stay busy doing mindless tasks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have any mindless tasks for me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Take one from the top of the pile.

setting: Office hallway and the boss's office
situation: Dilbert walks through the office thinking bitterly about the coworkers he must deal with all day. He decides his only escape is to keep busy with mindless work, so he asks his boss for some. The boss, seated behind a desk with a tall stack of papers, tells him to grab one from the top of the pile.
punchline: Dilbert goes looking for mindless tasks as a refuge from his coworkers, and the boss has an enormous pile of them ready, showing how plentiful pointless work is.
summary: Hoping to avoid his detested colleagues, an employee requests dull busywork and finds his manager has a towering stack waiting.

title: Hiring a Spy for Engineering Talent

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired an Elbonian spy who, I assume, will try to steal our intellectual property.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's hard to find good engineers in this economy, so that is a risk I am willing to take.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I'd like you to collaborate with him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can we call it something else?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and the tall, bearded Elbonian that he has hired the Elbonian as a spy who will probably steal company intellectual property. He justifies the risk by saying good engineers are hard to find in the current economy. He then asks Dilbert to collaborate with the spy, and Dilbert asks if they can call it something else.
punchline: Dilbert objects that working alongside a known thief isn't really 'collaboration' but something closer to being robbed, highlighting the Boss's willingness to knowingly accept theft in exchange for cheap talent.
summary: A manager knowingly takes on a foreign engineer he expects to steal company secrets and then cheerfully instructs an employee to work closely with him.

title: Tech Support Implies Caller Is Dumb

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I can't figure out how to use your product. What should I do?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend changing jobs to something less challenging.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Are you saying I'm dumb?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, no, no. I'm only implying it.

setting: Dogbert's tech support call center desk
situation: A customer phones Dogbert's tech support because he cannot work out how to use the product and asks what he should do. Dogbert, wearing a headset, advises him to switch to a less challenging job. When the customer asks if he is being called dumb, Dogbert says he is only implying it.
punchline: Dogbert's denial of insulting the customer is itself the insult, since he openly admits he is merely implying the caller is dumb.
summary: A confused customer seeking help is handed a backhanded career tip by an unapologetically snide support agent.

title: Regression Analysis Blames Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I did a regression analysis to find out which variables are common to all of our failures.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's me, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, it's him.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is this what winning feels like?

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: Dilbert tells his colleagues he ran a regression analysis to identify what all of the team's failures have in common. A bald coworker in a green shirt guesses it must be him, but Dilbert says the common factor is actually the person next to him. The bald coworker responds by asking if this is what winning feels like.
punchline: The bald coworker is so accustomed to failure that being named as the cause of a different person's failures feels like a victory to him.
summary: A data-driven post-mortem of repeated team failures singles out one culprit, and the colleague who feared blame treats his escape as a triumph.

title: Vague Pitch Earns Rejection

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you explain what your product does?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Our product was created by an experienced team of technologists to address the way content is surfaced.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Next time just say, "No."

setting: Conference room table in an office
situation: Dilbert asks a visiting salesman to explain what his product does. The salesman responds with a jargon-filled answer about an experienced team and the way content is surfaced, without ever saying what the product actually does. Dilbert tells him that next time he should simply say no.
punchline: The salesman's buzzword-laden non-answer is so meaningless that Dilbert says it would be more honest and efficient to just answer "no" to the question.
summary: A vendor dodges a simple question about his product with empty marketing talk, and the engineer he is pitching to tells him to just refuse next time.

title: Ship With Wrong User Guide

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The product is ready to ship as soon as the new user guide is complete.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ship it with the old model's user guide.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The user interface is totally different.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't let perfect be the enemy of shipping.

situation: At a meeting, Dilbert reports that the product can ship once the new user guide is finished. The boss tells the team to ship it with the old model's guide instead. Wally points out that the user interface is completely different, and the boss dismisses the concern by invoking a perfectionism cliche.
punchline: The boss treats shipping documentation that describes a completely different interface as an acceptable compromise, misusing the 'don't let perfect be the enemy of good' idea to justify a clearly broken deliverable.
summary: A manager waves away a missing manual by insisting the team release the product with instructions written for an entirely different version.

title: Failed Ideas and Cheese-Loving Rodents

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your idea won't work because others have already tried it and failed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Others have tried different things that simply remind you of my idea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I mean, you remind me of a rodent, but that doesn't prove you like cheese.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I love cheese.

situation: A coworker holding a paper rejects Dilbert's idea, saying others already tried it and failed. Dilbert objects that those attempts were merely different things that resemble his idea, and offers an analogy that the coworker reminds him of a rodent without proving he likes cheese. The coworker undercuts the analogy by admitting he loves cheese.
punchline: Dilbert's analogy about superficial resemblance not proving a trait backfires because the coworker really does love cheese, which also confirms the insult and unintentionally supports the coworker's point that resemblance can be a reliable predictor.
summary: A man trying to defend his proposal against claims of past failures compares his critic to a cheese-loving rodent, only to have the critic happily confirm the stereotype.

title: Psychic's Only Accurate Predictions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is the worst idea I have ever seen.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Didn't you once tell me you spent all of your savings on a fake psychic?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And the only prediction she got right was that you would lose all of your money?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She also predicted I would be unhappy.

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker holding a paper that the idea presented is the worst he has ever seen. The coworker counters by recalling that Dilbert once spent all his savings on a fake psychic, and that her only correct prediction was that he would lose his money. Dilbert deadpans that she also correctly predicted he would be unhappy.
punchline: Dilbert's judgment is undermined by his own history of gullibility, and his reply admits that the fraudulent psychic's only accurate predictions were about his misfortune.
summary: A man who dismisses a colleague's plan gets reminded of the time he squandered his savings on a phony fortune teller.

title: Meeting to Schedule Another Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need everyone to come to the Thursday meeting so we can decide when to schedule our next meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why don't we just have the meeting on Thursday?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: See me later so I can berate you for saying that.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do we need a meeting to schedule that?

situation: The Boss tells his team to attend a Thursday meeting whose only purpose is to decide when to hold the next meeting. Dilbert logically asks why they don't simply hold the meeting on Thursday, and the Boss responds by saying he'll berate Dilbert later. Another attendee then sarcastically asks if a meeting is needed to schedule that berating.
punchline: Management's obsession with meetings is so extreme that even scheduling a reprimand for questioning a pointless meeting could require yet another meeting.
summary: A manager convenes a gathering solely to plan the next gathering, and when a sensible objection is raised, the objector's punishment itself seems destined to need a meeting.

title: Employer of the Year, Bought

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm proud to announce that we've been named "Employer of the Year."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How much did that cost?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nothing! All we had to do was buy a million dollars' worth of ads.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did we need those ads?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You won't win any awards with that attitude.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The boss announces at a meeting that the company has been named "Employer of the Year." Dilbert asks what it cost, and the boss reveals the company simply bought a million dollars' worth of ads. When Dilbert questions whether the ads were necessary, the boss dismisses him for having a bad attitude.
punchline: The award was effectively purchased through advertising spending, and the boss deflects any scrutiny of this by treating skepticism as a bad attitude.
summary: A manager brags about a workplace honor that turns out to have been bought with an enormous ad spend, then scolds the employee who questions it.

title: Flag Me When You're Done Talking

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I find it a burden to listen to you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could wave this flag to signal when you are done talking, just in case I want to say something.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You are very rude.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Flag me when you are done with whatever this is.

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert that listening to him is a burden and hands him a small red flag to wave when he has finished talking. Dilbert objects that Dogbert is being rude. Dogbert responds by waving the flag himself, telling Dilbert to signal him when he is done with this complaint.
punchline: Dogbert turns Dilbert's protest into more of the same talking he finds tedious, dismissing the complaint of rudeness with even more rudeness.
summary: A dog finds a coworker's chatter tiresome, hands him a signalling flag, and then uses it to wave off his objection.

title: Sadist Designs Our User Interfaces

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a sadist to design our user interfaces.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I realize this isn't ideal, but no one else wanted the job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would our customers buy a product designed by a sadist?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's called Stockholm syndrome.

situation: At a meeting, the boss announces he has hired a sadist to design the company's user interfaces, admitting nobody else wanted the job. Dilbert asks why customers would buy a product designed by a sadist, and the boss answers that it is called Stockholm syndrome.
punchline: The boss implies that customers will grow to love or depend on a product made to torment them, treating bad user interfaces as a form of captive bonding.
summary: A manager casually justifies hiring a cruel designer for the product's interface by suggesting that customers will come to like their captors.

title: One-Hour Meeting, Zero Minutes Used

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How'd your meeting go?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We spent an hour trying to get the conference call audio to work.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And then?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was a one-hour meeting.

situation: A coworker in an orange shirt stops Dilbert in the hallway and asks how his meeting went. Dilbert explains that the whole hour was spent getting the conference call audio to work. When the coworker asks what happened next, Dilbert points out that the meeting was only scheduled for an hour.
punchline: The conference call technology problems consumed the entire meeting, so nothing was actually discussed or accomplished.
summary: A man reports that his meeting was swallowed whole by audio troubles, leaving no time for the actual agenda.

title: Boss Denies Remote Work for Power

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I work from home?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, because then I won't have the enjoyable sensation of wielding power over you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everything about that sounds wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Off you go.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for permission to work from home. The boss openly admits he refuses because he enjoys having power over Dilbert when he is physically present. Dilbert objects that this sounds wrong, and the boss simply waves him out of the office.
punchline: The boss's only reason for denying remote work is his own enjoyment of controlling his employee, and he is entirely unembarrassed to say so.
summary: A manager candidly admits he won't allow telecommuting because he likes feeling powerful over his staff.

title: Dogbert Blames Climate Change for Everything

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I can't figure out how to use your product.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The problem is climate change. There is nothing you can do.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: There must be something I can do.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you recycle?

situation: A customer phones Dogbert's tech support because she can't work out how to use a product. Dogbert, wearing a headset, blames climate change and says nothing can be done. When the customer insists there must be something, he asks whether she recycles.
punchline: Dogbert dodges responsibility for a product's usability by blaming a huge global issue, then offers a token gesture like recycling as the supposed fix, which is useless for her actual problem.
summary: A support agent deflects a user's product confusion onto global warming and then suggests recycling as the only remedy.

title: Bored Into a Technical Writer Coma

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tina is in some sort of technical writer's trance.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Apparently, I took too long to explain some new technology, and it bored her into a coma.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Should I report this?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Only if you can do it succinctly.

situation: Dilbert and Wally stand next to Tina, who sits motionless and glassy-eyed in a chair. Wally explains that his long-winded explanation of a new technology put her into a coma. He asks whether he should report the incident, and Dilbert says he should only do so if he can keep it brief.
punchline: Wally's tendency to ramble is so tedious it literally knocked someone out, and Dilbert's reply implies the only way to report it is by avoiding the very verbosity that caused it.
summary: A coworker's endless tech explanation leaves a colleague catatonic, and the advice for reporting it is to be concise.

title: Deep Fake Wally Attends Meetings

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I liked what you said on the video conference call yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've never seen you so engaged and helpful.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That wasn't me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That was "Deep Fake Wally." I created him to do all of my video calls.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I hired an Elbonian to do all of my coding jobs for a very affordable price.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: These days, I only come to the office for the free coffee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And the camaraderie?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sure.

situation: Dilbert compliments Wally on how engaged and helpful he was on a video conference call. Wally reveals it was a deep fake he created to attend all his video calls, and that he also outsources his coding to an Elbonian. He says he only comes to the office for the free coffee, and gives a flat answer when Dilbert asks about camaraderie.
punchline: Wally has automated and outsourced every part of his job, and his lukewarm "Sure" shows he has no real interest in coworkers either.
summary: A coworker's praise for a stellar video call turns out to be aimed at an AI impostor, since the real man has delegated everything but coffee drinking.

title: Best Places to Work Ad Shakedown

transcript.speaker: Publication Rep
transcript.text: Our publication is considering naming your company one of the best places to work.

transcript.speaker: Publication Rep
transcript.text: On a totally unrelated topic, our sales team will be contacting you about buying lots and lots of advertisements.

transcript.speaker: Company Rep
transcript.text: And if we don't?

transcript.speaker: Publication Rep
transcript.text: Who would want to work at a company that makes such bad decisions?

situation: A representative from a magazine tells a company's representative that the company may be named one of the best places to work. He then casually mentions that the sales team will be pitching lots of advertising. When asked what happens if they refuse, he implies the company would lose the honor and look bad.
punchline: The 'best places to work' award is effectively for sale, and the publication threatens to undermine the company's reputation if it doesn't buy ads.
summary: A magazine dangles a workplace ranking in front of a company while quietly tying it to an ad purchase, with a veiled threat if they decline.

title: Cluttered Desk, Cluttered Email

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did you see my project update?

transcript.speaker: Coworker in orange
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in green
transcript.text: I left it on your cluttered desk. Try excavating a few layers to find it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What happens when he realizes it isn't there?

transcript.speaker: Coworker in green
transcript.text: That's when I tell him to check his cluttered email.

situation: A coworker asks whether anyone has seen his project update. A colleague in green claims he left it on the asker's cluttered desk and suggests digging through the layers. When Dilbert asks what happens once he discovers it isn't there, the colleague reveals the next step: tell him to check his cluttered email.
punchline: The colleague never delivered the project update at all and is stalling with a chain of excuses that blame the other person's messiness.
summary: A coworker deflects responsibility for an undelivered report by sending its owner on a fruitless search through his own mess, with a second excuse already planned.

title: Bonus Incentives Ignore Tech Support Fallout

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our tech support staff is overwhelmed because we shipped the wrong user guide with our product.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: My bonus only depends on launching the product on time. Tech support isn't my department.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You caused the problem.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Who told you it was a fair world?

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker, a manager holding a coffee cup, that tech support is swamped because the wrong user guide shipped with the product. The manager says his bonus depends only on an on-time launch and tech support is not his department. When Dilbert points out that he caused the problem, the manager shrugs and asks who said the world was fair.
punchline: The manager openly admits he faces no consequences for the mess he created because his bonus rewards only the launch date, and he dismisses Dilbert's sense of fairness.
summary: A manager who shipped the wrong manual shrugs off the support chaos because his pay depends solely on hitting the launch date.

title: Software Already Done, Coworker Denies

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do you think?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: This will never work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This isn't a prototype. This is the finished software, and it's working.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I don't see how you can get this done in time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's already done. You are literally using it while we are talking.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: We don't have the resources to program this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's already done!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You. Are. Using. It. Right. Now!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You'd better settle down, or you'll never get this finished.

situation: Dilbert shows Asok his finished software and asks for his opinion. Asok insists it will never work, can't be done in time, and can't be programmed without more resources, even though he is using the software at that very moment. Dilbert grows increasingly frustrated while Asok keeps dismissing it.
punchline: Asok is so locked into his skeptical script that he ignores the working software in front of him and even warns the exasperated Dilbert that his temper will prevent him from finishing it.
summary: A programmer's colleague keeps insisting the project is impossible while actively running the finished product, driving the programmer to a furious breakdown.

title: Hire Someone Dumber Next Time

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why isn't your project done yet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because every time I walk past your office you give me three new tasks and tell me they are my highest priority.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was hoping you didn't know why.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hire someone dumber next time.

situation: The Boss stands by Dilbert's desk holding a coffee cup and asks why Dilbert's project isn't finished. Dilbert explains that the Boss keeps handing him three new top-priority tasks every time he passes by. The Boss admits he hoped Dilbert wouldn't figure that out.
punchline: The Boss knowingly sabotages his employees' projects with constant new priorities and only hoped Dilbert was too dim to notice, so Dilbert sarcastically suggests hiring dumber people.
summary: A manager blames his engineer for a late project, then sheepishly admits he caused the delay himself and hoped it would go unnoticed.

title: Saving Money in Elbonia, Ignoring Atrocities

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're moving our manufacturing operations to Elbonia to save money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you worried about the Elbonian government's reputation?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nah. I try to stay out of the weeds.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They're building concentration camps and rounding up dissenters.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They intentionally poisoned a hundred thousand people in this country.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They are habitual stealers of intellectual property, and they routinely ignore agreements they have signed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And they have a well-known goal of weakening other countries so they can dominate the world.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why can't you just admit I'm saving money?

situation: The Boss announces he is moving manufacturing operations to Elbonia to cut costs. Dilbert asks about the Elbonian government's reputation, then lists a string of serious abuses: concentration camps, mass poisoning, intellectual property theft, broken agreements and global domination plans. The Boss waves it all off and insists Dilbert should simply acknowledge the cost savings.
punchline: The Boss willfully ignores a litany of atrocities and hostile behavior by the host country, demanding credit only for the money he is saving, which satirizes companies that offshore to repressive regimes purely for profit.
summary: A manager cheerfully offshores production to a country with a dreadful record and gets annoyed when his employee won't just praise the savings.

title: Conference Call Ends From Exhaustion

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How did your conference call go?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Normal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It took us twenty minutes to get everyone connected, followed by forty minutes of garbled speech that no one understood.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The meeting ended when everyone got tired of pretending something useful was happening.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I didn't really care.

setting: Office break area or conference table, with an office building shown in the final panel
situation: Wally, holding a coffee, asks Dilbert how his conference call went. Dilbert describes a typical call: twenty minutes of connection trouble and forty minutes of unintelligible audio. The call only ended because everyone gave up pretending it was productive, and Wally says he didn't care anyway.
punchline: The call ended not because anything was accomplished but because everyone grew too tired to keep pretending it was useful, and Wally's indifference shows he never expected anything better.
summary: A routine conference call wastes an hour on technical glitches and mumbled audio before dying out from collective weariness.

title: Awkward Wait While Coworker Searches Phone

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I have something funny to show you.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Just give me a minute to find it on my phone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the protocol in this situation?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I just sit here and stare at her pawing at her phone?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't talk because she's focused on her task, and it would be rude to walk away.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would it be an insult to look at my own phone and mentally check out from this useless interaction?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Ah! I found it!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, good.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wait, that's not the right one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is this why people fake their own deaths?

situation: A coworker promises to show Dilbert something funny on her phone, then spends several panels searching for it while he sits there. Dilbert agonizes over etiquette: he can't talk, can't leave, and isn't sure if checking his own phone would be rude. When she finally finds it, she discovers it's the wrong item and has to keep looking.
punchline: Dilbert's social awkwardness over waiting for a coworker's phone search gets so unbearable that he wonders if it's the reason people fake their own deaths.
summary: A colleague's endless hunt for a funny phone video leaves Dilbert trapped in etiquette limbo, ending with a dark joke about escaping at all costs.

title: Co-workers Make Deadlines Impossible

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Can you have it done in a week?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not if I have to work with other employees.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Given the galactic incompetence of my co-workers, it would probably take seven to nine months.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: I'll give you two weeks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's how long it will take to set up the first meeing.

situation: A manager holding a coffee cup asks Dilbert whether he can finish a project in a week. Dilbert says it would take seven to nine months if he has to rely on his incompetent co-workers. The manager offers a two-week deadline, and Dilbert points out that this is only enough time to schedule the first meeting.
punchline: The manager's generous extension to two weeks is absurdly inadequate, since just scheduling the first meeting with the co-workers would consume all of it.
summary: Offered a slightly longer deadline, a programmer explains that coordinating colleagues will eat up the whole extension before any work begins.

title: Boss Refuses Mentoring To Avoid Competition

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can you mentor me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Heck, no.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're only one promotion away from competing for my job.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Well, maybe you could just stop thwarting my career?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, same issue.

situation: Alice asks the Boss to mentor her, and he flatly refuses. He explains that she is just one promotion away from being a rival for his own job. When Alice asks him to at least stop obstructing her career, he refuses that too for the same reason.
punchline: The Boss openly admits he will sabotage any employee who could threaten his position, so he refuses both to help Alice and to stop holding her back.
summary: A manager candidly explains that he blocks a talented subordinate's advancement because he fears she might one day take his job.
